pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized outputs under data_extra/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from specialized pretrained models with superior retrieval/recommendation performance to a benchmark of existing semantic encoders. v2 adds headline claims about disagreement with MTEB, task-dependent scaling, and Amazon-C4's usefulness as a proxy for real complex queries.

C2.justification: v1's explanations of BLAIR training benefits and curriculum-related overfitting are replaced by interpretations involving encoder discriminability, downstream complexity, metadata noise, and complex intent. v2 also introduces substantive limitations concerning English-only coverage, restricted model/category coverage, and incomplete review collection, plus failure analysis.

D1.justification: v1's checkpoint, GPU, batch-size, training-time, and pretraining-hyperparameter documentation is removed with its model study. v2 adds dataset-collection details, exact temporal cutoffs, generation and retrieval prompts, dataset-specific processing, a learning-rate search grid, and documented access to the BLaIR-Bench toolkit in Appendices A–C.

E1.justification: The Amazon dataset, Beauty/Games/Baby categories, ESCI, and Amazon-C4 remain. v2 adds MovieLens-1M and Yelp to sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering across six datasets including Book-Crossing, and real-world Reddit-Movies complex-query retrieval.

E2.justification: RoBERTa-large and SimCSE-large remain, while v2 adds Sentence-T5, three Qwen3 sizes, E5, SFR-Embedding-Mistral, GritLM, Gemini, and text-embedding-3-large. v1's BM25, GRU4Rec/SASRec, smaller encoders, and BLAIR/MLM comparison entries disappear from the corresponding evaluations.

E3.justification: Amazon item inputs change from concatenated titles, features, and descriptions to titles alone. v2 introduces protocols for the added tasks, including collaborative-filtering splits of 4:3:3 and filtered leave-last-out datasets, and adds NDCG@20 and Borda aggregation while dropping v1's additional sequential Recall and NDCG@50 reporting.

E4.justification: v1's MLM-only, multi-domain-training, and initialization-curriculum analyses are removed. v2 adds metadata and PCA-versus-MRL comparisons, encoder-scaling and cross-benchmark correlation analyses, and a concrete GritLM retrieval failure case in Appendix F.

E5.justification: v2 introduces focused Spearman and Pearson correlation tests with p-values in Section 5.2; v1 reports no corresponding significance analyses. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, or uncertainty intervals for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: v1's BLAIR results and pretraining-ablation entries are replaced by extensive encoder benchmark results, including new collaborative-filtering and Reddit-Movies outcomes. Retained scores also change: SimCSE-large's ESCI NDCG@100 is 0.0869 after rescaling v1's display, versus 0.1063 in v2. Changed metadata prevents interpreting this as a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: v1's proposed RoBERTa-based BLAIR models and review–metadata contrastive-plus-MLM pretraining are removed. v2 instead defines BLAIR as a benchmark using frozen external encoders with downstream UniSRec, AlphaRec, and representation adaptation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves forward, dataset and benchmark sections replace the original model-centered organization, and v2 adds limitations, ethics, and six appendices.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around the benchmark, and v2 adds correlation and metadata plots. Tables are substantially reorganized into consolidated dataset statistics, aggregate rankings, and appendix results grouped by encoder class. The original query example is retained as renumbered Table 4, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around benchmarking semantic encoders, including a first-benchmark claim. Related work expands to BEIR, MTEB/MMTEB, BRIGHT, shopping-agent benchmarks, and recent recommendation encoders, replacing much of v1's foundation-model retrieval and recommendation positioning.

T1.justification: The explicit BLAIR embedding and joint-loss definitions in v1's Equations 1–3 are removed. v2 supplies formal definitions for projected representations and sequential/collaborative prediction in Section 4.1. These change the limited mathematical specification; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's narrow encoder comparisons and lack of real-world complex-query validation through stronger comparators, broader domains, and Reddit-Movies validation of Amazon-C4. Detailed protocols and targeted analyses substantially strengthen the retained benchmark contribution. The original pretraining study is lost, and Table 6 swaps the Qwen 4B/8B Borda scores, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the improved evaluation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the evolving BLAIR work and retain Amazon Reviews 2023, Amazon-C4, and overlapping experiments. All material is readable, including v2's Appendices A–F; v1 ends with references and has no appendix. The substantial reframing does not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 11 encoders, including collaborative filtering and Reddit-Movies, with detailed results in Appendix D and additional analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original sequential-recommendation and product-search experiments, plus pretraining ablations, in Tables 4 and 7–9.

results.title: Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation: Benchmarking LLMs as Semantic Encoders

C1.justification: The central novelty and contribution—using a predictive side network to improve fMRI-to-text decoding—remain. The abstract replaces the Narratives-specific state-of-the-art statement and 27.8% BLEU-1 figure with a claim of outperforming decoding models on several metrics across two datasets, expanding the stated empirical scope.

C2.justification: v2 revises limitations after addressing the single-dataset, cross-subject-only, and fixed-prediction-length restrictions, and identifies visual stimuli and other signal modalities as remaining boundaries. Appendices F–G add distinctions between fluency and semantic fidelity across decoder families and recommend semantic-level evaluation. The predictive-coding debate and information-loss explanation are retained.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: explicit subject/stimulus separation rules, dataset-specific parcellation and tokenizers, PCA reduction from 768 to 20 dimensions, ridge penalization settings, 18 CNN layers, approximately 200 million parameters, and training from scratch. It also explains inference explicitly. Most are newly disclosed details, not demonstrated changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only Narratives, using 230 selected subjects. v2 retains this coverage and adds three subjects from LeBel's dataset for predictive-coding verification and language decoding, substantially extending the evaluated data and population.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates UniCoRN as its external decoding comparator. v2 additionally evaluates Tang's method, BrainLLM, and MapGuide on LeBel's dataset in Table 1, while retaining UniCoRN for Narratives in Table 2. Tang's method and BrainLLM were discussed but explicitly excluded from v1's experiments.

E3.justification: v2 adds within-subject evaluation using ten LeBel fMRI frames spanning 20 seconds, introduces BERTScore-F1, and evaluates prediction-length/distance grids. Appendix A.4 also changes the reported training budget from v1's 20 epochs to 40. This is a reported setting revision; unchanged Narratives scores do not establish whether those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds shuffled-fMRI controls testing reliance on ordered brain input (Tables 6–7) and extensive joint prediction-length/distance analyses (Figure 7 and Appendix C). ROI, side-network, and loss-weight analyses also extend to LeBel's subjects. The original Narratives positional-error analysis and decoding examples remain, rather than constituting new analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly specifies ten-fold held-out cross-validation for estimating each subject's brain score. The 95% confidence intervals across subjects were already reported in v1 Figure 1 and remain in v2 Figure 12. No increase in repeated training runs or new decoding-table uncertainty reporting is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including LeBel PREDFT BLEU-1 scores of 34.95, 32.46, and 33.22 in Table 1, BERTScores, and shuffled-input results. Original Narratives BLEU/ROUGE results are retained, so these additions are not same-setting performance gains. One added value is inconsistent: subject-2 PREDFT BERTScore is 83.52 in Table 1 but 82.52 in Table 6.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 adds a linear-layer encoder for 2D brain-surface inputs alongside the existing volumetric 3D-CNN encoder. The main and side Transformers, predictive cross-attention, and joint losses remain. The newly explicit description of discarding the side decoder during inference does not establish a change to the earlier procedure.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites explanatory passages and reorganizes the narrative. The main Discussion becomes a shorter Conclusion, while discussion and case studies move to dedicated appendices. Experimental documentation is divided into multiple subsections and appendices, and separate Limitations and Ethics sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout and substantially redesigns its displays. v2 adds simplified training/inference and encoder diagrams, a notation table, heatmaps, and additional comparison tables. The original detailed architecture moves to Figure 8, and retained ROI results appear both graphically and in appendix tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds MapGuide to the decoding literature, recent works by Xia et al. and Yin et al., and references supporting BERTScore, PCA, and scikit-learn. The central research positioning remains, including Antonello and Huth's alternative explanation, which moves into Appendix G.

T1.justification: Section 2 changes the definition of prediction distance from the distance to the last future word in v1 to the first future word in v2. For fixed distance and length, these definitions specify different word windows, without an explicit reconciliation. The principal attention, loss, and information-loss-slope equations remain.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important limitations explicitly acknowledged in v1 through a second dataset, within-subject evaluation, and variable prediction lengths. Additional external baselines, shuffled-input controls, and substantially fuller implementation documentation strengthen the evidence and reproducibility. The unexplained training-budget revision and conflicting subject-2 BERTScore limit precision, but do not outweigh these substantial gains. The improvement comes from stronger evaluation and documentation, not an established increase in same-setting performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PREDFT research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved into the expanded appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original Narratives results and adds LeBel dataset experiments, additional baseline comparisons, prediction-length analyses, and shuffled-input controls.

before.justification: v1 reports original Narratives decoding experiments, predictive-coding verification, ROI and prediction-distance analyses, ablations, and decoding-error analysis.

results.title: Language Reconstruction with Brain Predictive Coding from fMRI Data

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from differentiated learning rates specifically for benign IFT to SWAT for both benign and attack-contaminated IFT. v2 adds security-feature-space drift as a central explanatory claim and explicitly claims compatibility with existing pre-training and post-training defenses.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations involving early-layer drift amplification and allocation of low-level versus task-relevant learning across module subsets. It qualifies module-type sensitivity as model-dependent, including different behavior in Qwen2. Its new limitations section acknowledges coarse analysis granularity, security loss during warm-up, residual risks, and drift being only one possible cause.

D1.justification: The technical recipes are substantially revised: v2 documents model-specific warm-up durations, instruction-token training, attack-data additions, and defense implementation details such as IFTsafe's 1,000 security samples. v1's dual-learning-rate recipes and synthetic-mathematics construction appendix disappear. Search pseudocode remains, but v2 does not retain comparable explicit checkpoint-selection guidance.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Alpaca-based general instruction tuning and learning privately defined mathematical operators. v2 replaces these tasks with UltraInteract logical reasoning and GSM8K word problems, using Alpaca as supplementary training data, and adds training contaminated with malicious examples. Security coverage replaces Just-Eval with CatQA and removes GCG, while retaining Advbench and four other jailbreak methods.

E2.justification: v1 compares ML-LR principally with BASE and standard IFT. v2's Llama2-7B comparisons add evaluated defense baselines LoRAsafe, IFTsafe, Resta, and Resta integrated with DARE, labeled Restad (Tables 2–3). These are substantive additions to the comparator set.

E3.justification: ASR changes from GPT-judged harmfulness exceeding 1 to rule-based detection of security expressions, and the harmfulness judge changes from GPT-4-1106-preview to GPT-4o. v2 also revises training budgets and sample counts, adds 4- or 16-epoch warm-up stages before IFT, and changes the model suite, dropping Vicuna and 13B evaluations while adding Qwen2-7B. The default LoRA targets, rank 8, and alpha 16 remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds classifier transfer across base/tuned/SWAT representations, intermediate warm-up performance, parameter-update analysis, and an instruction-modeling ablation (Tables 1, 4, 7; Figure 5). v1's control for insufficient data fitting and all-module LoRA experiment disappear. Layer-depth verification remains, but its models change and the middle-layer condition is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Averages across attacks and deterministic perturbations do not establish uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v1's Alpaca and private-mathematics results are largely replaced by SWAT results on new tasks and scenarios. For example, v2 Table 2 reports UltraInteract ASR of 61.18% for IFT versus 27.82% for SWAT, with task accuracy of 66.00% versus 66.80%. Table 5 additionally reports complete language failure for one combined-defense configuration. These are newly reported outcomes under changed conditions, not demonstrated performance gains over v1's ML-LR.

M1.justification: v1's ML-LR applies different learning rates to robust and remaining modules throughout tuning. v2's SWAT instead warms up only robust modules, adding instruction modeling with loss over instructions and responses, then trains all targeted LoRA parameters. The classifier-guided search remains a foundation, but the training procedure and objective substantially change (Section 3.3).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten around SWAT and feature-space drift. Experimental preparation and results are reorganized into a consolidated main-experiment section, the scenario organization changes, and dedicated limitations and ethical-considerations sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. The framework diagram is redrawn, main radar-chart presentations give way to expanded safety/task tables, and the robust-subset map moves from the appendix into the main text. New parameter-update plots and ablation tables accompany substantial changes to existing figure and table structures.

R1.justification: v1 positions itself as pioneering mitigation for benign IFT. v2 reorganizes the landscape into pre-training, in-training, and post-training defenses, discussing Bianchi, Hsu, Bhardwaj, and Wei et al. (2024b) as relevant alternatives. Added feature-drift and instruction-modeling references support a substantially revised rationale and novelty positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds Equation 3, defining a contrast between SWAT and standard-IFT parameter-update L2 norms. The classifier and perturbation-accuracy equations remain substantively equivalent. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1: comparison chiefly against ordinary IFT. Evaluations against established defenses make safety/task tradeoffs substantially more assessable, while new mechanism checks and the instruction-modeling ablation strengthen support for the revised method. The gains are tempered by removal of earlier fitting and all-module controls and an overbroad compatibility claim: Table 5 reports complete language failure for one combination. Overall, the stronger comparative evidence represents a substantial quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on preserving LLM security during instruction fine-tuning, retaining the classifier-based module analysis and robust-subset search. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original safety/task comparisons, feature-space analyses, parameter-update measurements, and instruction-modeling ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier, module-perturbation, safety, usability, and mathematical-task experiments, including detailed appendix results.

results.title: Toward Secure Tuning: Mitigating Security Risks from Instruction Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a facial-forgery dataset and a model jointly producing masks and explanations; renaming this task does not establish a new objective. V2 expands the claimed dataset contribution to attribute editing and adds an explicit contribution claim about complementary effects between localization and report generation.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting pretraining to multimodal representations and manipulation categories to report quality and localization. It attributes low SynthScars scores to annotation-style differences. New limitations discuss training overhead and the absence of binary detection outputs, while the original FPN-quality bottleneck remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 changes reported hardware from four A100s to one H100 and newly specifies Flan-T5-XL, approximately 4B parameters, 48 GPU-hours, and the evaluation toolkit. Some earlier mask-generation and training details disappear. Appendix I introduces vetted academic access under a DUA and withholding generation pipelines, qualifying v1's general public-release promise.

E1.justification: MMTT expands from face swapping and inpainting to include semantic attribute editing using StyleCLIP and HFGI, increasing from 128,303 to 152,217 samples. V2 also evaluates transfer to DQ_F++ and the facial-manipulation subset of SynthScars, whereas v1 evaluates only MMTT.

E2.justification: The original SCA, LISA-7B, Osprey, and InstructBLIP comparisons remain. V2 additionally evaluates FFAA, FakeShield, PSCC-NET, IML-ViT, and general vision-language models including Seed1.5VL, Qwen2.5VL, LLaVA, and InternVL3 in Tables 2 and 6.

E3.justification: V2 introduces zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation, separates untuned general vision-language models from MMTT-trained methods, evaluates multiple model sizes, and trains on restricted manipulation-type subsets while testing on the full test set. The existing 8:1:1 split and reported FPN/main-model training schedules are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds pretraining ablation, leave-one-manipulation-type-out analysis, cross-dataset generalization tests, and qualitative comparisons with InstructBLIP. The original prompt/oracle ablation remains with updated results. V1's FPN loss/discount-factor analysis is retained unchanged as v2 Table 7, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for its experimental results.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces ForgeryTalker's 21.5 CIDEr and 70.81 IoU with 59.3 and 73.67, alongside extensively revised comparator scores. Changed data and training prevent interpreting these as controlled version-to-version gains. V2 adds transfer results, including 113.3 CIDEr on DQ_F++ and 2.20 on SynthScars, plus new ablation outcomes.

M1.justification: V2 adds forgery-aware pretraining with masked language modeling, text generation, segmentation, and contrastive objectives before FPN-guided report generation. V1 trains the FPN and then fine-tunes the Q-former and mask decoder without this additional stage. The underlying FPN, InstructBLIP, and SAM-based components are retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, and substantial dataset exposition are rewritten around attribution reports. Related work and experimental setup move into appendices, dataset statistics are reorganized, and dedicated limitations and statements sections are added. This constitutes substantial narrative restructuring beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the dataset overview and statistics, expands the architecture diagram into two training stages, and separates the FPN diagram. It adds qualitative comparisons, dataset examples, and a word cloud. Tables gain explicit zero-shot/fine-tuning groupings and additional transfer and ablation displays.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens engagement with explainable forensics, contemporary vision-language models, and multimodal misinformation research. Appendix A newly contrasts MMTT's human annotations with FakeShield's synthetic annotations. References also expand to attribute-editing methods and external evaluation resources; the original three related-work themes remain.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for the pretraining objectives and their weighted combination. Section 3.4 corrects v1's malformed mask-loss expression to summed pixel-wise binary cross-entropy. Existing FPN equations and the PLM definition are retained; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow, single-dataset validation through dedicated forgery baselines, two external transfer tests, and analyses of pretraining and data composition. These make generalization and component contributions more assessable. Important weaknesses remain: pretraining settings are incomplete, Table 9's full-set scores differ unexplained from Table 2, and some best-score claims conflict with table entries. These reporting problems qualify the substantial improvement in evaluative depth.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MMTT dataset and ForgeryTalker framework despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable throughout. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–I are available for comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, cross-dataset evaluations, qualitative comparisons, and ablations in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original dataset statistics, model comparisons, and FPN ablations in Section 5 and Tables 2–4.

results.title: Generating Attribution Reports for Manipulated Facial Images: A Dataset and Baseline

C1.justification: v2's conclusion drops the numerical headline bounds F1 greater than 0.90 and F1 below 0.63, expressing the detection-versus-relevance gap qualitatively. The proposed masking strategy, benchmark contribution, and novelty claims remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 interprets synthetic-real agreement as evidence of real-world validity, smaller-model failures as a barrier to on-device protection, and the new tradeoff scores as supporting selective masking. It removes the earlier PII-type mechanism explanation. The dedicated limitations section remains essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: New Appendices C-D substantially document consistency optimization, relationship constraints, scenario generation, and filtering. v2 also adds a scenario-generation template, detailed annotation guidelines, PII-Real sourcing information, the utility-judge prompt and model identities, and disclosure of top_k=1.

E1.justification: v2 adds PII-Real: 100 instances derived from 20 actual AI researchers' public profiles, with expert-written queries and manual annotations. This extends evaluation beyond synthetic profiles and generated queries to authentic biographical information; the original synthetic coverage remains.

E2.justification: Tables 11-13 add Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-3B as evaluated baselines across the three tasks. This extends the existing Qwen model family while retaining the earlier main model and prompting comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 4.5 and Appendix F.2 introduce a 200-description response-evaluation protocol using three masking conditions, GPT4o generation, BGE-M3 similarity, Claude-3.7-Sonnet judging, randomized response order, and equal privacy-utility weighting. Section 3.3 also corrects the stated sample counts from 2,000 each to 1,214 and 1,228, matching the existing Table 3 rather than establishing resampling.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative privacy-utility analysis, synthetic-versus-real consistency analysis, and an investigation of deployment feasibility using smaller models. It removes v1's Figure 5 and associated PII-type performance analysis, while retaining the original complexity and challenging-set analyses.

E5.justification: Table 14 adds Spearman correlation tests with reported p-values below 0.001. Table 21 newly reports Fleiss' kappa values of 0.912 and 0.873 alongside the retained observed agreement rates. Existing human uncertainty reporting remains; additional experimental runs or seeds are not documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for smaller models and PII-Real, plus Table 8's privacy, utility, and balanced scores of 0.83, 0.89, and 0.86 for query-unrelated masking. The original core benchmark tables and PII-multi results retain their values. The per-type accuracy results in v1's Figure 5 are removed.

M1.justification: The published construction prompts receive limited procedural refinements: Figures 10-11 add explicit conflict checks and relationship constraints, including a parent-child age gap of at least 18 years. The core masking strategy and detection prompts remain unchanged; regeneration of the existing benchmark is not established.

P1.justification: v2 condenses construction, human-evaluation, and results prose; clarifies seven PII types versus 55 subcategories; and corrects terminology and wording. New subsections and expanded appendices organize the additions, while the main narrative sequence and substantial portions of the text remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive displays for tradeoffs, smaller models, real-data results, consistency statistics, and annotation guidance. It redraws Figure 1, removes the per-type accuracy plot, adds a real-profile example and two prompt figures, and relocates appendix tables and interface screenshots.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Chen et al. (2017) and M3-embedding (2024), supporting the BiLSTM-CRF discussion and embedding metric respectively. The related-work discussion and positioning of query-aware privacy protection are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: The original task definitions and Equations 1-16 are retained. Appendix F adds formal definitions for privacy protection, utility evaluation, weighted privacy-utility balance, and Performance Consistency Score in Equations 17-21. These extend the scoring framework without adding theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidence gaps in v1 by adding quantitative response-utility evaluation and validation beyond synthetic data. Together with smaller-model experiments and substantially clearer construction documentation, these additions strengthen the paper's empirical support and reproducibility. The gains outweigh the lost per-type analysis, although PII-Real covers a narrow researcher population and the combination of the two utility measures remains unspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PII-Bench and retain matching core tasks, datasets, and experiments. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds privacy-utility experiments, smaller-model evaluations, and results on the new PII-Real dataset.

before.justification: v1 reports original human evaluations and model experiments, including Tables 2 and 4-7 and the additional PII-multi results in Appendix D.

results.title: PII-Bench: Evaluating Query-Aware Privacy Protection Systems

C1.justification: v1 describes the full 2.8-million-claim corpus as an estimate awaiting comprehensive processing. v3 presents that size without the estimate qualification, adds NSF-SCIFY-20K as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds high-precision extraction with lower recall. This materially strengthens and broadens the dataset contribution while retaining the three-task and fine-tuning claims.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantial limitations concerning funded-US-proposal coverage, availability bias, older publication links, generalizability, limited baselines, and LLM evaluation validity. It interprets lower claim recall as a deliberate precision-first choice and discusses error mechanisms and possible remedies. These qualifications go substantially beyond v1's advantages and brief future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds explicit code and checkpoint locations, stated Apache-2.0 release terms in Appendix A, and approximately one hour of training per epoch. Much of the release description and the extraction/evaluation prompts already existed and is relocated. The PDFs establish improved access documentation, not independently verified resource availability.

E1.justification: v1's downstream experiments use the materials-science subset. v3 additionally trains and evaluates on NSF-SCIFY-20K, spanning MPS, GEO, ENG, CSE, and BIO, and evaluates extraction quality across six areas by separating materials science from the rest of MPS. This substantially broadens the empirically studied domains while retaining the three tasks.

E2.justification: The Mistral and Qwen comparisons in Tables 2–4 remain unchanged. Section 7 and Appendix I newly use Claude-extracted claims as a comparison in the error analysis of fine-tuned Mistral outputs; Claude previously served as the dataset generator without this reported error comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds a validation protocol sampling 20 awards from each of six areas, using GPT-4o to identify missing or incorrect extractions and manually checking its outputs on 20 abstracts. It also reports pairwise-judge validation and a separate 120-award error-analysis sample. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original materials-science split, preprocessing, training budget, and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds claim and proposal taxonomies, extraction precision/recall analyses across scientific areas, human-assisted judge validation, a reported evaluation-prompt robustness check, and detailed error categories with examples in Appendix I. v1's abstract-style analysis and qualitative joint-versus-separate extraction observation are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports 95% confidence-interval ranges for Tables 2–4, which v3 retains. v3 additionally specifies standard-deviation error bars from 1,000 bootstrap resamples in Figures 5–6. Appendix F displays per-score uncertainties without clearly identifying their interpretation. No increase in training runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. New NSF-SCIFY-20K results in Tables A5–A7 include base versus fine-tuned Mistral claim F-scores of 0.5247 versus 0.7268, alongside lower recall of 0.8141 versus 0.7354. v3 also adds domain-specific extraction-quality results, taxonomy distributions, and error rates. These are additional results under new coverage, rather than improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: Both versions use joint zero-shot extraction with Claude-3.5, LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral and Qwen, and GPT-4o-mini pairwise evaluation. Renaming verifiable_claims to claims preserves its definition. Applying the approach to NSF-SCIFY-20K and proposing future remedies do not establish a changed extraction or training method.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, expands short task descriptions into explanatory paragraphs, substantially recasts the conclusion, and reorganizes the narrative around dataset validation, error analysis, and structured limitations. The appendices are reorganized to include reproducibility and separate analyses, with existing prompts and release material moved.

P2.justification: v3 adds two taxonomy treemaps, two extraction-quality plots, three results tables, two taxonomy-example tables, and formatted error-example panels. The original t-SNE figure moves to Appendix E as Figure A7, and existing example tables become A8–A9. Table 1 gains a subset row, and numerous captions gain emphasized summaries.

R1.justification: v3 adds Gu et al.'s LLM-as-judge survey, Liu et al.'s G-Eval, and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini references, and explicitly connects its claim definition to the already-cited Tang et al. The principal related-work comparison and grant-abstract novelty positioning remain largely unchanged; publication updates to existing references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: The pairwise support functions and mathematical precision/recall definitions are retained. The new true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative description explains standard evaluation quantities; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that change.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens a dataset paper whose earlier validation centered on materials-science downstream scores and qualitative extraction checks. Cross-directorate experiments, sampled extraction-quality and judge validation, and error analyses provide important evidence about reliability and incomplete coverage; explicit limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: human agreement remains described only as near-perfect, and the proposal taxonomy says eight categories in Section 4.2 but lists ten in Table A11, with some mismatched examples.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NSF-SCIFY with the same authors, extraction approach, and retained materials-science experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds cross-directorate experiments, extraction-quality evaluations, taxonomy analyses, and error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, abstract classification experiments, and fine-tuning results for three tasks in Tables 2–4.

results.title: NSF-SciFy: Mining the NSF Awards Database for Scientific Claims

C1.justification: The two-stage translation objective remains, but v3 redefines the verification contribution around co-produced specifications and synthesized harnesses. It drops v1's zero-shot characterization and adds explicit contribution claims about feedback benefits and temperature insensitivity. Its real-world claims distinguish full unidiomatic coverage from conditional, partial idiomatic coverage.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit limitations concerning test coverage, static-analysis precision, unsupported C features, harness stability, model dependence, and cost. New interpretations explain model-dependent feedback benefits and attribute Crown's contribution to otherwise unavailable ownership and pointer-shape information. The earlier AVL-specific generics/FFI discussion disappears with that case study.

D1.justification: Appendices B.1, L, and N add preprocessing and compile-flag instructions, supported SPEC mappings, converter checks, and concrete specification/fallback prompts. v3 also discloses baseline model and attempt settings. However, its configuration table removes v1's hosting-platform, H100, and explicit Q4 information. Reported code and dataset access links remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The two original 100-program suites remain. The AVL-tree and URL-parser case studies are removed and replaced by 50 CRust-Bench repository samples and libogg's 77 functions. This substantially expands the represented repository-level C programs and adds multimedia-container APIs with complex buffers and pointer manipulation.

E2.justification: The C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, and VERT comparisons remain, including VERT's TransCoder-IR-only participation. Appendix J.2 newly evaluates direct GPT-4o translation with minimal and interface-preserving prompts on CRust-Bench and libogg. These introduce a substantive comparison against using an LLM without SACTOR's translation pipeline.

E3.justification: v3 Table 6 reports temperature zero for the original five models, replacing v1's mixed settings, and specifies a dated GPT-4o version. New protocols include GPT-5 evaluation, function-level scoring, conditional idiomatic evaluation, and ten-repair-attempt direct-translation baselines. Actual sampling changes are unclear: v3 Section 5.1 says random sampling, but Appendix F.1 retains selection of the longest TransCoder-IR programs.

E4.justification: v1 provides failure breakdowns and case studies but no component ablations. v3 Appendices J-K add feedback removal, direct translation, Crown removal, unsafe-prompt variants, and temperature sensitivity experiments. Appendix F audits test coverage, while Appendix M adds detailed repository and libogg failure analyses. These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v3 Section 6.3 newly reports up to three complete translation runs per real-world sample; v1 specifies translation retries without a comparable outer-run count. This is a limited addition to run reporting, not evidence of increased statistical replication. Aggregation across runs, random seeds, and between-run uncertainty estimates remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Reported GPT-4o idiomatic success changes from 78% to 80% on TransCoder-IR and from 84% to 79% on CodeNet, under revised reported settings. Llama results, costs, and failure counts also change. New results include CRust-Bench's 788/966 unidiomatic and 249/580 conditional idiomatic successes, libogg outcomes, and ablations. Some revised failure-chart values conflict with accompanying prose.

M1.justification: v1 uses an LLM to generate idiomatic verification harnesses. v3 Section 4.3 and Appendix L introduce co-produced JSON interface specifications, rule-based harness generation, struct round-trip checks, and localized LLM completion of unsupported mappings. This substantially changes verification. Separately, v3 Section 4.1 rejects dependency cycles, while its retained Appendix B still describes grouping them; that behavior remains unresolved.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, related work, and methodology undergo extensive rewriting and consolidation. Failure and cost analyses move to Appendices H-I, illustrative material moves to appendices, and a dedicated limitations section is added. The title and author list also change. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview and success-rate plots, adds attempt breakdowns for both translation stages, merges failure displays, and places the lint plot beside the unsafe-code table. It removes the old case-study plot and adds translation examples, ablation and temperature plots, a SPEC diagram, and extensive new results and mapping tables.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references for RustBelt, long-context limitations, CRust-Bench, and libogg, and removes the introductory ChatGPT reference. The existing translation literature and its broad LLM-versus-static-method positioning remain, despite substantial rewriting of the related-work prose.

T1.justification: The task-ordering pseudocode and test-based soft-equivalence concept are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation. The SPEC schema and round-trip checks are procedural additions. Appendix J.3's information-theoretic interpretation is informal rather than a formal result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's empirical justification: Appendices J-K test previously unisolated design choices, Appendix F quantifies verification coverage, and Section 6.3 provides broader repository-level evidence. Detailed harness specifications and explicit coverage-dependent limitations also improve assessability. Sampling and dependency-cycle contradictions, along with stale result summaries, remain material weaknesses, but the added controls and transparent evaluation evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SACTOR and retain the original benchmark evaluations. The main text, figures, tables, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across reorganization. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports retained and revised benchmark results, new CRust-Bench and libogg evaluations, component ablations, temperature experiments, and test-coverage measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation success, cost, idiomaticity, and failure results on TransCoder-IR and CodeNet, plus AVL-tree and URL-parser case studies.

results.title: SACTOR: LLM-Driven Correct and Idiomatic C to Rust Translation with Static Analysis and FFI-Based Verification

C1.justification: V2 withdraws the claim that this is the largest long-context QA benchmark and narrows the categorical claim that other benchmarks lack explicit complexity levels. The main framework, dataset-release, and code contributions remain. The conclusion additionally invokes human performance to attribute failures to model limitations rather than dataset artifacts.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's generalization and model-size speculation with explanations involving abstention, answer coverage, verbosity, and metric disagreement. It prioritizes LLM-as-a-Judge for semantic interpretation, revises the Oracle-versus-Full discussion, and adds substantive limitations concerning ontology coverage and graph-representable deductive questions.

D1.justification: V2 documents annotation validation, QA normalization, duplicate removal, and logging; amends the financial template catalog and supplies counts; and explains stratified sampling for cost-constrained models. It also provides the medical schema/templates and replaces the planned generic evaluation-platform description with a specific leaderboard link. Hardware and core prompting details already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates financial credit agreements only. V2 Appendix F adds evaluation on a 225-page excerpt of HIV opportunistic-infection guidelines, covering pathogen, vector, disease, and medication relations. This introduces a distinct domain, although the demonstration uses one extracted document.

E2.justification: Tables 4 and 12 retain the original 13 models and add DeepSeek-R1, GPT OSS 120B, and Qwen3-Instruct. The retrieval comparison adds Dynamic RAG, and Appendix D.7 introduces human answering performance as a reference, substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds whole-document versus chunked evaluation, single-question versus 50-question batching, and a human-answering study with 100 questions balanced across five levels. These introduce substantial new controls and sampling designs. The main four metrics and batch/chunk setup remain; stratified sampling for existing cost-constrained evaluations is newly documented.

E4.justification: Appendices D.4–D.7 add subset-versus-full consistency checks, chunking and batching ablations, and human answerability validation. Appendix B.1 adds qualitative analysis of duplicate and noisy generated QAs. The earlier hop/set-operation error plots and document case studies are retained.

E5.justification: V2 newly quantifies annotation reliability with 80.76% inter-annotator agreement. The original Pearson/Kendall human-rating correlations remain unchanged, and no new repeated-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing protocol is specified.

E6.justification: The original 13 model rows remain unchanged, but new model, control, human, medical, and template-count results appear. Annotation statistics also change. The retrieval comparison replaces substantial values: Full-setting medium F1 changes from 0.6936 in v1 Table 13 to 0.3294 in v2 Table 17. The PDFs do not explain whether these replacements reflect corrections or different conditions.

M1.justification: The annotated RDF graphs, SPARQL extraction, three complexity dimensions, and batch-and-merge inference procedure remain. Revised template listings and newly documented cleaning do not establish a changed underlying algorithm; the medical study applies the existing framework.

P1.justification: V2 renames the framework and dataset and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, results interpretation, related work, and conclusion. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5; annotation motivation/details move into appendices; ethics moves into the main text; and the NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: The paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column formatting. Figure 1 becomes a redesigned first-page overview, Table 1 uses different comparison columns, and template tables gain count columns. New control/human/medical tables and Figure 12 are added, while most existing diagrams and error plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and Table 1 substantially redefine positioning around multi-hop reasoning, systematic question extraction, and multidimensional complexity. Newly discussed benchmarks include RULER, BABILong, Michelangelo, and MuSiQue, with explicit distinctions from their construction and difficulty schemes.

T1.justification: The complexity definition L = H + P + #SO and Easy/Medium/Hard thresholds retain their mathematical content. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; the expanded discussion and medical schema do not establish new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps through human answering, chunking/batching controls, subset validation, and a medical-domain demonstration. Expanded cleaning/sampling documentation and narrower novelty claims also substantially improve the paper's assessability. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unexplained Oracle/RAG score replacements, a duplicated template-count row in Table 7, and overconfident dismissal of chunking effects despite Table 14's substantial differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QA extraction framework and financial benchmark, renamed from KG-QAGen to KG-MuLQA. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, experimental controls, human question-answering performance, and a medical-domain evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 13 LLMs, retrieval comparisons, error analyses, and human-rating correlations.

results.title: KG-MuLQA: A Framework for KG-based Multi-Level QA Extraction and Long-Context LLM Evaluation

C1.justification: The main contribution remains learned nonlinear length debiasing with improved downstream alignment. However, v1's abstract explicitly claims three length-bias regimes; v2 removes that claim from the abstract and revises the introduction's characterization to linear behavior for short responses followed by flattening or occasional decline.

C2.justification: v2 strengthens the interpretation that reduced preference accuracy reflects removal of a length shortcut rather than diminished semantic ability, and extends this explanation to the newly reported BT-loss increase. It also interprets longer-response behavior as diminishing or reversing length effects instead of v1's noise regime. The limitation that legitimate preferences may favor longer answers is retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents generation settings, DPO hyperparameters, per-device batching, the fitting-model learning rate, detailed network layers and parameter count. Appendices C–D and Tables 6–7 specify stage allocations within 938 steps and measured training costs; additional algorithm settings appear in Appendices F and H. Length encoding and eight-device aggregation were already documented in v1 and are relocated.

E1.justification: v2 retains Dahoas-rm-static and AlpacaEval but adds MT-Bench multi-turn evaluation and IFEval instruction-following evaluation in Table 4. Appendix G additionally trains on the eight-source RLHFlow preference dataset. These substantially broaden task and preference-data coverage.

E2.justification: Length Penalty, discussed but not experimentally compared in v1, becomes an evaluated baseline in v2 Tables 1–3 and the corresponding distribution plots. Vanilla RM and ODIN remain, so the main baseline expansion is one additional method.

E3.justification: The reported SFT sample count changes from approximately 15k to 30k, and Gemma2-9B replaces Qwen2.5-1.5B alongside retained Qwen2.5-7B. v2 also introduces SimPO and GRPO evaluation protocols, MT-Bench turn-level scores and IFEval prompt accuracy. Newly specified DPO hyperparameters are additional documentation, without evidence that those particular settings changed.

E4.justification: Appendix A adds tests of staged versus joint training, alternating updates, and linear, polynomial, CNN and MLP fitting alternatives. Appendices D and E add computational-cost analysis and BT-loss monitoring, while Appendix B extends length-bias diagnostics to Gemma. v1 contains distribution and fitting-trajectory analyses but lacks these component ablations and cost/loss analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, uncertainty intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures. The retained BoN candidate count N=8 is a sampling setting, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v1's description of long-response behavior as statistically indistinguishable from noise provides no accompanying statistical test.

E6.justification: The main numerical results are replaced, and numerous results are added. For example, Qwen2.5-7B FiMi-RM DPO LC-WR changes from 70.19 in v1 Table 3 to 62.17 in v2 Table 3; changed training settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting decline. New results include MT-Bench, IFEval, ablations and GRPO, where v2 Table 10 reports LC-WR 67.42 for FiMi-RM versus 58.80 for Vanilla RM.

M1.justification: The fitting objective drops MSE: v1 Section 3.2 combines negative absolute Pearson correlation with MSE, whereas v2 uses only negative absolute correlation. This changes one training objective while retaining the three-stage framework, length encoding, residual fitting network, debiasing objective and eight-step alternating schedule.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted language edits, clarifies stop-gradient and Pearson-loss explanations, shortens the abstract and conclusion, and relocates technical material into named appendices. It also adds acknowledgements and author contact information. The main section sequence and overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document to two columns and substantially reorganizes the visual presentation. It revises Figure 1, expands comparison plots with Length Penalty, removes numerical reward-axis ticks, and adds difference histograms and appendix displays. Figures 4 and 6 redisplay differences from existing histograms rather than representing independent experiments.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of Park et al.'s DPO length regularization, SamPO and ALBM. References also expand for Gemma 2, MT-Bench and IFEval. The central positioning against approaches that leave bias unmodeled or assume linear length dependence remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of the fitting objective is revised by removing its MSE term, and the accompanying discussion of MSE-driven reward expansion is removed. Other central definitions remain equivalent, including length encoding relocated to Appendix C. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation through component ablations, independent task benchmarks, GRPO evaluation and broader preference-data testing. Detailed architecture and training-cost disclosures also substantially improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: uncertainty is still unreported, and Vanilla RM LC-WR is inconsistent between v2 Tables 2 and 5 (68.25 versus 69.25). The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, not cross-version score gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FiMi-RM research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 also includes readable Appendices A–I.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments throughout Section 4 and Appendices A–H, including downstream evaluations, ablations, training-time measurements and BT-loss monitoring.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model accuracy, BoN and DPO evaluations, response-length distributions and fitting trajectories in Section 4, Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–5.

results.title: Bias Fitting to Mitigate Length Bias of Reward Model in RLHF

C1.justification: v1 centers on the disconnect between trace correctness and answer correctness. v2 adds a second central claim about divergence between training effectiveness and human interpretability, and advocates separating model-supervision objectives from user-facing explanation design in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 proposes structural-pattern learning as an explanation for incorrect-trace success and qualifies the earlier broad outperformance statement with dataset-specific outcomes. It adds interpretations about cognitive workload and separate explanation objectives. The limitations shift from extreme trace mixtures and alternative decompositions toward QA-domain and model-size generalization.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B newly provide category-level dataset counts, summarization/explanation prompts, participant demographics, compensation, consent, instructions and study stimuli. v2 also adds project, code and dataset links. These substantially expand documentation; the original hardware and fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: CoTemp QA, Microsoft MARCO QA and the same eleven bAbI categories are retained. v2 adds a distinct human-evaluation task: 100 US-based participants assess interpretability and cognitive workload for CoTemp reasoning traces, substantially expanding the evaluated population and task coverage.

E2.justification: The original prompting, answer-only SFT and correct/incorrect-trace comparisons remain. Figure 3 adds evaluated SFT comparators using DeepSeek R1 traces, GPT-4o-mini summaries and GPT-4o-mini post-hoc explanations, compared against decomposed correct traces.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, correct-answer filtering of R1 training outputs, and a between-subjects study with 25 participants per trace type evaluating five fixed examples using Likert and NASA-TLX measures. The original QA sample counts and stated three-epoch QLoRA settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted model-size robustness check for the correctness findings using Llama-3.1-8B (Table 4) and descriptive trace-length distributions for four formats (Appendix A.3). The original confusion matrices and associated error analysis are largely retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides descriptive comparisons without formal hypothesis tests. v2 adds chi-square independence tests for trace/answer correctness and Bonferroni-corrected Mann–Whitney U tests for human ratings (Sections 5.2 and 5.4.3). Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty or seed variation.

E6.justification: Tables 4–5 and Figure 3 add larger-model performance, trace-format comparisons and human ratings. Figure 3 shows R1 leading for three models, with Qwen3-8B favoring summaries or explanations. Existing results are mostly retained, but Table 3 changes Qwen3-1.7B's bAbI classification accuracy under correct-trace SFT from 61.7% to 60.64%.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 retain classification-plus-retrieval decomposition, correct or incorrect traces paired with correct answers, and supervised fine-tuning. The added R1-based trace formats are experimental comparators, rather than revisions to the proposed decomposition procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, conclusion and limitations are extensively rewritten. Experimental and results sections are reorganized around correctness and interpretability questions, and new appendices organize supporting details. This substantially changes the narrative beyond simply inserting additional results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and combines v1's Figures 2–3 into one rearranged Figure 2 using the same confusion-matrix images. It adds a performance chart, trace-length histograms, survey screenshots and multiple results, distribution and example tables.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces the QA/decomposition discussion with sustained positioning on CoT interpretability and faithfulness, adding works such as Arcuschin, Barez and Lanham alongside human-centered evaluation literature. The conclusion also relates the findings to a separately cited maze study and an anti-anthropomorphism position paper.

T1.justification: The decomposition remains unchanged, and neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. The added hypothesis tests are empirical statistical analyses rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1 discusses human interpretability largely without direct user evidence; v2 supplies a documented 100-participant study linked to trace-format training comparisons. Larger-model checks, dataset-specific qualifications and detailed appendices substantially improve evidential support and reproducibility. These gains outweigh a material new statistical overstatement: Section 5.2 incorrectly treats failure to reject independence as proving it. The expanded conclusions therefore still require qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, retaining the decomposition method and original QA experiments. Text, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–B were included in the assessment.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional larger-model evaluations, trace-format comparisons and a 100-participant human study.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original fine-tuning experiments on three QA datasets, including answer accuracy, trace accuracy and error analyses.

results.title: Interpretable Traces, Unexpected Outcomes: Investigating the Disconnect in Trace-Based Knowledge Distillation

C1.justification: v2 explicitly claims state-of-the-art NQ R@1, whereas v1 emphasizes competitive retrieval and acknowledges lower R@1. It extends headline performance claims to competitive zero-shot OTT-QA retrieval and adds up to 33-fold fewer online embedding calls as an explicit contribution. These broaden the claimed scope and computational benefits.

C2.justification: v1 explains SPLADE's unchanged description-ablation scores through context saturation; v2 reports a benefit and removes that explanation. v2 also adds interpretations concerning contextual noise, ambiguous entities and retrieval-versus-answerability failures, alongside offline/online computation trade-offs. Its limitations explicitly distinguish oracle-passage evaluation from full open retrieval and identify unaddressed multi-hop retrieval and multimodal tables.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project link advertised for code and data, and documents precomputed row embeddings, sparse indexing, ANN search and on-demand mini-table encoding in Section 4.4. Table 2 and Appendix A clarify checkpoint provenance. The baseline hyperparameter table and three prompt templates already existed in v1; the newly documented execution details do not establish that the earlier implementation changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only NQ-Tables. v2 adds retrieval over OTT-QA's 419,183-table corpus and answer generation on its table-and-passage questions. This substantially extends coverage to a hybrid multi-hop benchmark, although the answer-generation evaluation supplies gold passages.

E2.justification: The main NQ retrieval comparison adds Re2G and released DTR(M)+HN and DTR(S)+HN checkpoints in v2 Table 2. Those DTR variants previously appeared only in v1's perturbation comparison. v2 Figure 2 also includes DTR variants in downstream QA comparisons. The established comparator set is otherwise largely retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an oracle OTT-QA protocol pairing retrieved tables with gold passages, a gold-table-plus-passage control, full-table versus mini-table QA configurations, and additional model evaluations including GPT-4o. These substantially expand the evaluation design. Figure 1 also changes the intermediate shortlist label from 1,000 to 100; because v1 already evaluated 100-candidate reranking, this does not establish an actual change to the earlier runs.

E4.justification: v1 already contains stage, paraphrase, few-shot and token-count analyses. v2 adds full-table versus mini-table F1/context-length comparisons on NQ-Tables and OTT-QA (Figures 2, 6 and 7), plus two failure case studies (Tables 16–17). These investigate whether context filtering prevents missed answers and incorrect answer extraction, extending the earlier analysis beyond token savings.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The new curves continue point-estimate reporting. Average recall changes in the perturbation tables are not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds OTT-QA results and GPT-4o F1 scores of 56.76 and 67.72 at n=1 and n=5. Its new large-reranker NQ results are 49.84/86.83/97.17 at R@1/10/50; the original small-reranker results remain. Existing entries also change: Qwen's n=1 zero-shot F1 goes from 33.33 to 39.73, THYME's n=5 Mistral F1 from 39.29 to 37.20, and SPLADE's without-description R@1 from 32.64 to 31.06. These comprise new configurations and revised results, not uniformly established same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: The training-free three-stage architecture remains. v2 Section 3 introduces dataset-specific component substitutions: Jina Embeddings v3 for OTT-QA row ranking and dense retrieval, and gemini-embedding-001 for final reranking. It also adds a text-embedding-3-large variant for NQ-Tables. These adapt the existing pipeline without introducing a new training objective or retrieval architecture.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative into dedicated benchmark, numbered results, computational-efficiency and ablation sections. Much of v1 Appendix A moves into the main text, and the remaining appendices are redistributed. The abstract, contribution list, conclusion and limitations receive substantial rewriting, beyond the insertion of new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds three context-length performance figures, OTT-QA result tables and two case-study tables. It expands the dataset-statistics and stage-wise tables and relocates existing token-count and ablation displays into the main text. Figure 1's shortlist annotations and table emphasis conventions change. The original prompt figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2's introduction adds discussion of earlier cascaded systems, including Wang et al. (2011), Hu et al. (2019) and Re2G, positioning CRAFT against trained retrieval pipelines. References supporting OTT-QA and the additional embedding models also appear. This expands context while retaining the central positioning around modular, training-free table retrieval.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs or a mathematical framework. v2 adds informal computational accounting and model-choice explanations, without introducing substantive formal definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by addressing v1's explicitly acknowledged single-benchmark limitation and testing full-table versus mini-table answer quality beyond token savings. Failure cases and explicit oracle-setting limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: OTT-QA Stage 2 R@10 conflicts between Tables 3 and 8 (81.88 versus 87.35), and the 33-fold online-call claim does not clearly separate baseline precomputation from inference. Those issues limit specific conclusions but do not erase the substantial gains in validation and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CRAFT research work. Their text, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated from v1's appendices into v2's main text.

after.justification: v2 retains original NQ-Tables experiments and reports additional OTT-QA evaluations, model configurations, context comparisons and qualitative failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original NQ-Tables retrieval and answer-generation results, query-perturbation experiments, stage ablations, few-shot evaluations and token-count measurements.

results.title: CRAFT: Training-Free Cascaded Retrieval for Tabular QA

C1.justification: v2 removes the headline average 10% absolute-gain claim and replaces the contribution centered on proposing a general combined-policy framework with claims about evaluator reliability, environmental feedback, and future task evaluations as memory-quality labels. Experience-following, error propagation, and misaligned replay remain central, but the claimed contribution shifts substantially toward understanding and selecting evaluators.

C2.justification: v2 recasts misaligned replay around intrinsic record errors and incompatibility with current task context, develops reasoning-versus-imitation explanations using RegAgent, and qualifies deletion benefits according to evaluator reliability and memory dependence. Appendix B.5 identifies a failure case where AgentDriver retains worse records under GPT-4o-mini. A new Limitations section restricts generalization to other memory mechanisms and acknowledges the absence of theoretical guarantees.

D1.justification: v2 supplies RegAgent's data-generation recipe, retrieval settings, thresholds, and prompt; identifies the three automatic evaluators and 300-example fine-tuning setup; and substantially revises EHR/CIC-IoT prompts. The code/data link is retained. Reproducibility remains imperfect: v2 Appendix A.1 specifies 100 initial CIC-IoT records, whereas Table 1 reports 50, and its EHR termination-signal description conflicts with the new judging prompt.

E1.justification: v2 adds RegAgent's synthetic six-dimensional regression task and changes CIC-IoT classification from 34 labels to 8 selected categories. MIMIC-III and nuScenes remain. The CIC-IoT constrained-memory scenario shown in v1 Figure 7 is absent from the corresponding v2 Figure 17.

E2.justification: The single coarse-evaluator condition expands into C1, C2, and C3: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, and fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini for the real agents. These variants are actually compared in addition and history-based deletion experiments (v2 Table 1 and Figures 5 and 14). Fixed-memory, add-all, strict evaluation, and the existing deletion approaches remain.

E3.justification: CIC-IoT evaluation changes from 1,200 test-split cases to 1,000 training-split cases. AgentDriver's reported periodic-deletion interval changes from 300 to 500 steps, alpha from 1 to 0, and minimum retrieval count from 5 to 3. EHRAgent's strict evaluation changes from answer containment to exact matching. RegAgent introduces a separate 4,000-query protocol. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds evaluator-quality comparisons, RegAgent error-free controls, and direct analyses of deleted versus retained record quality using error distributions and correctness rates. These substantially revise the misaligned-replay investigation previously based on input/output-similarity heatmaps. v1's noisy-initialization experiment and similarity-versus-performance plots are removed. Existing alternative-backbone analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces kernel-density estimation of deleted and retained record errors (Figure 6 and Figures 15–16), adding a statistical distribution-estimation procedure. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; existing correlation-coefficient reporting is retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise many existing scores and add RegAgent and evaluator variants; Table 4 adds record-correctness results. For example, reported fixed-memory AgentDriver success changes from 40.53 to 40.11. CIC-IoT strict accuracy changes from 63.33 to 85.40 under different class and sampling settings, so this is not a comparable-setting performance gain. New results also show that history-based deletion reduces RegAgent performance despite improving several real-agent configurations.

M1.justification: The selective-addition and frequency/history-deletion framework remains. Local revisions include changing the stated combined-deletion predicate from multiplying indicators to logical OR (v1 Section 5.1; v2 Section 4.1) and revising EHR/CIC-IoT judging prompts. The PDFs do not establish whether the Boolean edit also reflects changed implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around evaluators. The standalone evaluation-setup section is absorbed into the addition section and appendix, the former Appendix C is reorganized within Appendix B, and a Limitations section is added. This substantially changes the narrative and organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, simplifies Figure 1 by removing its challenge illustrations, expands Tables 1–3, and adds Table 4. Figures are extensively regrouped and replaced with evaluator bar charts and record-error density plots. Some backbone and memory-capacity plots are carried over, while other panels are added or removed; these changes exceed simple renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes evolving, noisy agent memory from static retrieved-demonstration learning and revises its relationship to memory-bank optimization research. New discussions cite works including Luo's survey, Lampinen's latent learning, A-MEM, and AgentFly, while several general agent references disappear. Publication updates to AgentDriver and Agent Workflow Memory concern retained works, not new citations.

T1.justification: The stated memory-size bound changes from M ≤ alpha(t'−t)K to M ≤ alpha(t−t')K. The combined-deletion definition changes from a product of indicators to logical OR. These alter mathematical statements, while the rewritten history-utility expression is equivalent. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's evaluator recommendations relied on one coarse condition and an oracle, with fine-tuning suggested but untested. v2 compares stronger and fine-tuned evaluators and adds controlled RegAgent experiments plus direct measurements of stored-record quality, substantially strengthening the evidence behind its central explanations and practical guidance. The new limitations also clarify applicability. Narrower IoT coverage, removed robustness checks, and inconsistent implementation details reduce breadth and reproducibility, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same memory-management study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten, with framework terminology changed to recipe. The detailed pass@16 discussion moves to Appendix D.3, while a limitations section and appendices on licensing, AI assistance, and potential harms are added.

The former main-text pass@16 Tables 3–4 become appendix Tables 6–7; the existing training-time table is also relocated and renumbered.

The earlier IPO discussion and citation are removed, changing positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Proposition B.3's proof replaces the bare gradient factor with its norm in the final scalar bound, correcting the mathematical expression. The proposition, small-beta argument, and Appendix A convergence theorem otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens external validity: Tables 4–5 address v1's reliance on one student model and predominantly mathematical evaluations through additional architectures, scales, and tasks. These reporting weaknesses temper the transfer conclusions but do not outweigh the broader validation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds evaluations across model architectures and scales, scientific question answering, and code generation.

improvement.justification: V1 supported its coordination explanation mainly through learning dynamics, similarity trends, and a case study. Appendix D supplies conditional formal reasoning, while the limitations and entropy-collapse caveat improve interpretation. C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims about coordinated reasoning/search and effective multi-hop verification. The introduction newly claims that HARIS is among the first RL-based cooperative-agent approaches for claim verification, adding a limited novelty claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning human alignment of the reward judge and the advantages of agent separation beyond simply increasing model size. Its limitations newly exclude open-domain QA and counterfactual detection. The original explanations concerning retrieval noise, agent coordination and binary-verification limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a HARIS code-repository link and single-agent/SFT prompt templates in Table 9. It provides more specific GPU allocations, explicitly states one epoch per training stage, and documents SFT target generation and human-annotation instructions. Existing optimizer, retrieval and context-length details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover EX-FEVER with 2–3 hops, HOVER with 2–4 hops and positive CHECKWHY claims, using Wikipedia retrieval. The added comparisons and human checks reuse the existing claim-verification and synthesized-QA setting; they introduce no new domain or verification task.

E2.justification: v2 adds BiDeV to the main comparison in Table 1 and introduces supervised fine-tuning and ReAct comparisons in Tables 6 and 7. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives. The original main-table comparators remain present.

E3.justification: v2 adds comparisons using Qwen3-4B across baselines, SFT with correct-answer-filtered training targets and matched epochs/learning rates, and ReAct evaluations at 4B, 8B and 14B. Appendix D introduces a human-validation protocol using 150 held-out questions and two annotators evaluating 75 responses each. These are additional protocols; the reported main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 extends the reward ablation from training curves to final verification scores in Table 4. It also adds SFT-versus-RL comparisons, model-size sensitivity analysis and human validation of the reward judge in Appendices B and D. The earlier role-separation and coordination-round ablations and qualitative cases remain.

E5.justification: v2 introduces human–LLM agreement estimation, reporting Cohen’s kappa of 0.81 and 93.3% agreement. v1 contains no corresponding reliability statistics. Neither version reports benchmark seed-based variability, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–3 and the original training curves are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results for BiDeV, reward choice, matched backbones, SFT, model scaling and human validation. For example, Table 4 reports HOVER 4-hop F1 of 52.38 with F1 rewards versus 57.42 with LLM-judge rewards. Table 5 shows FOLK tying HARIS on both EX-FEVER settings. These are additional comparisons, not improvements to the original HARIS scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the returned agents from L_N and H_N to L_{N+1} and H_{N+1}, matching the final alternating update. This is a limited correction to the algorithm specification; the architecture, rollout actions, rewards and GRPO objective remain unchanged. It does not establish that the underlying experiments changed.

P1.justification: v2 edits and condenses passages throughout the introduction, methodology, ablations and case study, and clarifies the foundation and alternating training stages. It regroups appendices into settings, additional experiments, prompts/examples and human evaluation. The main section sequence and narrative remain substantially unchanged.
