P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables, a single-agent/SFT prompt table and a human-evaluation screenshot. It revises Figure 1’s labels/caption, expands the captions of Figures 8–9 and relocates existing tables. Figures 2–9 retain identical embedded images; v1’s prompt, signature and synthesis-example tables are preserved under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liu et al.’s BiDeV and explicitly contrasts HARIS’s cooperative RL training with prompt-based LoCal and BiDeV. The new early-work novelty claim sharpens this positioning, while the broader related-work coverage remains intact.

T1.justification: The reward definitions and GRPO objective in Equations 1–4 are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, proofs or substantive derivations are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support by addressing backbone differences between methods, comparing RL with supervised training, testing model scaling, and validating the previously unchecked LLM reward against human judgments. Final reward-ablation scores also connect training behavior to verification performance. Appendix B.1 overstates uniform superiority—Table 5 shows FOLK ties on EX-FEVER—but this limited interpretive flaw does not outweigh the stronger controls and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HARIS research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated prompts and image-based case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds baseline comparisons, model-size experiments, supervised-fine-tuning results and human evaluation of the reward judge.

before.justification: v1 reports original HARIS evaluations on EX-FEVER, HOVER and CHECKWHY, together with single-agent, coordination-round and reward ablations.

results.title: Coordinating Search-Informed Reasoning and Reasoning-Guided Search in Claim Verification

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about computational efficiency, long-context and causal ASR, quantized representation quality, and scale-dependent bidirectional performance. Added evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications concerning training scale, batch size, hardware, and memory optimizations in Section 8. Section 6.3 and Appendix D hypothesize training instability as an explanation for ExtBiMamba Base's weakness. Section 6.2 also introduces an intra-class consistency versus inter-class discriminability explanation for the phone-purity/probing discrepancy.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies LibriSpeech pretraining and causal-ASR data, optimizer scheduling and learning rates, V100 hardware, front-end specifications, and implementation sources. It adds a code-access link, architecture diagrams, score-normalization details, and loss-scaling rules. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that the underlying method or retained experiments changed.

E1.justification: Appendix E expands frozen-backbone SUPERB evaluation from four to ten tasks for four representative Base models. Added coverage includes keyword spotting, query-by-example, speaker verification, speaker diarization, and slot filling, plus ASR probing beyond the retained ASR fine-tuning experiments.

E2.justification: Corresponding Tables I–V and 1–5 retain the same comparator and variant membership, including Transformer + Causal Mask. The added full SUPERB evaluation uses existing Causal Transformer/Mamba+MLP and Transformer/ExtBiMamba comparisons without introducing a new comparison method.

E3.justification: V2 extends the reported TEDLIUM3 duration filter from training/validation to all train/dev/test splits; unchanged WERs do not establish rerunning. The added ten-task evaluation introduces additional metrics and SUPERBFULL aggregation. Appendix C names SF instead of IC for the four-task score, conflicting with Section 6 and Tables 3–5 rather than reliably establishing a changed original protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix D and Figure 7 add a focused training-stability diagnostic comparing loss-scale and overflow behavior across Mamba, InnBiMamba, and ExtBiMamba. Existing architectural ablations, CCA, and phone-purity analyses remain; the higher-k purity plots are relocated. V1's brief mutual-information corroboration is removed.

E5.justification: Section 3 newly discloses that results come from a single training run without averaging; v1 did not specify this count. Ten-run RTF averaging and the paired long-context WER t-test remain unchanged. This is additional disclosure, not increased replication.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain v1's numerical results. New Table 6 supplies six additional probing tasks and ten-task aggregates: Mamba+MLP Base versus Causal Transformer Base scores 651.6 versus 608.1, while Transformer Base versus ExtBiMamba Base scores 772.4 versus 683.5. These are newly reported evaluation results, not changes to the original four-task scores. Figure 7 additionally reports persistent ExtBiMamba training instability.

M1.justification: The HuBERT block replacement, Mamba variants, optional MLPs, and two-stage pretraining procedure remain unchanged. Expanded descriptions of the feature encoder and bidirectional branches, including Appendix A's diagrams, clarify existing components rather than establish a different method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, the contribution list, and the main section sequence are retained. V2 expands explanations, revises selected interpretive paragraphs, and adds Limitations, Acknowledgments, and appendices with corresponding cross-references. It does not extensively rewrite the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reformats typography, headings, citations, and tables. It adds two architecture diagrams, a training-dynamics plot, and the full SUPERB table. V1's three-panel phone-purity figure is split between the main text and Appendix B, reorganizing existing visual evidence rather than adding new purity results.

R1.justification: V2 adds Transformer foundation references, visual Mamba stability studies, and the SUPERB journal extension, while removing or replacing some speech-unit and probing references. These support expanded explanations; the central positioning relative to earlier Mamba speech SSL and Audio Mamba work remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The state-space and selection equations remain equivalent. Projection explanations and Appendix C's standard SUPERB normalization formula document existing mathematics; no new theoretical result, substantive derivation, assumption, or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves essential pretraining and causal-ASR settings unspecified and supports cross-task generality through four probing tasks. V2 fills important documentation gaps, directly checks the principal rankings across ten tasks, and adds evidence and qualifications concerning training stability and resource limits. These substantially strengthen reproducibility and assessment of the central claims. Appendix C's IC/SF mismatch weakens score transparency, but does not outweigh the broader evidential and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mamba-based HuBERT study. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and references are readable and matchable. V1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–E are available for comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds ten-task SUPERB evaluation and training-stability measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original ASR fine-tuning, computational-efficiency measurements, representation analyses, SUPERB probing, and architectural ablations.

results.title: An Exploration of Mamba for Speech Self-Supervised Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim joint functional and PPA optimization through EDA feedback. v2 makes CDPO and controllable, prompt-specific PPA optimization central contributions. Its title and abstract replace v1's explicit human-surpassing, 27-design emphasis with claims centered on the new optimizer and fine-grained design objectives.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of reward-scale mismatch, curriculum effects, SFT-related PPA degradation and transfer across synthesis configurations. It also identifies computational cost and weaker control/memory optimization as limitations, hypothesizing insufficient representation of those circuits. This substantially expands v1's predominantly positive cross-layer optimization discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices B, C and I add extensive implementation, evaluation and prompt documentation, including batch size, clipping bounds, sampling parameters, sequence limits, training cost and metric aggregation. v2 newly states benchmark-exclusion filtering, revises hardware/framework information, and replaces the anonymous artifact reference with a named GitHub repository link.

E1.justification: VerilogEval and RTLLM coverage is retained. v2 adds evaluations on larger AutoSilicon CPU/NPU blocks averaging approximately 560 lines of code (Appendix G, Table 10), plus RTLLM tasks with explicit power, delay, area and paired optimization requirements.

E2.justification: The functional comparison adds GPT-o1, ReasoningV and untuned Qwen2.5-Coder, while removing BetterV and several foundational-model comparators from v1 Table II. v2 also broadens the PPA comparator set and explicitly evaluates GRPO and DAPO against CDPO (Table 5 and Figure 8).

E3.justification: Training expands from one to four base models. Reported RL sampling changes from 10 to 8 responses per prompt, and the learning rate changes from 1.5e-6 to 1e-6. PPA evaluation adds mean and worst scores alongside best-of-10 results; priority-specific evaluations use best-of-five selection. New experiments vary synthesis tools, libraries and optimization targets.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's SFT/RL comparison and design examples, v2 adds individual-reward ablations, CDPO-component ablations, expanded training-stage comparisons, synthesis-sensitivity tests, runtime analysis and optimization-category analysis. The barrel-shifter case is expanded, while the edge-detector case analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's best/mean/worst EDAP summaries characterize generated candidates, and its additional training trajectories do not introduce a defined statistical uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: The six Qwen-based VerilogEval scores are retained, but RTLLM v1.1 pass@5 changes from 82.8% to 87.2%. Several per-design PPA entries change; for example, adder_16bit delay changes from 0.07 ns in v1 Table III to 0.84 ns in v2 Table 11. Extensive new ablation, robustness, runtime and scalability results are added. Revised methods and settings prevent interpreting all differences as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v1 uses GRPO with a fixed weighted scalar reward. v2 introduces CDPO with separately normalized component advantages, success-dependent curriculum weights, prompt-conditioned power/delay/area preferences and a revised token-level objective. Preference-aware data augmentation also changes the training procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, background and method narrative are extensively rewritten around CDPO and design preferences. v2 adds dedicated ablation, runtime, optimization-analysis and limitations sections, and reorganizes evaluation definitions, implementation information and detailed results into appendices. The title, model terminology and author block also change.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the framework diagram, replaces the introductory adder illustration, removes the win/tie/loss chart and adds radar, optimization, runtime and training plots. The detailed PPA table moves to the appendix with fewer comparator columns. New ablation tables and full prompt/code displays substantially change the visual presentation and layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially refocuses the literature discussion, removing broad image/video and general-LLM citations while adding relevant work such as ReasoningV, SymRTLO, Spec2RTL-Agent and DAPO. It also positions CDPO through explicit comparisons with existing policy-optimization methods, extending v1's emphasis on SFT, RAG and external search.

T1.justification: v2 substantively revises the mathematical optimization formulation: componentwise normalized advantages, an exponential-moving-average curriculum recurrence, preference-weighted aggregation and an asymmetric clipped token-level objective replace v1's scalar-reward GRPO formulation. These are changed mathematical definitions and update rules, not equivalent notation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation through component ablations, synthesis-tool/library robustness tests and larger-design experiments, while substantially improving reproducibility through algorithm and prompt documentation. These gains outweigh reporting inconsistencies, including Section 4.2's baseline-improvement claim and Table 4's pass@1 header versus pass@5 prose. The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, not simply additional content or higher scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChipSeek RTL-generation work, despite substantial revision and renaming. Text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–I.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, runtime measurements, synthesis-sensitivity experiments and larger-design evaluations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original ChipSeek training, functional-correctness evaluations and synthesized hardware measurements, including Tables II–III and design case studies.

results.title: ChipSeek: Optimizing Verilog Generation via EDA-Integrated Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from a multilingual test benchmark diagnosing model weaknesses to a benchmark plus training resource claimed to improve multilingual chart understanding across model families and sizes. The original benchmark novelty and multilingual performance-gap claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's blanket preference for fully localized inputs with a model-family-dependent interpretation: English inputs help several families but hurt Qwen2.5-VL. It adds explanations involving OCR failures, language bias, training-data saturation, and visual adaptation. Limitations now explicitly discuss inherited source biases and cultural or semantic shifts introduced by generation and translation.

D1.justification: v2 adds LoRA ranks, learning rates, epoch budgets, alignment-data composition, detailed filtering counts, annotator qualifications and instructions, source-dataset access links, and additional inference settings. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v1's explicit METEOR/Gemini translation-acceptance cutoffs and four-shot chart-reconstruction detail are no longer documented.

E1.justification: The ten-language test benchmark is retained. v2 adds POLYCHARTQA-Train from ChartQA and ChartLlama, including training chart types such as Gantt and scatter charts. Appendix E.2 also introduces chart-to-JSON and document/chart OCR training using MTVQA, Pangea-OCR, and reconstructed SMPQA, expanding represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds five evaluated chart specialists: TinyChart, ChartGemma, ChartInstruct, ChartLlama, and ChartAssistant. The LLaVA-v1.6-7B-Vicuna row disappears. In the corresponding cross-lingual comparison, v2 replaces the two Qwen2-VL variants with InternVL3-2B/8B, PaliGemma2-3B, and LLaVA-v1.6-7B, while retaining Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce training-data fractions, English-mixture sweeps with a fixed 70K-example budget, and alignment/fine-tuning stage controls. Dataset-quality evaluation changes from Chinese human assessment plus multilingual model proxies to human assessment across languages. Its sample size is inconsistently documented as 20% per language in Section 3.4 and 250 items per language in Table 7.

E4.justification: v1's 0/2/4/8-shot study is removed. v2 adds error decomposition by failure category, chart type, and question type; training-data-size and English-proportion sensitivity studies; and alignment-stage/vision-encoder freezing ablations. These analyses investigate failure mechanisms and adaptation choices beyond v1's few-shot and cross-lingual analyses.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports a single run, whereas v2 reports averages over eight independent runs. v2 also adds weighted Cohen's kappa and disagreement counts between human annotators across languages, replacing the earlier human-versus-model exact-agreement reporting. Run-level variability and confidence intervals remain unreported.

E6.justification: The 21 retained zero-shot result rows match after converting proportions to percentages. Substantial new results concern chart specialists, expanded cross-lingual comparisons, human validation, and training analyses. For example, v2 Table 5 newly reports fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B averages of 61.1%/66.9%; these use new training conditions. The earlier few-shot results are removed.

M1.justification: The core JSON/Plotly chart-generation pipeline is retained, but v2 adds model-adaptation procedures absent from v1. These include LoRA instruction tuning and Appendix E.2's chart-to-JSON/OCR alignment followed by QA fine-tuning, with different vision-encoder freezing strategies. This introduces substantive training stages and objectives beyond the earlier inference-only experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and methods undergo extensive rewriting and compression. Quality control and data statistics become dedicated subsections, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and appendices expand from A-C to A-F with clearer thematic divisions. Duplicate source-selection prose and a duplicated rewriting prompt are removed.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline diagram, replaces the opening Chinese example with Hindi, adds error-analysis and training-sensitivity plots, and substantially restructures result and dataset-statistics tables. Prompts become colored figure panels and the annotation-interface illustration changes. Existing dataset examples and distribution plots are retained and relocated, rather than newly generated analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused references on chart-specialist models, LoRA, translation, and multilingual instruction tuning, plus benchmark-comparison tables. It explicitly attributes the decoupled chart representation to Shinoda et al. (2024). The central positioning against English-centric chart benchmarks remains; publication and bibliographic updates to retained works are not new research relationships.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. v2's training descriptions and use of standard agreement statistics do not introduce a theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper through training-resource validation, controlled adaptation studies, chart-specialist comparisons, and human quality assessment across languages, addressing v1's reliance on a Gemini proxy beyond Chinese. The revised cross-lingual interpretation is also better supported. Reporting problems remain, notably conflicting annotation sample sizes and Table 2/Table 7 agreement summaries, plus Table 14's inconsistent baseline row. These limit precision, but the broader validation and explanatory evidence provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe POLYCHARTQA. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including visually inspected prompts that are embedded as images in v2. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, multilingual human assessments, fine-tuning experiments, error analyses, and training ablations, including the additional experiments in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot, few-shot, and cross-lingual model evaluations in Tables 2-4, together with human and model-based assessments of dataset quality.

results.title: POLYCHARTQA: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models with Multilingual Chart Question Answering

C1.justification: The four headline contributions remain. V2's conclusion additionally asserts that the identified heads are conflict-specific rather than generically visual, strengthening the mechanistic claim. Dataset novelty is also qualified through an explicit combination of requirements rather than the earlier broad first-dataset formulation.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of weak MLP interventions, cross-dataset head overlap, and POPE invariance as evidence of specialized conflict resolution. It adds fusion-architecture generalizability limits while dropping v1's explicit synthetic-data caveat. Appendix E also strengthens diminishing returns after 20 heads into a peak/no-further-gains assertion, although Figure 10 shows continued gains.

D1.justification: V2 adds exact judge model identifiers, OpenRouter usage, judge and human evaluation prompts and rubrics, and Visual CounterFact prompt instructions. Reported total compute changes from 15 to 20 GPU hours. Hardware, Transformers usage, and the code/dataset link are retained; the reproducibility paragraph is relocated.

E1.justification: V2 adds Visual CounterFact's color split, covering independently constructed, more photorealistic attribute conflicts, and POPE's object-presence questions for ordinary visual understanding. These substantially extend evaluation beyond WHOOPS-AHA!'s anomalous-scene completions. The original WHOOPS-AHA! coverage remains.

E2.justification: Appendix C adds MLP-block interventions as a comparison with attention-head interventions. Table 4 adds random heads to the localization comparison against gradients. Random heads already appeared in v1's intervention controls, but their participation in this localization comparison is new.

E3.justification: New protocols include interventions on the last three MLP blocks, dataset-specific head identification on Visual CounterFact, a 1,000-question POPE control, and SAM3-mask localization on 20 images. V2 also adds two-model dataset judging and validation by two humans on 20 items. The original models and retained WHOOPS-AHA! sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 tests whether MLP interventions reproduce the effects, whether selected heads support ordinary visual understanding, whether findings replicate across datasets, and whether attention aligns with counterfactual object masks. It also adds dataset-quality validation. V1's random-head control, head-count sensitivity, patch ablations, and generation-quality analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 adds rating summaries with plus/minus values, exact and adjacent agreement rates, localization medians and interquartile ranges, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against baselines. These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1's plotted error bars. Neither version establishes an increase in repeated experimental runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Original WHOOPS-AHA! result curves are retained, while substantial new results appear. Table 3 reports unchanged POPE accuracy of 0.84/0.87 after head suppression, versus 0.50 without images. Table 4 reports localization medians of 4.41/2.05 for counterfactual heads versus 1.74/1.88 for gradients. V2 also adds MLP, dataset-validation, and Visual CounterFact intervention and head-overlap results.

M1.justification: Logit Lens head identification, bidirectional attention intervention, and attention/gradient patch selection remain unchanged. V2 reverses the equations' lambda signs to match the steering direction already described and plotted in v1; this does not establish a changed underlying procedure. New controls and localization metrics extend evaluation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, related work, discussion, and conclusion; separates Dataset from Background and Methods; condenses existing explanations; and reorganizes limitations and appendices. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds MLP-intervention and Visual CounterFact plots plus dataset-validation, POPE, and localization tables. It substantially reorganizes appendix displays, relocates existing figures and the caption-generation table, revises captions, and restyles prompt boxes. Original main-result plots are preserved.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded and reorganized around multimodal conflicts, VLM interpretability, and internal conflict dynamics. Added discussions include Hua, Basile, Neo, Nikankin, and other works. Positioning now emphasizes implicit commonsense conflicts and conflict-specific heads relative to explicit modality conflicts and general visual processing.

T1.justification: Appendix I introduces the mathematical definition of Average Ratio, comparing mean attribution inside counterfactual object masks with background attribution. This adds a formal metric definition, but no theorem, proof, or substantial theoretical development.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens empirical support through independent-dataset replication, MLP/POPE controls, and object-mask localization measurements with significance tests, extending v1's single-dataset study and patch-ablation evidence. Documented dataset validation also improves transparency. These gains outweigh the small validation subsets, overly categorical conflict-specificity interpretation, and new Appendix E assertion that accuracy peaks at 20 heads despite further gains in Figure 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WHOOPS-AHA! study, models, and intervention framework. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds dataset validation, MLP interventions, Visual CounterFact evaluation, POPE controls, and quantitative localization results.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3, including head attribution, interventions, image-patch ablations, and generation-quality analyses.

results.title: When Seeing Overrides Knowing: Disentangling Knowledge Conflicts in Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The main narrative removes the claim of exceeding the closed-source per-dataset upper-bound average by 2.04 points, while retaining the scalable collaboration contribution and comparisons with GPT models and open-source best results. The longer-output closed-source upper-bound claim remains in Appendix A.5, so it is not removed throughout the paper.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning inexpensive APIs and parallel inference, generalization supported by question-bank diversity, prospective online bank expansion, perplexity normalization, and budget trade-offs. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability. The original limitations concerning computational resources and uniform inference configurations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 revises the embedding dimension and newly specifies eight responses for Self-MoA, while most generation settings and the supplied prompts remain unchanged. The abstract changes a promised code release into a stated release at the renamed SMCS repository.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original eight benchmarks and adds HumanEval, FinQA, and LiveMathBench as unseen-benchmark evaluations using the existing question bank (Appendix A.6). Section 4.5 also introduces a distinct retrieval-transfer scenario: an MMLU-PRO-only bank supporting evaluation on AIME, MBPP, GPQA-Diamond, and MedMCQA.

E2.justification: The new question-bank comparison includes an evaluated random-selection control without a question bank (v2 Table 3). Table 1 retains the same six collaboration baselines and individual LLMs. Newly discussed GraphRouter and MODEL-SAT are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds restricted-bank and unseen-benchmark evaluation protocols, API cost and latency measurements, and MMLU-PRO sweeps over referencer count, aggregation count, and retrieval-bank support size. Appendix A.3 also changes the stated embedding dimension from 4,096 to 8,192; this documents a setting revision without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test retrieval under distribution mismatch, the numerical scale of perplexity, and accuracy/cost sensitivity to three hyperparameters (Section 4.5 and Appendices A.6, A.7, A.10). The original component ablation is retained unchanged, moving from v1 Section 4.4/Table 2 to v2 Appendix A.9/Table 10.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports three runs with different random seeds and mean/standard-deviation results for SMCS and three comparators across four datasets (Appendix A.8, Table 9). Table 8 also adds perplexity distribution summaries. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-run or uncertainty reporting; v2 does not add formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Shared scores in the main and longer-output tables remain unchanged, including system averages of 76.78 and 81.01. v2 adds substantial results, including 95.12 on HumanEval, 75.24 on FinQA, and 74.38 on LiveMathBench (Table 7), plus cost/latency, repeated-seed, perplexity, and budget-sweep results. Closed-source upper-bound summary rows are removed.

M1.justification: Despite the SMACS-to-SMCS rename, Section 3 retains the unified question bank, similarity-weighted model selection, prior-based dropping, repeated aggregation, and hybrid similarity/perplexity scoring. No new algorithmic component or changed inference procedure is established.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract is rewritten, and the introduction and related-work narrative are substantially recast around multi-LLM collaboration. Terminology changes throughout from SMACS/MACS to SMCS/MCS. The experimental narrative is reorganized, including moving component ablations into the appendix and shortening the conclusion.

P2.justification: v2 adds the conceptual comparison diagram in Figure 2 and eight tables covering efficiency, distribution mismatch, perplexity, uncertainty, and budget sweeps. Existing displays are relocated and relabeled, including the component-ablation table. The main results table also changes its highlighted comparison rows and removes the closed-source upper-bound row.

R1.justification: Related work adds GraphRouter and MODEL-SAT, expands the RouterDC discussion, and places MoA and Self-MoA under posterior collaboration. Some general NLP and repeated-sampling background is removed, and references supporting the new benchmarks are added. The central prior-versus-posterior positioning remains.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(8), including the selection, sampling, scoring, and ranking definitions, are retained. Appendix A.7 discusses the existing perplexity score's numerical scale and empirical behavior without introducing a substantive new formal definition, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: The new unseen-benchmark evaluations, three-seed results, and cost/latency and budget analyses address important gaps in v1's evidence for generalization, reliability, and practical scalability. They substantially strengthen the empirical case while preserving the original results. Some new interpretations overreach the evidence, particularly treating perplexity summaries as strict bounds, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the added direct experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with SMACS renamed SMCS. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original efficiency, out-of-distribution, repeated-seed, perplexity, and cost-versus-accuracy experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original eight-benchmark evaluations, scaling experiments, component ablations, aggregator comparisons, and longer-output experiments, including appendix results.

results.title: A Scalable Multi-LLM Collaboration System with Retrieval-based Selection and Exploration-Exploitation-Driven Enhancement

C1.justification: V1 presents a 30,000-persona temporal dataset with competitive survey alignment and stronger narrative consistency. V2 presents a framework claiming improved alignment and fairness with smaller generators and demonstrated network utility. Temporal evolution leaves the main contributions, while population fidelity, bias reduction, and homophily become central.

C2.justification: Temporal specificity/coherence interpretations disappear. V2 introduces interpretations concerning subgroup representational harms and latent network homophily, explicitly limits validity to population/subgroup simulation, and discusses imperfect judge agreement, model and prompt sensitivity, and static-network scope. The existing concern about Bluesky's demographic representativeness remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds exact ATP questions and options, software/CUDA and hardware-memory specifications, graph and baseline construction details, and expanded privacy and licensing descriptions. These substantially expand documentation. Conversely, v1's six-source Bluesky inventory (Table 6) and temporal-analysis implementation examples disappear, reducing documentation of those aspects.

E1.justification: English Bluesky content and ATP Waves 34 and 99 remain. V2 adds human-authored PersonaChat personas and evaluates follower-link prediction and semantic homophily under global and dense local graph scenarios. These introduce substantial task and evaluation-data coverage beyond v1's persona and survey evaluations.

E2.justification: V1 principally compares against the original Anthology collection, retained as ANT_LLaMa. V2 adds Gemma-generated Anthology and human-authored PersonaChat to survey screening, and PersonaChat to contradiction analysis. Network experiments add random and recency-based extractive baselines (Tables 1, 4, and 6).

E3.justification: The sampled population changes from 10,000 to approximately 3,000 users, and the stated generation cap increases from 400 to 1,500 tokens. V2 adds Gemma generation, screening, and a 3-by-3 demographic/response-surveyor design beyond v1's Llama-3-8B surveying. It drops the fixed temporal-window evaluation and introduces revised judging, a 250-persona faithfulness protocol, graph evaluation, and response-scale coarsening.

E4.justification: V1's temporal perplexity, named-entity, narrative-evolution, and demographic-distribution analyses are removed. V2 adds human validation of consistency judges, source faithfulness across post-count ranges, generator/surveyor and response-scale sensitivity, subgroup fairness analyses, and two network case studies. This substantially changes the questions investigated beyond aggregate survey performance.

E5.justification: The 40 demographic responses per question are retained. V2 adds means and standard deviations across surveyor configurations, case-study seed 42, 20 random human-population splits, and 10,000 bootstrap resamples with specified 95% confidence intervals and McNemar tests (Table 2; Appendices A, D, and E). Configuration variability does not establish additional independently seeded repetitions.

E6.justification: V1 Table 5 reports SYNTHIA FULL survey distances of 0.47 and 0.44; v2 Table 2 reports SYN_Gemma means of 0.35 and 0.38 under changed populations and model configurations, so these are not same-setting gains. Contradiction results are replaced and temporal results removed. New results include faithfulness of 0.5762–0.7534 across post-count bins and global/local link-prediction accuracies of 0.72/0.59.

M1.justification: The core post-conditioned persona-generation approach remains. However, v2's generation prompt explicitly requests selecting significant post_ids and returning a backstory based on them; v1 requests only a story (v1 Figure 7; v2 Figure 9). This adds source selection and provenance to the specified output.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's separate evaluation/results organization and temporal narrative become an integrated alignment section followed by dedicated fairness and network sections. The appendices are substantially reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: The pipeline diagram is redrawn, temporal and demographic-distribution displays are removed, and fairness plots, bootstrap distributions, homophily plots, surveyor heatmaps, and expanded comparison tables are added. The grounding example moves from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Figure 8; unchanged demographic prompts are also relocated. Table structures and placement change extensively.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to recent persona-generation and population-simulation research, including BluePrint, Co-persona, and PersonaCraft. New factuality and fairness analyses are positioned through FActScore, SummaC, Q2, and fairness literature. Core Anthology and Park references remain, while several earlier citations disappear; this exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The demographic-matching objective is retained across v1 Appendix D and v2 Appendix F. V2 adds formal definitions for atomic-claim faithfulness and hallucination, Fidelity Gap with a human-split reference, and Parity Gap. These are limited mathematical extensions; no theorem or proof contribution is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through matched-generator comparisons, multiple surveyors, human-checked judging and source faithfulness, and statistical network evaluation. These address v1's explicit single-model limitation and its lack of direct faithfulness testing. Removing the temporal study and source inventory sacrifices useful evidence and reproducibility, and broad superiority language needs qualification by exceptions in Table 10. Nevertheless, the improved controls and direct validation provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SYNTHIA research project. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained content across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original survey comparisons, source-faithfulness measurements, fairness analyses, judge validation, and social-network experiments, with detailed appendix results.

before.justification: V1 reports original persona-generation evaluations covering consistency, demographic matching, ATP survey alignment, and temporal effects, including Tables 3–5 and Figures 4–6.

results.title: Synthia: Scalable Grounded Persona Generation from Social Media Data

C1.justification: V3 retains the reliable-search contribution but makes efficient test-time computation a central additional claim in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. It claims that four confidence-weighted samples match 16-sample majority voting, yielding a fourfold inference-compute reduction.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations concerning retrieval-independent calibration, improved information extraction, verification behavior and transferability of adaptive constraints. Its new limitations section explicitly acknowledges text-only evaluation and that intermediate confidence scores are not optimized by the training objective. Appendix E also substantially expands the interpretation of the retained training curves.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D add training epochs, batch sizes, rollout counts, sequence limits, GPU resources and training times, the Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge and its full prompt, the training prompt, and document truncation/ID handling. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v1's dated closed-source model identifiers disappear from Table 1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, GAIA and xbench-deepsearch, retaining Wikipedia retrieval and real-world web search. V3 clarifies training versus out-of-distribution roles and text-only evaluation, but does not establish newly added dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster in Table 1 is retained, accounting for renamed labels. V3 adds majority voting as the comparator for confidence-weighted inference (Figure 3), and compares against the existing Qwen-7B and Qwen-72B models under identical-document controls (Table 2).

E3.justification: V3 adds equal-budget aggregation comparisons over 1–16 rollouts, identical-document evaluation controls and an evaluated DeepSeek-70B trained variant. Appendix E also describes fixed lambda = 0.1 throughout training, whereas v1 introduces it after the first quarter. This is a reported setting revision; the unchanged ablation plots do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds binary-versus-continuous reward comparison, a controlled analysis holding retrieved documents constant, inference-budget analysis and a confidence-evolution case study. V1's adaptive-versus-fixed-weight ablation is retained as Figure 5 in Appendix E, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or performance uncertainty estimates. V3's added rollout counts describe training and inference sampling, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All 216 numerical entries in the retained Table 1 rows are unchanged. V3 adds continuous-reward and DeepSeek-70B results, Table 2 controls, and Figure 3 aggregation results. Newly reported examples include DeepSeek-70B average accuracy/reliability/FC of 0.41/0.75/0.09 and 7B accuracy of 0.551 versus 0.532 for weighted versus majority voting at 16 rollouts.

M1.justification: V3 adds confidence-weighted aggregation of multiple inference trajectories as a substantive inference extension (Section 2.4), and evaluates a continuous alternative reliability reward. The original constrained-GRPO objective and adaptive multiplier update remain; expanded descriptions of search, reading and confidence reporting largely document existing behavior.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, experimental narrative and conclusion, adds an explicit contribution list, and reorganizes the method around the interaction framework. Dedicated related-work and limitations sections and Appendices A–E substantially restructure the document; the original training ablation moves to Appendix E.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column layout, replaces the rotated Table 1 presentation with a horizontal color-highlighted table, and adds framework diagrams, aggregation plots, a case-study panel, tables and prompt listings. The original ablation plots are retained but reduced and relocated. Figure 3 introduces a caption error that reverses the plotted legend's colors.

R1.justification: V3 adds a substantial related-work section positioning the method against agentic retrieval, confidence-calibration training and adaptive self-consistency. New cited comparisons include WebGPT, ReAct, FLARE, SaySelf and confidence-informed self-consistency. RQ-RAG is removed; publication-year and title updates to retained works are not separate additions.

T1.justification: V3 adds mathematical definitions for the continuous reliability reward and confidence-weighted answer selection (Equation 7). The original constrained optimization equations, strong-duality argument and multiplier update remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is provided.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves the interaction protocol, evaluation judge and most training details unspecified. V3 substantially improves assessability and reproducibility through Appendices A–D, adds controlled retrieval and reward comparisons, evaluates an inference extension, and states important limitations. These gains outweigh the inconsistent ablation-schedule description and Figure 3 caption error, although performance uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Deliberative Searcher and retain identifiable methods, experiments and results. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. V1 has no appendices; v3's Appendices A–E are available and readable.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds reward-variant, DeepSeek-70B, controlled-retrieval and inference-aggregation results, plus a confidence-evolution case study.

before.justification: V1 reports original five-benchmark evaluations in Table 1 and an adaptive-versus-fixed reliability-weight training ablation in Figure 1.

results.title: Deliberative Searcher: Improving LLM Reliability via Reinforcement Learning with Constraints

C1.justification: The main steering contribution and headline performance claims remain. However, v2 narrows claims about identifying causally influential tokens to identifying tokens with large attribution-based contributions, particularly in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning attribution and baseline sensitivity, gradient access, scaling costs, and absent behavioral guarantees. It discusses undercorrection and hypothesizes a mismatch between global steering strength and instance-specific needs, while expanding interpretations of PCA, normalization, modality variation, and transfer results.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies GPT-4o as the hallucination judge, clarifies inference implementation, describes heatmap clipping and normalization, and adds license and artifact-use statements. Most existing implementation settings, hardware disclosures, precomputation timings, prompts, and the code link are retained or relocated.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original benchmarks and adds Toxigen-to-RealToxicityPrompts and MMHal-Bench-to-POPE transfer evaluations (Section 5.3). These substantially extend coverage to unseen input distributions and adversarial object-hallucination questions.

E2.justification: v2 adds RUDDER and SHARP to the MMHal-Bench and SPA-VL comparisons and the VLM capability checks (Tables 2 and 4). Existing VLM comparators and the LLM comparator set remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include source-to-target dataset transfer, Qwen2.5-VL-72B evaluation on 500 held-out SPA-VL examples, a nine-annotator judge-validation study, and inference-throughput measurements. The original data splits, 50-example vector construction, and five-shot reasoning evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond relocating existing ablations, v2 adds PCA-versus-mean, last-token-versus-every-step, single-layer-versus-all-layer, and normalization controls. It also adds steering-sample sensitivity, modality-composition analysis, TruthfulQA objective ablations, transfer tests, and heatmaps for existing qualitative examples (Sections 5.3 and A.1–A.4).

E5.justification: v2 newly reports Pearson correlation 0.82 and Spearman correlation 0.85 between GPT-4o and human judgments, based on evaluations from nine annotators (Section 4.2). Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals for the steering benchmarks.

E6.justification: Original per-model benchmark scores are retained, while v2 adds substantial comparison, transfer, ablation, efficiency, and scaling results. For example, Table 5 reports RTP toxicity of 1.15 for GrAInS versus 2.89 for CAA, and Table 16 reports 72B SPA-VL scores of 76.2 versus 74.0. These are newly reported experiments rather than improvements to matched v1 results.

M1.justification: Both versions use preference-based Integrated Gradients, signed token selection, masking, PCA aggregation, and normalized layer-wise steering. The additional token/layer explanations and ablations document and test the existing procedure; the combined normalization equation is algebraically equivalent.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work, and experimental narrative are substantially compressed and rewritten. Main-text ablations move to Appendix A.3, alignment-related work moves to Appendix C, and the analysis/conclusion structure is reorganized around transfer and computational overhead, with new limitations and artifact sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, merges v1 Tables 2–3 into one VLM-results table, adds average columns and numerous analytical tables, reformats figures, and introduces attribution heatmaps in Figure 8. The original sensitivity plots and Figure 7 examples are retained rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against SteerVLM, VisEdit, and SHAP, alongside citations for RUDDER, SHARP, transfer benchmarks, and methodological explanations. The central positioning of attribution-guided steering remains; moving the multimodal-alignment discussion to Appendix C does not itself add related work.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, attribution definitions, PCA construction, and intervention rule retain their substance. Combining addition and normalization and clarifying SmoothGrad's Gaussian-noise notation do not introduce new theoretical results, substantive derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 left same-attribute transfer, several key steering-design choices, and decoding overhead largely untested. v2 supplies direct transfer tests, targeted ablations, throughput measurements, and human-judge validation, while narrowing causal language and documenting concrete limitations. These changes substantially strengthen the paper's evidential basis. Benchmark uncertainty remains unreported, and some superiority claims still conflict with table entries, such as the Qwen MMHal-Bench comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GrAInS and contain readable methods, experiments, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds transfer evaluations, further ablations, larger-model results, throughput measurements, and human-judge agreement estimates.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM and VLM benchmark results, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples.

results.title: GrAInS: Gradient-based Attribution for Inference-Time Steering of LLMs and VLMs

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes a human-verified trajectory dataset, reinforcement fine-tuning and smaller models' capability ceilings. V3 replaces those central contributions with logic–language separation and the LightManus-Jarvis architecture, claiming stronger execution and substantially lower token/time costs. This changes the paper's scientific focus.

C2.justification: Interpretation shifts from fine-tuning's benefits and limitations to semantic drift, hybrid perception, reasoning–execution tradeoffs and cumulative errors. V3 also explicitly identifies restricted task diversity, exclusion of dynamic/irreversible scenarios, human-verification bottlenecks and inference-induced state drift; v1's limitations discussion is substantially narrower.

D1.justification: V3 supplies a code-access URL, emulator/VM specifications, accessibility-tree and action implementation details, knowledge-graph construction and verification procedures, and an execution listing. V1's trajectory-curation and four-A100 training disclosures disappear with the training study. Earlier details deferred to missing appendices cannot be checked.

E1.justification: The reported study removes the trajectory-training corpus and A3 evaluation on six unseen-application subsets. V3 adds AndroidWorld and a browser-only NaturalGAIA scenario in Appendix E. The benchmark remains described as 276 tasks; the PDFs do not establish which individual tasks were regenerated.

E2.justification: V3 adds UI-TARS-1.5-7B to the main comparison, M3A on AndroidWorld and Mind2Web on the browser-only subset. PC-Agent and Mobile-Agent-e remain named comparators. However, PC-Agent's citation changes from Liu et al. (2025b) to a different work by He et al. (2024b), leaving that comparator's continuity uncertain.

E3.justification: Backends change substantially, including GPT-o3 to GPT-5.2 and Claude-Sonnet-4 to 4.5, with Gemini-3 and newer Qwen configurations added. New protocols include matched-backend external comparisons and efficiency measurement across five shared Level-3 tasks using Gemini-3.0-Flash. Newly disclosed emulator specifications alone do not establish an environment change.

E4.justification: V3 extends the existing MAe/LightManus comparison with a Jarvis executor ablation and adds token/time analysis. RFT-focused diagnostics are replaced by architecture/backend failure comparisons, illustrated error cases in Appendix F and generalization tests of the revised framework.

E5.justification: Both versions report Pass@1 and, where available, Pass@4 without seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. V3's five-task efficiency averages specify an evaluation sample rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Reported values change even for retained labels: MAe with Gemini-2.5-Pro has overall WPSR 23.2% in v1 Table 1 and 21.1% in v3 Table 2. V3 adds Jarvis, efficiency and external-test results while removing RFT/A3 results. The headline 34.6% versus 45.6% uses different model/executor combinations and does not establish a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: V1 delegates execution to Mobile-Agent-e/PC-Agent and proposes trajectory-based reinforcement fine-tuning. V3 introduces Jarvis with screenshot/accessibility-tree fusion, filtered element identifiers and identifier-based Android actions; fine-tuning disappears from the reported method. Hierarchical decomposition and dynamic scheduling remain underlying components.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the revised contribution. Benchmark subsections are reorganized, the trajectory-training sections disappear, and a separate limitations section and structured appendices substantially alter the document's organization.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the architecture diagram, replaces the failure pie charts with a radar chart and restructures the main results table. It adds construction diagrams, observation-space and efficiency tables, appendix comparison tables, task examples, screenshots and a formatted execution listing.

R1.justification: Positioning moves from trajectory-data scarcity and experiential learning toward realistic verifiable evaluation, context management and hybrid execution. V3 adds substantial discussion and citations around OSWorld, UI-TARS, agentic context engineering and hierarchical planning, plus a systematic benchmark comparison in Table 6.

T1.justification: Changes concern methodological definitions: v3 formalizes application information spaces, constrained graph-walk steps and Jarvis's observation/action mapping, while v1's training-trajectory tuple disappears. The WPSR, MATCR and positional success-rate equations remain equivalent. Neither supplied PDF contains theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's underspecified fine-tuning procedure and missing referenced appendices, v3 makes benchmark construction and execution substantially easier to audit. Component comparisons, efficiency measurements and explicit applicability limits strengthen support for its revised contribution. Reporting weaknesses remain: Section 5.2 claims a Gemini-3 Flash WPSR advantage although Table 2 shows an 81.2% tie with Pro, and uncertainty estimates remain absent. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in transparency and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NaturalGAIA and LightManus, retaining the 276-task benchmark and core evaluation metrics. All supplied pages are readable. However, v1 references Appendices A–C that are absent from its nine-page PDF, limiting comparison of earlier construction, trajectory and training details. V3 includes Appendices A–F.

after.justification: V3 reports original architecture comparisons, efficiency measurements, failure analyses, AndroidWorld evaluations and browser-only comparisons in Tables 2–3 and 7–8 and Figure 4.

before.justification: V1 reports original NaturalGAIA evaluations, Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tuning results, A3 generalization results and failure analyses in Tables 1–2 and Figure 2.

results.title: NaturalGAIA: A Verifiable Benchmark and Hierarchical Framework for Long-Horizon GUI Tasks

C1.justification: Both versions claim to formalize multilingual and cross-lingual attribution, evaluate existing approaches across 18 languages and eight author classes, and identify substantial cross-lingual generalization challenges. The added experiments support these retained contributions without redefining their central meaning.

C2.justification: V2 adds empirically informed qualifications about generalization beyond news and connects the Russian-transfer explanation to results from other Slavic languages. Its new Limitations section explicitly addresses fixed generator coverage, future models and decoding strategies, and the clean-text assumption. This substantially expands applicability boundaries beyond v1's shorter future-work discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code/data repository link and specifies mGPT-13B outputs for StatEnsemble features. Reported cumulative computation changes from approximately 200 to 500 GPU-hours, while the main hardware description remains unchanged. V1's Jupyter Lab and four-core preprocessing disclosure is removed; existing learning-rate and sequence-length details remain.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates MULTITUDE news texts in 18 languages; MultiSocial appears only in the dataset overview. V2 actually evaluates MultiSocial social-media texts in 22 languages, adding a different domain and four languages marked ca, ga, gd, and et in Table 5. The original MULTITUDE coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds separately fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Base to the multilingual, cross-lingual, family-level, and multilingual per-generator comparisons. V1 includes only mdok as a Qwen-based detector. Existing comparators remain, including the same exclusion of Fast-DetectGPT and Binoculars from the main cross-lingual comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation of news-trained models on MultiSocial and separate fine-tuning of Qwen, mdok, and XLM-R-large on seven additional Slavic source languages. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original Table 1 splits, F1 metrics, English/Spanish/Russian training settings, and balanced three-language sampling remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds domain-shift robustness testing. Appendix D/Table 7 tests whether the Russian-transfer finding extends to other Slavic training languages, beyond redisplaying existing family averages. A new Section 5.1 footnote also reports a qualitative scoring-backbone comparison favoring mGPT-13B. Existing generator-confusion analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1's Computational Resources appendix and v2's Appendix A both specify a single run for each fine-tuned method version. Neither reports confidence intervals, repeated-seed variability, or significance tests. The increased cumulative GPU-hours do not establish additional repetitions.

E6.justification: Retained methods' numerical results match across corresponding main and appendix tables. Substantial new results include Qwen's overall multilingual macro F1 of 0.93, additional Slavic-source outcomes, and MultiSocial scores of 0.24 for OTBDetector, 0.21 for XLM-R-large, 0.20 for mdok, and 0.19 for Qwen. These are added comparisons and test conditions. Table 2 averages also change because Qwen joins the method set.

M1.justification: The existing attribution adaptations remain unchanged, including XLM-RoBERTa-based OTBDetector and QLoRA-based mdok. The separately fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Base expands the comparison set; additional descriptions of mdok and statistical features do not establish revisions to existing procedures.

P1.justification: Most of the main narrative and section order are retained. V2 edits wording, clarifies the RQ2 exposition, rewrites parts of the conclusion, introduces numbered headings, and reorganizes the technical appendix into Appendices A–E. Limitations and Ethical Considerations receive separate sections, without a wholesale rewrite of the existing exposition.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reformats typography and page layout, including converting the appendix discussion to two columns. It adds full-width MultiSocial and Slavic-training tables, expands existing tables with Qwen rows, and moves v1's main-text family-level Table 4 to appendix Table 6. The map and confusion-matrix figures are retained, while several captions are shortened.

R1.justification: The cited works and central research positioning remain the same after matching publication updates. For example, Deng et al. (2023) and Miao et al. (2024) refer to the same Bayesian-surrogate paper, and MultiSocial's changed year reflects its publication update. These are not additions to the related-work coverage.

T1.justification: The ML-MGT and CL-MGT problem definitions, classification mapping, language-selection assumptions, and training/test language relation are unchanged. Neither version adds proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of generalization, the paper's central concern. MultiSocial testing probes a previously untested domain boundary and reveals poor transfer to social texts, while seven additional Slavic training languages test the broader relevance of the Russian-transfer finding. The standalone Qwen comparator and explicit applicability limits make the conclusions better supported and more informative. These address important validation gaps in v1, although single-run reporting and sparse details for the preliminary domain test remain limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched reliably despite reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds Qwen comparisons, MultiSocial evaluation, and experiments with additional Slavic training languages.

before.justification: V1 reports original multilingual and cross-lingual attribution experiments, including F1 scores, generator-level results, and confusion matrices.

results.title: Authorship Attribution in Multilingual Machine-Generated Texts

C1.justification: V1 presents a complete self-organizing memory architecture built around two cognitive principles and aimed at agent self-evolution. V4 redefines the central contribution as assessing retention utility through prediction error, separating distillation from management, and providing a transferable distillation layer. Third-party compatibility and storage reduction become explicit headline contributions.

C2.justification: V4 adds explanations of episode-level construction efficiency, limited benefits of consolidation on LoCoMo, and dependence of open-domain answers on backbone knowledge. Its new limitations identify simple management/retrieval and case-specific integration as constraints. V1's discussion of a model-dependent performance ceiling and loss of fine-grained assistant details is removed.

D1.justification: V4 adds construction and response pseudocode, management-interface implementations, full pipeline and ablation prompts, answer-generation and judge prompts, and a code-availability link. These substantially improve implementation transparency beyond v1's short reproducibility subsection. The newly supplied prompts document procedures; their disclosure alone does not establish that every prompt changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use LoCoMo's 10 dialogues and 1,540 questions across four categories, plus 500 LongMemEvalS conversations. V4's scalability section retains the earlier long-context evaluation; its additional ablations and manager integrations introduce no new datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds A-MEM and MemoryOS to the LoCoMo accuracy and response-efficiency comparisons in Tables 2 and 4. Full Context, RAG-4096, LangMem, Zep, and Mem0 remain. The added systems also support substantive comparisons of ordinary operation against NEMORI-assisted integration.

E3.justification: V4 evaluates a default 20-message partitioning window, replacing v1's detector with a 25-message buffer cap. New protocols include window lengths from 5 to 40, fixed-chunk and management controls, crossed narrative/raw indexing and retrieval, and third-party input substitution. It adds construction-cost and storage measurements and a Core accuracy metric excluding Temporal Reasoning.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained memory-type and direct-extraction ablations, v4 tests adaptive partitioning, native management, observation-window sensitivity, and narrative versus raw indexing/retrieval. It adds component cost analysis and an open-domain UNO case study. The mentorship example already appeared in v1 and is relocated to Appendix B.1.

E5.justification: V1 Table 1 reports uncertainty terms with every LoCoMo LLM score; the corresponding v4 Table 2 reports only point estimates. Neither version explains repeated-run counts or the meaning of those earlier uncertainty terms. V4's remaining ± expressions describe variation across configurations, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: On a common 0–100 scale, NEMORI's LoCoMo average LLM scores change from 74.4 to 73.0 for gpt-4o-mini and 79.4 to 80.8 for gpt-4.1-mini, accompanying the revised method. Existing baseline means and LongMemEvalS results are retained. V4 adds extensive ablation, cost, and integration results, including 45.3–64.3% storage reductions with temporal-accuracy losses.

M1.justification: V1's per-message, confidence-based boundary detector is replaced by partitioning a filled observation window. V4 adds associative merging of related episodes and management-agnostic context-evocation and consolidation interfaces, including third-party adapters. These substantially change the procedure while retaining prediction-error distillation and dual-memory retrieval.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, methodology narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around distillation and three priors. Research questions and experimental sections are reorganized, the existing temporal example moves to an appendix, and dedicated limitations and appendices are introduced.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. V1's three conceptual/system illustrations are replaced by a consolidated framework figure; v4 adds a taxonomy table, window-sensitivity plot, multiple experimental tables, algorithm displays, and prompt boxes. Retained tables and the retrieval-sensitivity plot are substantially reformatted.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from static RAG versus conversational memory and granularity gaps to a distillation/management/retrieval taxonomy in v4 Table 1. Predictive-coding references such as Rao and Ballard and Clark, and systems including A-MEM, MemoryOS, and LightMem, are added. Much of v1's broader survey and Event Segmentation Theory positioning is removed.

T1.justification: V1's formal sequential boundary-trigger rule is replaced by a disjoint, exhaustive partition of message indices in v4 Section 3.2.1, permitting nonconsecutive messages within an episode. V4 also defines merge and conflict state updates. These are limited changes to mathematical definitions and procedural formalization; neither version presents theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially improves reproducibility and component-level validation: Appendices A and D supply implementation contracts and prompts missing from v1, while new controls test partitioning, management, and retrieval choices. Construction and integration measurements also make efficiency claims more assessable. Removing uncertainty reporting weakens small-margin performance claims, and Table 14's temporal losses qualify claims of preserved integration performance, but the gains in transparency and diagnostic evidence remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NEMORI, with shared prediction-gap distillation, benchmarks, and retained results despite substantial revisions and a changed title. All 12 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v4 are readable, including v4's Appendices A–D; v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–C report original benchmark, ablation, construction-cost, retrieval, and third-party integration results. Attribution of some baseline costs to prior work does not affect the original NEMORI results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original NEMORI results on LoCoMo and LongMemEvalS, component ablations, retrieval sensitivity, and response efficiency.

results.title: What Deserves Memory: Adaptive Memory Distillation for LLM Agents

C1.justification: V2 replaces the unqualified zero-shot and unseen-activity framing with parameter-frozen, training-free inference using labeled references, emphasizing evidence-grounded reasoning. Its contributions also explicitly claim transferable motion priors, and the conclusion extends the state-of-the-art claim to cross-dataset settings.

C2.justification: New Section 7 acknowledges labeled retrieval requirements, limited architectural comparisons, and computational overhead. Section 4.3 explains why retrieval remains target-domain and attributes transfer asymmetries to source-user diversity and data density, including cases where transferred knowledge hurts. These substantially expand applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 adds Qwen checkpoint identifiers, detailed transfer preprocessing and mappings, token-cost information, and clearer UniMTS checkpoint-use documentation. It corrects Opportunity's appendix class count from 12 to 4. Conversely, v1's default retrieval k=100 is omitted. The code URL, feature catalog, prompts, and most implementation details remain.

E1.justification: The eight original datasets remain. V2 adds eight directed transfer scenarios among UCI-HAR, USC-HAD, PAMAP2, WISDM, and MHealth, using shared activities and aligned sensor placements. These extend evaluation from held-out subjects to knowledge transfer across heterogeneous datasets.

E2.justification: The ten baselines in Table 1 and the supervised Moment-S, Moment-L, and Mantis comparators in Table 2 are retained. Added Qwen/GPT rows are ZARA configurations; the transfer experiments extend comparisons using its existing full-knowledge and no-knowledge conditions.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3.2 introduce transfer protocols with shared labels, placement mappings, resampling, and pair-specific evaluation samples while retaining target-domain retrieval. V2 also evaluates Qwen-30B, Qwen-80B, and GPT-4.1-mini backbones. Existing subject splits largely remain; PAMAP2's reported test total changes from 210 to 240, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of whether knowledge transfers across datasets, comparing absent, target-domain, and source-domain knowledge with retrieval held fixed. It also examines additional LLM backbones and token consumption by agent stage. The original component ablations, retrieval-backbone comparisons, and per-class analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify temperature zero and report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Feature means and standard deviations supplied to agents, and cross-validation used for knowledge construction, are retained rather than newly introduced uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds Qwen-30B, Qwen-80B, and GPT results with average macro F1 of 70.2, 73.0, and 77.2, plus transfer results and token measurements. Original Gemini results and matched ablations remain unchanged. Table 1 exchanges Gemini Plot's UCI-HAR accuracy/F1 from 31.7/20.6 to 20.6/31.7 while retaining the old averages, introducing an inconsistency.

M1.justification: Both versions use pairwise feature-importance knowledge, frozen placement-specific embeddings, class-wise retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, and three agent roles executed in four stages. The appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged. Expanded explanations and additional backbone evaluations do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodological motivation, result discussions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around training-free, evidence-grounded reasoning. V2 introduces numbered sections, separates cross-subject and cross-dataset evaluation, organizes the appendix into subsections, and adds limitations and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 are substantially restructured into paired accuracy/F1 columns, and Figure 1 is rearranged. V2 adds the transfer figure and token table, consolidates dataset statistics into another table, and extensively reflows appendix displays and prompt panels. Retained ablation and per-class plots are matched across renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted references on retrieval, agent memory, TableTime, Qwen, LLaSA, and RelCon, while removing the conventional-HAR paragraph and several associated citations. Positioning emphasizes statistical grounding and explains excluded recent comparators, but retains the principal HAR and foundation-model comparison landscape.

T1.justification: V2 removes v1's explicit O(|F|) update-cost assertion for adding an activity. The pairwise knowledge representation and cosine-similarity/RRF mathematics remain equivalent; neither version presents formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the alignment of claims with the actual labeled-support setting and directly tests knowledge transfer and robustness across LLM backbones, addressing important weaknesses in v1's broad zero-shot framing. Explicit limitations and token accounting improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized reporting regressions, including the inconsistent Gemini Plot row and omitted retrieval default, although cross-dataset state-of-the-art wording remains supported only by internal comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZARA and retain matching methods, benchmarks, and results. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds LLM-backbone evaluations, cross-dataset knowledge-transfer results, and measurements of token usage.

before.justification: V1 reports original recognition results on eight HAR datasets, component ablations, retrieval latency measurements, and per-class results.

results.title: ZARA: Training-Free Motion Time-Series Reasoning via Evidence-Grounded LLM Agents

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a lightweight, training-free safeguard using attention-guided safety reflection and sampling. The abstract broadens its explicit effectiveness claim from three attacks and seven safeguards to four attacks and nine safeguards; the introduction also extends the claimed model-family coverage.

C2.justification: v2 interprets high IAS as sufficient but unnecessary for safety, connects utility preservation with reasoning-length consistency, and explains complementary roles and streaming limitations of post-hoc filters. It also qualifies comparison coverage because of unavailable training data and computational limits. These substantially extend the scientific interpretation; the IAS sufficiency wording exceeds what the conditional observational analysis establishes.

D1.justification: v2 specifies last-layer attention, identifies 14B/32B models as quantized, documents IAS-analysis sampling and filtering, and supplies implementation/checkpoint references for added attacks and defenses. GPU hardware and task-time estimates are retained. Exact evaluation subset sizes and random seeds remain unspecified.

E1.justification: AdvBench, SorryBench, MMLU, GPQA Diamond, MATH500, and XSTest are retained. Attack-input scenarios change: automated AutoRAN replaces manually constructed H-CoT attacks, and cipher-based Mousetrap attacks are added. This extends adversarial conditions within the existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RealSafe-R1, SafeKey, SAFEPATH-FT, and SAFEPATH-ZS comparisons, plus Llama Guard 3 and GuardReasoner filtering baselines. Gradient Cuff disappears. PPL remains in a narrower appendix comparison, while SafeDecoding is restricted to the 7B/8B models. These substantially change comparator membership.

E3.justification: v2 replaces the AdvBench Llama Guard classification metric with the proportion receiving GPT-4o harmfulness score 5, retaining mean GPT scores. It adds Phi-4 and Qwen3 model configurations, controlled IAS sampling and NF4-versus-unquantized experiments, and reasoning-length metrics. Its reported decoding policy also extends nucleus decoding beyond utility evaluations; these statements do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine IAS–harmfulness associations, varied instructive/misleading/irrelevant safety phrases, quantization sensitivity, reasoning-length preservation, and combinations with guard filters. A mathematical utility case is added and the failure example is replaced. Existing window, sampling, scaling-factor, decoding, and phrase-component ablations are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Spearman rank-correlation estimation for reasoning lengths and IAS boxplots reporting distributional spread, means, and medians. These extend descriptive statistical reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, attacks, and analyses, while removing detailed QwQ utility, jailbreak, and XSTest results. Retained entries also change: ReasoningGuard's R1-Llama-8B no-attack GPT harmfulness scores change from 1.02/1.00 in v1 Table 10 to 1.40/1.00 in v2 Table 17.
