Changed metrics and incompletely specified subsets prevent interpreting the overall revisions as matched performance gains.

M1.justification: The core attention-sink identification, safety phrase, IAS ranking, and adaptive sampling procedure remain unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates ReasoningGuard combined with Llama Guard 3 or GuardReasoner, adding optional post-generation filtering to the inference pipeline (Appendix D.5.2, Table 15).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative receive broad paragraph-level revisions. v2 reorganizes the appendices around a dedicated IAS analysis, restructures utility and ablation subsections, adds a model-transferability section, and separates limitations and ethical considerations from their earlier locations.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1–2 are reorganized, the radar chart and ablation panels are revised, and tables are restructured with comparator groups and average columns. New IAS boxplots, phrase-example tables, and analysis tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 shifts from a general jailbreak-defense taxonomy to LRM-specific training-based and training-free alignment, positioning ReasoningGuard against closely related SAFEPATH and SafeKey approaches. AutoRAN, GuardReasoner, and additional model references are introduced, while several general defense references are removed.

T1.justification: The attention, sink-selection, IAS, and token-complexity mathematics are substantively retained. Last-layer notation clarifies implementation, and the added Spearman formulas explain a standard evaluation statistic. The new IAS-sufficiency discussion supplies an empirical interpretation, not a formal theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central safety–utility claim through direct comparisons with closely related LRM alignment methods and guard models, addressing an important gap in v1. The IAS, phrase-robustness, quantization, and reasoning-length analyses also test important assumptions behind the method. Reduced QwQ reporting and overstrong IAS-sufficiency wording are drawbacks, and reproducibility remains incomplete, but the more relevant comparisons and targeted validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReasoningGuard. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including algorithms, equations, tables, and figures. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds attention-score analyses, robustness experiments, model-transfer tests, and guard-filter comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original defense, utility, efficiency, ablation, and human-evaluation results in Sections 3–4 and Appendix C.

results.title: ReasoningGuard: Safeguarding Large Reasoning Models with Inference-time Safety Aha Moments

C1.justification: v2 narrows the multi-step conclusion from state-of-the-art to competitive performance, while retaining the principal single-step performance and speed claims. It also explicitly presents the enhanced architecture and broader experimental analysis as contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of component roles, long-caption alignment, scaling, and music-generation applicability. A new limitations section identifies restrictions from 10-second training segments, noisy public data, and the inability to generate intelligible speech; v1 lacks these explicit applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D add listening-test procedures, scaling configurations, dataset statistics, and caption-source details; v2 also specifies SwiGLU and revises training-time information. However, v1's explicit train/test-overlap filtering disclosure disappears, and the large variant is inconsistently described as having 448M versus 480M parameters.

E1.justification: v1 trains on AudioCaps, Clotho, and WavCaps; v2 omits Clotho and adds broader AudioSet coverage, VGGSound, and LP-MusicCaps. Evaluation expands to MusicCaps and a long-caption scenario emphasizing multiple sound events and temporal order.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds IMPACT-Large and ETTA to the reported comparison. Appendix C.3 also introduces FluxMusic and AudioLDM-2-Large as music-generation comparators, substantially broadening comparison methods beyond the retained baselines.

E3.justification: Reported pre-training increases from 200k to 400k iterations, fine-tuning batch size changes from 72 to 32, and the threshold for segmenting long recordings changes from 20 to 10 seconds. Ablation training protocols are revised, and new listening tests and model-scaling experiments introduce additional evaluation settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds CLAP, RoPE, and ConvMLP removal tests, a long-caption dual-encoder listening test, and expanded data/model scaling analyses. Existing curriculum and flow-mixing studies are revised; guidance analysis adds scale 5 but removes the 25-step cases, and the original per-variant GPU-hour comparison disappears.

E5.justification: Tables 2 and 8 introduce human-rating scores with ± terms, whereas v1 reports point estimates only. v2 does not define these uncertainty or dispersion terms, and neither version provides repeated-run or seed-based uncertainty for automatic metrics.

E6.justification: MeanAudio's Table 1 scores change, including one-step FD from 15.40 to 14.30 and 25-step FAD from 1.74 to 2.30. These accompany changed training settings, rather than establishing controlled performance gains. v2 also adds substantial human-rating, architectural, scaling, and music results and replaces existing ablation values.

M1.justification: The MeanFlow objective, integrated guidance, dual-encoder transformer, and two-stage curriculum are retained. v2 newly specifies SwiGLU activations, but v1 does not identify its activations, so this disclosure does not establish a method change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and experimental discussion receive substantial rewriting. Sections become numbered, related work moves to Appendix A, metric explanations move to Appendix B, and the document gains a limitations section and organized supplementary material.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands into a detailed transformer-block diagram, Figure 1 is redrawn, and a listening-interface screenshot is added. Tables expand from four to ten, existing ablation displays are reorganized, and typography and page layout change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting new comparators, datasets, captioning sources, and activation choices, while removing the Clotho reference. The central positioning against distillation remains substantially intact; most existing related-work discussion is relocated to Appendix A.

T1.justification: The flow-matching definitions, MeanFlow identity, derivative expansion, guidance equations, and sampling equations retain their mathematical content. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears in the appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that v1 lacked: human listening tests assess perceived quality and relevance, and component ablations directly test architectural choices. Music/scaling evaluations, more precise multi-step claims, and explicit limitations further strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including undefined ± terms, conflicting parameter counts, removal of the overlap-filtering disclosure, and scaling interpretations that overlook some worsening metrics.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe MeanAudio, with matching methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. v1 ends with references; v2 adds Appendices A–D, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original generation experiments, human evaluations, architectural ablations, scaling experiments, and MusicCaps results in the main text and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original AudioCaps generation results and curriculum, flow-mixing, and guidance ablations in Tables 1–4.

results.title: MeanAudio: Fast and Faithful Text-to-Audio Generation with Mean Flows

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and long-step reasoning claims remain. v2 extends the proof-shortcut finding into a claim that limited answer hints improve process correctness while explicit answers undermine it. It also narrows the auxiliary-annotation novelty claim from the first and only benchmark to the first large benchmark.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes auxiliary-construction awareness from construction capability and offers new explanations for strategy differences and harmful prompting effects, qualifying v1's broadly beneficial account. It adds substantive limitations concerning Zhongkao-level coverage, evaluator costs, and the difference between using supplied constructions and generating them autonomously. These qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds model identifiers and generation settings for the expanded panel, manual annotation and format-verification details, and the 150-problem/three-prompt, character-based leakage-probe description. It also reports releases of translated and perturbed data and specifies licensing. Existing prompts, hardware descriptions, and shared-model parameters are retained; these additions mainly extend documentation.

E1.justification: The 2,186-problem Chinese geometry corpus and 330-problem GeoLaux-mini subset remain. v2 adds evaluation of an English translation of GeoLaux-mini and 159 numerically perturbed problems (Appendices A.2 and F.2), extending language and input conditions within the existing domain.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from 13 to 23 models through 12 additions and removal of InternVL2.5-78B and its MPO variant. Additions include Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.1V, Claude-4/4.5, and InternVL3/3.5 models. Diagnostic comparator panels also change, and v2 Table 2 introduces a four-model evaluator comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces validation against manual review of 1,000 solution instances, reference-free evaluator controls, construction-rate measurement, and PCS conditioned on actually constructing auxiliary lines. It also adds paired translation and numerical-perturbation protocols. Existing one-shot prompts, main dataset assignments, and shared-model generation budgets remain unchanged; the additions do not establish reruns of retained results.

E4.justification: v2 adds evaluator/reference ablations, translation and numerical-perturbation robustness checks, and cases testing alternative solution paths and constructions. It separates multiple-choice from free-response analysis and expands auxiliary-line diagnostics. The first-error-position analysis is removed and replaced by PQS-versus-length analysis. Appendix B adds analytical comparisons of weighting functions and activation parameters, rather than empirical model ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical tests. The new robustness and evaluator tables still report point estimates; statements about insignificant changes do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All 11 shared main-table model rows retain their scores, while added and removed rows change the comparison landscape. Qwen3-VL-32B becomes the leading non-thinking model with PCS 51.9 and PQS 73.6. v2 adds evaluator, translation, perturbation, and construction results, and replaces the leakage table's 2.28–3.77% ROUGE-L figures with 0.01–0.13%. These are expanded or replaced results, not demonstrated same-model performance improvements.

M1.justification: The core dataset-building and solution-scoring pipeline is retained, including the solver/evaluator prompts, o4-mini evaluator, and effective ACS/PCS/PQS calculations. Alternative-path acceptance is clarified rather than established as a changed procedure. Added construction-rate measurements are evaluation diagnostics.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, dataset description, and experimental interpretation. Related work moves into a substantive main-text section, evaluator reliability receives its own treatment, and the appendices are reorganized around dataset details, PQS discussion, and leakage analysis. Dedicated limitations and ethical-considerations sections are added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the document and expands table structures and visual comparisons. Figure 7 separates three problem types, Figure 9 presents simple/complex auxiliary-line PCS deltas, and new evaluator, robustness, function-comparison, and case-study exhibits appear. Existing dataset examples, prompts, and error examples are retained with relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: The benchmark comparison and research positioning are substantially revised. v2 adds discussion of SolidGeo, GeoInt, general mathematical benchmarks, and trajectory evaluation, while removing comparisons such as GeoGen and GeoMath-QA. The blanket claim that earlier benchmarks stop at 11 steps is replaced by more specific coverage comparisons, including GeoSense's reported 16-step maximum, and auxiliary-line novelty is qualified against existing work.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 corrects the weight formula from e^(i/n) to e^(-i/n) and changes the required curvature from concave to convex. This aligns Equation 4 with the negative exponent already present in v1 Equation 5. Appendix B additionally defines alternative weighting functions and develops their mathematical comparison; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 largely asserted the reliability of automated step grading. v2 tests four evaluators against manual review of 1,000 instances and includes reference ablations (Table 2), substantially strengthening support for the benchmark's central measurement. Translation and perturbation tests, direct construction diagnostics, and explicit limitations further improve validity and interpretation. These gains outweigh small new reporting errors, such as Table 6's incorrect signed delta, although uncertainty reporting remains absent and some hint and leakage conclusions remain overconfident.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GeoLaux and its evaluation framework. All 17 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison. Relocated sections and retained exhibits can be matched without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v2 reports evaluations of 23 models and additional original evaluator-validation, language-robustness, numerical-perturbation, and auxiliary-construction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 13 models, auxiliary-line prompting experiments, error analyses, and a leakage assessment.

results.title: GeoLaux: A Benchmark for Evaluating MLLMs’ Geometry Performance on Long-Step Problems Requiring Auxiliary Lines

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the attack-label-free defense claim based on hierarchical encoding and corruption-guided detection. Generalization across attacks and superiority in generalization over supervised baselines were already claimed in v1; new experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning simulated environments and mitigation after intrusion, plus failure conditions involving malicious semantic mimicry and benign reasoning diversity. New discussions explain topology, corruption, backbone, and collusion effects. Appendix H's directional-negative explanation, however, is not reconciled with the unchanged uniform-noise rule in Equation 5.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses exactly three compromised agents, fixed corruption strength alpha=0.8, prompt construction following G-Safeguard, and latency of 0.53 versus 0.56 minutes without versus with BlindGuard. These supplement existing optimizer, hidden-width, and GPU details. The code repository destination is unchanged.

E1.justification: The five benchmarks and original attack/topology coverage remain. v2 substantially broadens tested operating conditions through sacrificial-decoy collusion, defense-aware prompt injection, and attack-free CSQA evaluation in Appendices E.4, E.5, and E.7.

E2.justification: The main comparator set remains G-Safeguard, DOMINANT, PREM, TAM, and No Defense. Table 9 adds Raw SentenceBERT plus Equation 7 as an explicit comparator for assessing the learned encoder's contribution.

E3.justification: v2 adds an explicit PI-to-MA transfer comparison, Qwen3-8B experiments, corruption-strength sweeps, threshold-based remediation, and K=2 testing (Tables 2, 4–6, and 13). These substantially expand the evaluation design. The original backbones and main K=3 rule are retained.

E4.justification: The original neighborhood/global-feature ablation remains. v2 adds corruption-strength sensitivity, threshold and budget studies, complete encoder removal, collusion and adaptive-attack tests, clean-data utility checks, and topology-dependent and failure case analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional results do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises many retained comparisons. For example, BlindGuard's random-topology CSQA PI AUC/ASR@3 changes from 76.89/23.67 to 75.11/30.00, while chain CSQA MA changes from 74.67/12.33 to 73.78/7.00. v2 also adds extensive transfer, robustness, ablation, utility, and timing results. The PDFs do not explain all numerical revisions.

M1.justification: The core encoder, corruption rule, contrastive loss, anomaly scoring, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds an evaluated remediation variant using a 0.5 anomaly-score threshold instead of fixed top-K selection, providing a limited inference extension.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the introduction, rewrites the generalization discussion, numbers sections and subsections, and organizes the expanded appendix analyses. Affiliations and contact details also change. Most methodological prose and the main narrative order remain.

P2.justification: v2 updates Figure 2's example and labels, introduces dedicated displays in Tables 2, 4–10, and 13, and changes typography, spacing, and figure/table placement. This substantially expands and revises the visual presentation; retained displays were matched across relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds contrastive-learning and newer GAD, MAS, and reasoning references, and broadens related-work discussion to intrinsic LLM vulnerabilities. Appendix G makes comparisons with rule-based and output-consensus defenses explicit. The central positioning against supervised G-Safeguard and generic unsupervised GAD remains.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the generic supervised objective in Equation 1 to use cross-entropy. New Appendix C derives computational costs for BlindGuard and G-Safeguard, including BlindGuard's O(Ed + Nd^2 + N^2d) complexity. These are limited mathematical additions and corrections.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the retained defense claim through direct cross-attack comparison, collusion and adaptive attacks, clean-data utility checks, and targeted sensitivity and encoder studies. Concrete failure cases also clarify applicability beyond v1's largely positive account. These gains outweigh documentation weaknesses, including absent uncertainty estimates, overstated uniform superiority around Table 9, and Appendix H's unreconciled explanation of the unchanged corruption rule.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BlindGuard, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison; extraction artifacts were resolved through visual inspection.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative results and additional transfer, collusion, adaptive-attack, ablation, and clean-data evaluations in the main text and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection and defense experiments, including Table 1, scalability results, feature ablations, and additional evaluations in Appendix D.

results.title: BlindGuard: Safeguarding LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems under Unknown Attacks

C1.justification: The central claim of efficient forward-only data valuation remains. v3 emphasizes last-layer gradient approximation and batch scalability and extends its advertised empirical contribution to selecting useful subsets for actual fine-tuning, beyond the identification and detection claims demonstrated in v1.

C2.justification: New limitations identify pretraining as outside direct applicability and acknowledge that data value changes during training (Section 7). v3 also interprets the Hessian-free comparison as support for last-layer valuation and attributes noisy-data baseline failures to convergence or uniqueness assumptions (Appendix A.4).

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds warm-up procedures, LoRA ranks, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, gradient accumulation and GPU counts for the fine-tuning experiments. v3 also documents new data-pool sizes and corruption construction and supplies a GitHub code-access link. Earlier detection settings and licensing information are retained.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original sentence/math, image subject/style and cat–dog tasks. It adds fine-tuning data selection on GSM8K, Noise-Huatuo-Complex-CoT and PMC-Reasoning, with five medical QA and six VLM evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain Hessian-free, DataInf, HyperINF and Emb. New fine-tuning comparisons add base-model and full-data training references, including a PMC full-data row attributed to Huang et al. (2025). These new comparisons use the three existing gradient baselines and exclude Emb.

E3.justification: New protocols select 1%/5% of GSM8K, 5%/10% of Huatuo and 10%/20% of PMC data, with warm-up training, full-parameter fine-tuning and greedy-decoding accuracy evaluation. GSM8K uses test examples for valuation; medical experiments use separate valuation pools and held-out tests. Original detection settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 extends robustness evaluation to fine-tuning selection under corrupted medical reasoning data. It adds clean-data recovery among the top 10% of selected samples (Table 8) and mislabel-ratio sensitivity at 40% and 60% alongside the original 50% (Table 7). Existing prediction-error ablation, model-size analyses and qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: v1 already contains plus/minus values and error bars. v3 explicitly identifies mean and standard deviation in Table 1 and Figure 3 and explains nonzero deviations after rounding. No seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the original Tables 1–2 are retained. New results include 48.3% GSM8K accuracy with 5% selected data and 62.35% mean medical QA accuracy with 10% Huatuo data. On PMC, For-Value leads at 10% selection but trails HyperINF at 20%: 52.67% versus 53.04%. These are newly reported experiments.

M1.justification: The scoring rule, Algorithm 1, batching, vocabulary restriction and averaging over valuation examples already appear in v1. v3 makes the restriction explicit in Equation (2) and clarifies the last-layer gradient interpretation without changing the scoring procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions and method explanations are substantially rewritten around last-layer gradients and batch scalability. Preliminaries move into Appendix B, and the appendices are reorganized into experimental details/results and proofs. Contents, limitations, acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure are added; the title and author block also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds the performance–efficiency overview in Figure 1, fine-tuning Tables 3–5, diagnostic Tables 7–8 and corruption examples in Figure 7. The original complexity table and qualitative figure move into the appendix as Table 6 and Figure 5. Table styling, figure sizing and appendix layout are also substantially revised.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Bae et al. (2024), LAVA by Just et al. (2023), Razin et al. (2024), and literature supporting the new benchmarks. The basic positioning against gradient, Hessian and Shapley approaches remains. Wang's Data Shapley in One Training Run is retained with updated publication metadata.

T1.justification: Theorem 2, Equation (3), explicitly adds an unembedding-dependent term. Related mathematics existed conditionally in v1's proof, but v3's standalone statement omits the matching-input/prefix restriction retained in its derivation. This is a limited formal revision with an unresolved condition; the principal assumptions and most proof equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacks direct evidence that selecting high-value subsets benefits downstream fine-tuning. v3 addresses this important empirical gap through held-out medical evaluations in Tables 4–5, supported by noise analyses, implementation details and explicit limitations. GSM8K's test-informed valuation and the missing condition in revised Theorem 2 qualify the gains, but the new medical evidence substantially strengthens the paper's practical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same For-Value framework. Their text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these results and adds original fine-tuning evaluations, noise-sensitivity measurements and clean-data selection diagnostics in Tables 3–5 and 7–8.

before.justification: v1 reports original influential-data identification, mislabel detection, ablation and runtime results for LLMs and VLMs, including Tables 1–2 and Figures 2–4.

results.title: For-Value: Efficient Forward-Only Data Valuation for finetuning LLMs and VLMs

C1.justification: The central claims remain the introduction of personalized distractor generation, a training-free two-stage MCTS framework, improved personalized distractors, and applicability to group-level generation. V2 broadens the supporting experiments and foregrounds diagnostic validation in its contributions and conclusion, while retaining these scientific claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about sparse histories, reconstructed reasoning being an approximation of actual cognition, and computational feasibility. Appendices D.6 and D.8 explain low compiler-principles/operating-systems accuracy through matching difficulty and discuss incidental errors, noisy histories, and retrieval overload. These substantially expand the earlier interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously unavailable supplementary documentation: seven MCTS algorithms, API version identifiers, baseline and evaluation prompts, dataset statistics and filtering rules, a 15-concept cap, and intermediate-output logging. It also adds a project-page pointer. These are substantial documentation additions, although Algorithm 1 omits incrementing its iteration counter, limiting literal reproducibility.

E1.justification: Student_1361 adds evaluated Python programming, Java programming, compiler principles, and operating-systems domains to the original elementary and discrete mathematics coverage (Tables 4 and 7). Eedi_100, Discrete_40, and the existing MMLU/CEval evaluations remain; those retained benchmarks are not new coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Random, Similarity, Level, Level+Random, Level+Similarity, Mastery, IO, and CoT. The group-level comparison retains D-GEN, O&A, and DiVERT, moving from v1 Table 4 to v2 Table 11. Additional evaluations reuse CoT; no existing comparison replaces or removes a comparator.

E3.justification: The user-study sample increases from 10 to 30 students. New protocols include 20 human assessors with two ratings per output, blinded mechanism judgments covering 30 questions and 90 distractors, and 25 numerical-variant questions across five students. Table 2 also changes average history/test counts from 57/10 to 49/9, but v2 associates the latter with the expanded corpus, so this does not establish resplitting of the retained subsets.

E4.justification: V2 adds human quality evaluation and intermediate-output validation: concept precision/recall, agreement with expert error rationales, and behavioral consistency on isomorphic questions (Section 5.3.4 and Appendix D.7). Existing component ablations and search-iteration analysis remain. Appendix D.4 supplies depth, branching, and reward-weight sensitivity results; v1 referenced such supplementary analyses but did not include them.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2 averages human ratings but provides no uncertainty or inter-rater reliability estimates. Its additional rater counts and blinding concern evaluation design.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 3 and the relocated group-level results are numerically unchanged. V2 adds cross-subject, human-rating, sensitivity, and intermediate-validation results, including Behavioral Match@1 of 0.68. Under the enlarged user-study sample, treatment CEval error rate changes from 0.25 to 0.21, abstention from 0.04 to 0.06, and personalized-distractor selection from 0.35 to 0.40; these are revised results under different sample conditions.

M1.justification: The shared method retains concept extraction, MCTS with terminal nodes, UCT selection, match-plus-plausibility rewards, misconception summarization, and concept-based prediction. Equations 1–5 are unchanged. Appendix C supplies procedural explanations and pseudocode without establishing a revision to the underlying algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method explanations and introduces a more detailed numbered subsection structure. It reorganizes the experimental narrative, moves group-level analysis to Appendix D.5, and adds organized appendices and separate limitations and ethics sections. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reformats the document and adds dataset examples, filtering illustrations, a full-page MCTS walkthrough, prompt panels, and multiple result tables. The group-level table moves to the appendix and gains explicit method-group headings. Existing core figures and tables remain recognizable; the change extends well beyond numbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds option-tracing research by An et al. and Ghosh et al., distinguishing predefined-option prediction from open-ended generation. Appendices add citations and connections to adaptive assessment and noisy behavioral profiling. The central positioning against group-level distractor generation and latent cognitive-diagnosis models remains.

T1.justification: The task notation, reasoning-node definitions, UCT formula, reward formulation, and summarization/prediction equations remain equivalent. Neither PDF presents a theorem or proof. V2's pseudocode and worked search illustration elaborate the existing procedure rather than introduce a new formal result.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens evidence beyond v1's LLM quality scores and small user study through human ratings, expert mechanism checks, behavioral validation, four additional subject domains, and a larger user study. It also makes previously missing methodological details inspectable and states important limitations. Validation samples remain small, uncertainty estimates are absent, and the new pseudocode contains an iteration-counter omission, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching core methods and several identical result tables. However, v1 ends after its references and omits the Appendices 1–4 it cites; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Main-text comparisons are reliable, but some earlier supplementary details cannot be checked.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports expanded subject coverage, human ratings, a 30-student user study, and concept-extraction, mechanism-alignment, and behavioral validation results.

before.justification: V1 reports original personalized and group-level generation experiments, component ablations, search-budget analysis, and a 10-student user study.

results.title: Tailoring Diagnostic Modeling to Individual Learners: Personalized Distractor Generation via MCTS-Guided Reasoning Reconstruction

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims about SIG-guided proactive questioning, two-stage training, benchmark construction, superiority, and OOD generalization. The headline 6.29% and 54.45% gains are unchanged; additional experiments primarily broaden support for these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning cautious over-questioning, adaptive versus rigid clinical questioning protocols, simulator dependence, and computational tradeoffs. Limitations now acknowledge tested open-ended tasks while retaining the need for real clinical validation; population differences are also discussed. Some new interpretations overreach the evidence: Figure 7 does not support uniformly favorable comparisons with GPT-4o-mini.

D1.justification: v2 adds vLLM batching and prompt-logprob details, greedy-first/asynchronous sampling descriptions, stage-specific runtime and data-construction costs, baseline adaptations, evaluation prompts, and clinician annotation procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Hardware reporting remains inconsistent: Appendix F specifies four A800 GPUs, while Appendix H states two.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's exam-derived MedQA/CMB tasks, v2 evaluates MedQA without answer options, CMB-Clin clinical reasoning, Abg-CoQA clarification, and MIMIC-IV outcome/readmission prediction. These additions substantially extend task requirements, domains, and represented clinical data.

E2.justification: The principal Table 1 baselines and HuatuoGPT-o1/OpenBioLLM comparison remain. v2 adds GPT-4o-mini (Figure 7) and an explicit Best-of-5 versus MCTS data-construction comparison (Table 11). The MedQA-to-CMB DPO comparison from v1 Table 2 is no longer reported.

E3.justification: The original benchmark splits, training hyperparameters, and exact-match metric remain largely unchanged. New protocols include LLM-judged free-form answers, BLEU/ROUGE and clarification-action metrics, information-availability sweeps, and blinded ratings by five clinicians using 25 cases per model. Simulator validation changes from 1,000 MedQA interactions to 250 each from MedQA and CMB per simulator.

E4.justification: The original component ablations, Shapley/LOO noise analysis, and arthritis example are retained. v2 adds sensitivity to initial information and reward weights, robustness across simulator backbones and mechanisms, clinical questioning-protocol tests, clinician/LLM question-quality assessments, computational-sensitivity analyses, and two MIMIC-IV case studies.

E5.justification: Bootstrap-based accuracy means and standard deviations remain unchanged as a reporting practice. v2 additionally reports a fitted linear trend and mean-plus-standard-deviation convergence summaries in Figure 9, alongside timing deviations in Tables 9–10. Neither version specifies independent training seeds or repeated-training-run counts.

E6.justification: All ProMed scores in Table 1 remain unchanged, but several baseline values change: LLaMA3.2-3B/CMB Vanilla rises from 1.78 to 33.45 and CoT from 0.84 to 34.79; several DialogT entries also change. Extensive new results include MIMIC-IV accuracies of 69.50% and 76.20%. CMB-to-MedQA is reported as 57.50 in v2 Table 3 versus 52.08 in v1 Table 2, but v2 Figure 6 retains 52.08, preventing interpretation as a clear performance gain.

M1.justification: The SIG reward, two-stage training framework, and optimization objectives are retained. However, Algorithm 1 replaces sequential fact-subset scoring with batched prefix evaluation, a limited procedural revision to Monte Carlo Shapley computation.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten, analysis becomes a dedicated main section, related work moves to Appendix A, and limitations and ethics move into the main document. The appendices are substantially reorganized, including separate algorithm, runtime, evaluation, case-study, and notation sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds information-availability curves, question-quality radar charts, simulator diagrams, sensitivity/runtime plots, comparison tables, and an annotation-interface screenshot. Retained material is also reorganized: v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 6, and the arthritis case changes from Table 8 to Figure 11. Typography and page layout change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds ORPO, TPO, and LearnAT citations to its revised SFT critique, plus references supporting new datasets, clinical interviewing, metrics, and implementation. WebRL, ReTool, and Branzei's cooperative-game-theory reference disappear. The central positioning against prompting, dialogue SFT, and conventional RL remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds computational-complexity arguments for batched Shapley evaluation and SIG-guided MCTS in Appendices D–E. The reformulated Shapley equation is algebraically equivalent, and the existing reward and optimization mathematics remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow task coverage and limited direct assessment of generated questions through broader clinical/general-domain tests, clinician ratings, and simulator robustness checks. Detailed computational and evaluation documentation further strengthens assessability. Conflicting OOD scores and hardware descriptions, plus overstatement of Figure 7, weaken individual additions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ProMed and its SIG-guided training framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds broader task evaluations, MIMIC-IV prediction, simulator robustness tests, computational measurements, and clinician ratings.

before.justification: v1 reports original MedQA/CMB experiments, cross-dataset evaluations, component ablations, simulator assessments, and Shapley noise-injection results.

results.title: ProMed: Shapley Information Gain Guided Reinforcement Learning for Proactive Medical LLMs

C1.justification: V2 replaces the abstract's broad state-of-the-art assertion with a quantified improvement exceeding 4% on Llama and Qwen, also emphasized in the introduction. The central contribution remains adaptive bandit-guided construction of preference data; no new central method contribution is claimed.

C2.justification: V1 credits random chunking itself with improvements over full-context sampling; v2 instead argues that chunking without UCB is insufficient. V2 develops explanations involving chosen-response quality, selective exploration, and alpha sensitivity, and adds explicit computational, model-scale, and training-context limitations. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix A.5 claims consistently improving rollout performance although Table 6 average F1 falls from 46.44 at T=4 to 45.22 at T=8.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies alpha=1.0, supplies the GLM-4-Plus judging prompt and scoring rubric, and lists dataset licenses. Conversely, it removes the earlier 500-example disclosures for sampling/reward analyses and the explicit answer-containing definition of ground-truth chunks. Existing training-framework, hardware, seed, and future code/data-release information is retained.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix A.6 adds HotPotWikiQA-mixup from LV-Eval at 16k, 32k, 64k, and 128k context lengths, extending coverage within long-context QA. The original training data and five evaluation tasks remain. FakebookQA becomes En.QA, with matching sample counts, context statistics, and retained scores.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 newly evaluates Logo-PO, previously only discussed, and LongMab-SFT, trained on the proposed method's chosen responses. Diagnostic comparisons also replace Initial-Dist and Final-Dist with no-initialization and separate chosen/rejected no-UCB controls. Random-Dist corresponds to the retained random-chunk strategy called w/o UCB.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B evaluations, context-length-stratified LV-Eval testing, and GLM-4-Plus judgments using four three-point quality scales. New experiments vary rollout budgets and the exploration coefficient. The previously stated main training settings remain unchanged; the newly disclosed default alpha is documentation, not evidence of a changed original setting.

E4.justification: V2 adds initialization removal, separate chosen/rejected sampling ablations, judged chunk quality, selection-frequency analysis, chosen-response quality, and rollout-count/alpha sensitivity studies. Initial-Dist and Final-Dist analyses and mean response-similarity comparisons disappear. The reward-design experiment, K sensitivity curves, and Lago District case study are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions describe common inference seeds and a training seed typically set to 42. Neither adds repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Response-similarity variance remains a diversity measure rather than run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All retained main comparison rows are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds extensive baseline, ablation, sensitivity, backbone, and LV-Eval results. The corresponding random-chunk variant's average F1 changes from 44.93 to 44.19 for Llama and 40.97 to 38.76 for Qwen, without an explained setting change. Newly reported LongMab average F1 scores include 45.84 on Qwen2.5-14B, 46.82 on Qwen3-8B, and 26.28 on LV-Eval. Fixed-distribution results and mean-similarity entries are removed.

M1.justification: The probing, UCB selection, reward updates, and DPO workflow remain intact. However, v1 uses answer-extracted SubEM for preference ranking in Eq. 3 but full-response SubEM for rollouts in Eq. 11; v2 uses full-response scoring throughout via Eq. 4. The PDFs do not establish whether this corrects an inconsistent description or changes preference-pair selection.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodological explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. K sensitivity moves into the ablation section and expanded appendix, while Section 5.3 is reorganized around mechanisms. The framework is renamed LongMab, and the author list and affiliations change.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reformats the document and redesigns Figures 3–4 into chunk-quality, selection-frequency, and preference-quality displays. Prompt boxes are enlarged and restyled, captions expanded, and numerous sensitivity/generalization tables added. Dataset statistics and retained K curves move to the appendix; the earlier case study is reformatted rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 adds bandit foundations and related methods, including Auer et al., Komiyama et al., ClusterUCB, and LongPO, while removing several compression and dynamic-chunking references. Probe initialization is more explicitly attributed to prior work. The central positioning against static relevance-based sampling remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: V2 revises the written preference-reward definition to full-response SubEM, eliminating the disagreement between v1 Eqs. 3 and 11. It also makes context conditioning explicit in the DPO equation. The substantive formal change is limited to reward-definition consistency; UCB scoring and updates remain unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 closes important validation gaps by evaluating the chunk-based Logo-PO competitor and a matched-data SFT control, then testing initialization/UCB contributions and transfer across models and context lengths. These comparisons substantially strengthen attribution and applicability of the retained main results. Removed fixed-distribution diagnostics, omitted sample counts, and overstated rollout trends are meaningful reporting costs, but they do not outweigh the stronger validation and explicit applicability limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core methods and original main results. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite renaming and restructuring.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, component and sensitivity experiments, additional backbones, and LV-Eval results.

before.justification: V1 reports original preference-training evaluations on Llama and Qwen, component ablations, sampling analyses, and appendix reward-design experiments.

results.title: Chunks as Arms: Multi-Armed Bandit-Guided Sampling for Long-Context LLM Preference Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims remain a unified survey and taxonomy of 134 papers, a synthesis of 300 metrics, and a research agenda. V2 refines the taxonomy from four dimensions to three independent facets, treating LLM integration as a complementary analysis while retaining its coverage.

C2.justification: V2 adds practical distinctions between core and contextual evaluation dimensions, detailed metric limitations in Table 9, and substantive discussion of multimodal evidence and hybrid attribution. Its new Limitations section addresses search coverage, annotation subjectivity, English-language selection and restricted visibility of proprietary research.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: initial retrieval and deduplication counts, search-string selection details, the sensitivity query, publication-date conventions, and all 134 paper annotations in Table 7. Appendix A adds BSD 3-Clause licensing information for the repository already linked in v1.

E1.justification: The main survey retains 134 studies under the same inclusion scope, with 16 identified tasks, 231 datasets and 11 benchmarks. V2's expanded dataset table documents more of that inventory. The additional search tests coverage within the same research field.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates baselines against a proposed system. V2 expands the inventory and discussion of evaluation frameworks, but these are surveyed resources rather than newly evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: V1 Section 3.2 states that both authors independently screened all titles and abstracts; v2 Appendix B.1 reports divided screening with an independent check on 50 studies. V2 also adds an expanded-query sensitivity protocol on ACL Anthology and arXiv. These substantially revise the reported validation design without establishing that the original screening was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's aggregate distributions, v2 adds search-coverage sensitivity analysis and extensive task-specific and temporal analyses of attribution approaches, citation characteristics and evaluation practices. Appendices D–E and Figures 7, 8 and 11 investigate relationships and trends absent from v1.

E5.justification: V2 introduces statistical reliability reporting absent from v1: Krippendorff's alpha for screening 50 studies and annotating 30 publications. Appendix B specifies label-frequency filtering and macro-averaging; Table 4 reports agreement from 0.73 to 1.00. Agreement for parametric attribution could not be estimated because the sample contained no such studies.

E6.justification: Figure 2 changes the 2023/2024 publication counts from 16/106 to 28/96 and reported growth from 6.6-fold to 3.4-fold; v2 documents dating studies by their earliest available versions. V2 also reports five additional relevant sensitivity-search papers, new task/time breakdowns, individual paper annotations, and 19 frameworks instead of 17, adding Attributed Information Retrieval and Attribution Bias.

M1.justification: Neither version proposes a generation algorithm or model. The seven surveyed attribution approaches and training/prompting strategies remain; their expanded descriptions and the separate treatment of LLM integration do not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten around concise descriptions and takeaway boxes. Methodology and detailed analyses move into organized appendices, LLM integration becomes a separate section, and evaluation guidelines and a dedicated limitations discussion reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the taxonomy and adds a PRISMA diagram, task-conditioned charts, an evidence-level timeline and citation-style illustrations. New tables provide guidelines, agreement statistics, paper annotations and metric limitations. Existing figures and tables are also relocated or expanded; the evaluation-metric overview is retained.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands citations and comparative discussion of attribution methods and evaluation metrics in Appendices D–E. It adds positioning relative to AI-generated plagiarism detection, cites faceted-classification and PRISMA foundations, and incorporates previously uncited work such as Pride et al. and Wallat et al. Publication-version updates alone are not counted.

T1.justification: Neither version develops mathematical theory, formal assumptions, theorems or proofs. V2's faceted-taxonomy rationale and expanded descriptions of existing evaluation metrics remain conceptual and explanatory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the survey's transparency and practical usefulness. Search-sensitivity checks, agreement measurements and complete paper annotations address v1's lack of reported validation evidence, while Tables 1 and 9 provide actionable evaluation guidance and limitations. Some inconsistencies remain: Section 3.2.5 reverses the single/multiple-citation examples relative to v1 and v2's own Table 7. These local problems do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological documentation and critical synthesis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same systematic survey. Their main texts, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated into v2's expanded appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original literature-analysis results and adds search-sensitivity findings, inter-annotator agreement measurements, and task-specific and temporal analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original quantitative analysis of its annotated literature corpus, including publication trends and distributions of attribution approaches, citation styles, tasks and evaluation resources.

results.title: Attribution, Citation, and Quotation: A Survey of Evidence-based Text Generation with Large Language Models

C1.justification: v1 presents a proposed paraphrasing method and its translation gains as a headline contribution. v2 replaces that contribution with a reusable evaluation framework and analyses claiming degradation primarily originates from VMWEs rather than general sentence difficulty. Paraphrasing remains in the appendix, and the limitations explicitly disclaim proposing a new improvement method.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of error localization and controlled associations, including stronger causal language. It explains WMT anomalies through sparse sampling, cautions about small GPT samples and qualifies rankings conditioned on excluding invalid outputs. New limitations address reliance on QE, English-source coverage and omitted language phenomena.

D1.justification: v2 reports releasing code and an evaluation framework and supplies a repository link. Appendix A newly identifies model checkpoints, sizes and hardware comprising eight RTX 6000 Ada GPUs; Appendix M provides the GPT translation prompt. These improve documentation without establishing changes to previously unspecified model configurations.

E1.justification: The same EPIE, MAGPIE, Tu–Roth, BNC and WMT data, three VMWE categories and seven English-to-target directions remain represented. Both versions actually display WMT comparisons for Czech, German, Russian and Chinese. New experiments reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.1 as direct translators compared with Google Translate on a sampled subset (Tables 4 and 8). This is a targeted extension; the eight primary translation systems and four extraction-model comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported EPIE sampling changes from 1,182 to 1,000 sentences, and the VPC split changes from 876/472 to 878/470. v2 adds a 100-sentence-per-category GPT comparison and pooled regression over 305,428 outputs. Model rankings change from separate categories over four languages to aggregation across categories and seven languages. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds aligned error-span localization, regression controls, readability analysis and investigation of sparse 2018 WMT human assessments (Section 6; Appendices D, K and N). Existing paraphrasing and ten error examples are retained. The Google Translate screenshot case study is removed, while a new LVC example is added.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates, v2 reports regression standard errors, significance thresholds and model fit statistics, plus Pearson correlations and fitted slopes. This introduces substantive statistical analysis. Appendix G mentions optional bootstrap estimation without establishing its use; no additional repeated runs or seeds are documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds overlap, regression, readability and GPT results; Table 3 reports VMWE coefficients of -0.0813 for xCOMET and +0.9954 for MetricX. Heatmap values also change alongside revised sampling, including Madlad's VID en-zh MetricX gap from 1.90 to 1.96. GPT-4o accuracy, precision and recall entries disappear. The WMT heatmap and all four detailed paraphrasing tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: The heuristic-plus-GPT-4o extraction pipeline and Llama-3.3-70B paraphrasing procedure remain intact, including their prompts. Paraphrasing moves to Appendix O and is repositioned, but its actual procedure is unchanged. The new diagnostic analyses do not revise these methods.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning; results and analysis become separate sections; paraphrasing, rankings and qualitative discussion move to appendices. New takeaway paragraphs, limitations and acknowledgments further reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds an opening illustration, additional-language heatmaps, correlation plots and analysis tables, and removes seven translation screenshots. Category-specific ranking panels become aggregate charts, and the GPT-4o table is reduced to F1 scores. The WMT heatmap caption also corrects the subtraction direction.

R1.justification: Appendix O recasts paraphrasing as an existing strategy, explicitly crediting Castaldo and Monti (2024) and Donthi et al. (2025), substantially revising the positioning of v1's claimed contribution. New citations support difficulty controls, SimAlign and WordNet. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained references are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: Section 6.2 adds an explicit additive regression model and definitions of its VMWE indicator and normalized difficulty predictors. This is a limited formal model specification, without new theorems or proofs. The retained paraphrasing score definitions remain equivalent; the DA normalization formula merely explains the existing procedure.

improvement.justification: The new localization analyses, difficulty controls and modern LLM comparisons substantially strengthen v1's largely aggregate evidence. Corrected paraphrasing attribution, explicit limitations and much fuller reproducibility information provide additional substantial gains. These outweigh remaining weaknesses: observational controls do not establish the asserted primary cause, and Table 11's Chinese VID paraphrasing summary reports 1.73 although the corresponding Table 12 values average 1.17.

A1.justification: Both complete 29-page PDFs describe the same research work. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds regression, error-localization, readability and GPT translation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation evaluations, VMWE extraction results, paraphrasing experiments and analyses of WMT human judgments.

results.title: Evaluating the Impact of Verbal Multiword Expressions on Machine Translation

C1.justification: The central claims about high-rank updates, parameter efficiency, and zero inference overhead remain. The conclusion newly claims suitability for hundreds of thousands of task- or user-specific adapters, replacing v1's general future-work statement about applications beyond LLMs.

C2.justification: New Section 7 identifies tensor-contraction training costs, absent low-bit quantization, and remaining tensorization-search requirements. Appendix J adds a tentative explanation linking factor sharing to consistent update subspaces across layers. These materially expand the practical qualifications and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code URL, Kaiming initialization details, hyperparameter candidates, batch size, evaluation frequency, baseline ranks, software versions, and dataset licenses. However, v1's explicit three-epoch commonsense training, 120-example validation set, and checkpoint-selection descriptions disappear.

E1.justification: Both versions use Commonsense170k's eight tasks, ConvAI2's self-persona dialogue setting, and Math10k with AQuA/SVAMP evaluation. The additional experiments use this existing coverage; the personalization discussion introduces no evaluated population or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds MoRA and QuanTA to the commonsense and dialogue comparisons, cited Full FT results to Table 2, and TopLoRA, PiSSA, and DoRA to Appendix L's Table 10. The arithmetic comparison's baseline membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New experimental settings include rank-128 LoRA/HiRA, query-only and value-only adaptation, and layer-specific frozen factors as controls. The principal backbones and metrics remain unchanged. Newly disclosed hyperparameters do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices E, I, and J add analyses of adapter placement, higher LoRA/HiRA ranks, and shared versus layer-specific frozen cores and factors. These substantially extend the original tensorization and identity-initialization studies, which remain present.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging TeRA over five independent runs. v2 additionally introduces Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons and p-values against multiple baselines in Appendix H, adding formal significance analysis. No increase in run count is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline and ablation results, including the TeRAunique averages of 7.74 and 26.59 in Table 8. Table 3 revises the Llama-3-8B LoRA dialogue average from 47.63 to 47.94 and changes its component scores. The main TeRA benchmark scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: TeRA retains the same tensorization, Tucker-like parametrization, shared frozen random factors, trainable diagonal vectors, initialization procedure, and inference-time weight merging. Newly specified initialization details and experimental variants do not establish a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 polishes wording, numbers sections, consolidates LoRA background, moves the elementwise TeRA formula into Appendix B, and organizes new limitations and appendix sections.

P2.justification: v2 changes page format, typography, spacing, and figure placement; expands Figures 1 and 3 and Tables 2 and 3; and adds appendix Tables 5–10. New Figure 7 provides a zoomed display of the high-rank comparison, while Figures 4–6 retain their analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds QuanTA discussion and references covering additional PEFT variants, tensor research, initialization, and statistical testing. The central positioning between high-rank expressivity and vector-based parameter efficiency remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 states three theorems but omits the promised technical appendix. v2 supplies their proofs in Appendices B–D, explicitly assumes nonzero core entries for Theorem 3, and changes its error-bound multiplier from g_max in v1 Eq. (10) to g_max^2 in v2 Eq. (9).

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps through inspectable proofs, broader competitive comparisons, and controlled placement and sharing analyses. Additional implementation information and concrete limitations improve reproducibility and balance. Some training/validation details disappear, and statistical pairing remains underspecified, but the gains in empirical scrutiny and transparency constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TeRA research and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–M. All supplied material supports comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, adapter-placement experiments, and factor-sharing ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original TeRA experiments on commonsense reasoning, personalized dialogue generation, and arithmetic reasoning, alongside tensorization and initialization ablations.

results.title: TeRA: Vector-based Random Tensor Network for High-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central benchmark and shortcut-generation contributions remain. v2 broadens the stated contribution to comparisons across workflow, general-purpose, and specialized GUI agents, explicitly adds exposing shortcut misuse, and frames predefined structural shortcuts as a reference upper bound.

C2.justification: v1's broad finding that weaker models benefit more becomes a qualified account involving nonmonotonic model-size effects and reliable shortcut selection. v2 also discusses specialized-model failures, controlled retrieval, application-version stability, emulator-only evaluation, and evaluator limitations, materially sharpening applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies snapshot resets, isolated test accounts, GPU hardware, intent-accessible ADB endpoints, UI-tree-based RPA, application-keyword retrieval, prompt injection, human-baseline collection, and Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro evaluator roles. These substantially expand implementation disclosure without necessarily establishing changes to existing procedures.

E1.justification: The 139 tasks, 11 applications, and 69-task shortcut-generation subset remain. v2 adds targeted environmental conditions: irrelevant-only shortcut pools on 23 existing cross-app tasks and shortcut testing across at least five versions of each application.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evaluated comparators with Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.5V, UI-TARS-1.5, GUI-Owl, ScaleCUA, and MAI-UI models, including matched MAS variants where supported. Earlier workflow baselines and the shortcut-generation comparator set in Table 3 remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds ground-truth shortcut-selection scoring, a controlled relevant-shortcut removal protocol, and automated-versus-human evaluation on 278 trajectories. The original task and shortcut-generation evaluation designs remain. The advertised seven-to-nine metric count largely consolidates measures already used in v1.

E4.justification: New analyses examine shortcut-selection precision and redundancy, resistance to irrelevant shortcuts, stability across application versions, and automated scoring reliability. These address substantial robustness and measurement-validity questions absent from v1. Earlier difficulty analyses and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly documents three independent human demonstrations per task and selection of their minimum step count for the human baseline (Appendix A.5). This adds replication and aggregation information without establishing increased runs. Neither version reports agent seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive model, interference, and evaluator results, including MAS-GLM-4.5V's 68.3% overall success rate. Retained results also change: Gemini-2.0-Flash MAS-MobileAgent's cross-app MSRS changes from 0.738 to 0.938 in Table 5, and several difficulty-level values change. Shortcut-generation Table 3 remains unchanged.

M1.justification: The hybrid agents and shortcut-generation procedures are retained; additional model families explicitly use the same shortcut injection strategy. However, v2 specifies the two-stage MAS-Bench-Eval pipeline, while v1 only briefly describes a SPA-Bench adaptation. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the evaluator's procedure or documents its existing implementation.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: detailed metrics move to Appendix A.6, experiments separate setup and protocols, and appendices reorganize implementation, detailed results, and evaluator reliability. The abstract, findings, and interpretations are revised, and limitations become a standalone section.

P2.justification: Table 2 becomes a grouped overall comparison with relative-change annotations, while expanded single-app and cross-app breakdowns appear in Tables 9 and 10. v2 adds task-category, metric-summary, robustness, and reliability tables plus evaluator Figure 7. Existing workflow and failure figures are largely retained or relocated within a reformatted layout.

R1.justification: The cited literature is substantially revised, adding newer general-purpose and specialized GUI-model families while removing much earlier automation, testing, and survey literature. Automated evaluation also shifts from an explicitly attributed SPA-Bench adaptation to a separately named MAS-Bench-Eval protocol. The central hybrid-benchmark positioning remains.

T1.justification: The written action-ratio definition changes from GUI operations divided by shortcut operations (GSAR) to shortcut operations divided by GUI operations (S2GR; v2 Appendix A.6). This corrects a mathematical definition beyond renaming, although many reported ratios remain identical. No theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited baseline coverage and unvalidated automated scoring through broader comparisons, shortcut-misuse tests, and human-validation results. Added implementation details and qualified interpretations strengthen reproducibility and credibility. Reporting inconsistencies temper these gains: v2 Tables 5 and 10 disagree on some cross-app values, and Section 3.7 presents single-app validation figures as covering the full sample. Nevertheless, the added evidence resolves important weaknesses in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAS-Bench and retain identifiable tasks, agents, experiments, and shortcut-generation methods. The main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds model comparisons, shortcut-interference tests, cross-version validation, and automated-evaluator validation against human judgments.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations, shortcut-generation comparisons, difficulty analyses, and failure cases, including Tables 2, 3, 5, and 7.

results.title: MAS-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Shortcut-Augmented Hybrid Mobile GUI Agents

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on a projection-based bias selector outperforming Magnitude and Fisher. v2 centers the analytical and empirical finding that directly tuning value biases generally works better in low-data regimes without post-hoc evaluation, and extends that central claim to bias-free models and PEFT combinations.

C2.justification: v2 introduces expressiveness, softmax sensitivity, and additive-gating interpretations of the value-bias advantage. Its limitations specify standard softmax attention and query/key/value projections, and discuss unresolved superposition and scaling questions. These replace v1's limitation about relating importance scores to performance; its learning-rate and transfer interpretations are also removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and Appendix D's regime sizes, validation sizes, learning rates, batch sizes, training epochs, metrics, sequence limits, and gradient-accumulation information. It also documents classifier use and bias-reparameterization details. These substantially improve documentation without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: Appendix C.7 adds PAWS-X evaluation in English, Chinese, and French, plus CommonsenseQA experiments. These introduce multilingual coverage and a commonsense reasoning domain beyond the retained GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and DROP evaluations.

E2.justification: The main comparator suites remain. v2 adds standalone VeRA and DoRA comparisons on three retained OPT-1.3B tasks (Table 15), and output-projection bias tuning as a comparator to value-bias tuning (Table 7). These are limited additions to the existing comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce LLaMA2-7B, GPT-J-6B, DeepSeek-Coder-Base-1.3B, and XLM-RoBERTa configurations. Added protocols include PAWS-X with 3333 training examples per language and 1998 test examples, plus batch-size controls of 8 versus 16. Appendix D mostly discloses previously unstated settings; it does not establish changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds attention-distribution and attention-sink analyses, Fisher-ranking sensitivity across epochs and batch sizes, value-versus-output bias comparisons, and layer-wise bias-change analysis. Conversely, v1's task-bias averaging experiment and learning-rate/epoch sensitivity findings are removed. The original geometric explanation is partly relocated and redrawn, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports uncertainty only in Table 2 without identifying its run count or meaning. v2 identifies those entries as mean and standard deviation over three seeds, adds extensive repeated-seed reporting, and introduces paired t-tests, including additional five- and ten-seed SST-2 analyses (Appendices C.2-C.3).

E6.justification: Table 5 revises LoRA results: OPT-6.7B SST-2 changes from 50.5 to 95.1, and OPT-1.3B RTE from 50.5 to 73.2, exceeding BEFT's unchanged 71.5. Identical LoRA settings across versions are not established. Numerous new results accompany the extensions, while v1's merging results disappear; Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The projection score and direct value-bias tuning are retained. v2 substantially extends the procedure by injecting trainable biases into bias-free attention modules and introducing bias-update variants using LoRA, VeRA, VeRA1d, DoRA, PiSSA, and BA-LoRA (Sections 3.4 and 3.6; Appendices C.4-C.5).

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, method narrative, extension discussion, conclusion, and limitations are extensively rewritten around direct value-bias tuning. Selection-method details move into Appendix A, the main method section gains an attention-based explanation, and structured Appendices A-D reorganize supporting material.

P2.justification: v2 adds a performance-versus-parameter overview, attention diagrams and distributions, heatmaps, and numerous result and configuration tables. It redraws and relocates the original geometric diagrams into Figure 6, reorders Figure 4's panels, adds colored table highlighting, and adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its positioning through gated attention, attention sinks, representation editing, bias-only steering, and newer PEFT methods. In particular, it interprets BEFT relative to Qiu et al.'s additive gating and adds relevant VeRA, PiSSA, and BA-LoRA literature, beyond v1's emphasis on bias-selection approaches.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds mathematical arguments concerning key-bias cancellation, query-bias sensitivity through the softmax Jacobian, and value-bias additivity. Appendix B.2 derives the relationship between value and output-projection biases. These substantially expand the analysis beyond v1; the original projection-score derivation is retained in Appendix A.3.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's sparse reproducibility and uncertainty reporting through detailed experimental settings, repeated-seed results, and significance tests. Added mechanism analyses and broader comparisons make the central value-bias claim more assessable. The loss of task-merging and learning-rate analyses removes useful evidence, and some new extensions report only relative gains, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BEFT by the same authors, with matching core equations and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-D.

after.justification: The main text and appendices report original experiments, including retained benchmark results and additional bias-free model evaluations, attention analyses, PEFT variants, and multilingual experiments.

before.justification: Sections 3.2-3.5 report original fine-tuning results, runtime measurements, and task-bias merging experiments across GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and DROP.

results.title: BEFT: Bias-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Language Models in Low-Data Regimes

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: prompt-injection fingerprints provide uniqueness and post-processing robustness, unified gray-/black-box verification, and strong detection relative to prior methods. Additional experiments support these claims without substantially redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning tokenizer-independent token preferences, negative-token necessity, partial model reuse, computational practicality, and attacker knowledge. Section 7 newly identifies API restrictions, changing prompt-injection susceptibility, and computational overhead as limitations. Section 5.6 acknowledges full-knowledge evasion, although its broad robustness language insufficiently qualifies the low detection rate under gray-box attacker knowledge.

D1.justification: v3 states that code is publicly available and supplies an access link. Section 5.5 newly documents RTX 6000 and H200 hardware and construction/verification costs, including approximately 60 GPU-hours for 300 Llama fingerprints, 14-second gray-box verification, and 28-minute black-box verification. These substantially expand access and resource information; original hyperparameter and word-category disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds descendant populations of GPT-OSS-20B and Phi-4-14B, 70 merged Meta-Llama-3-8B variants, and adaptive-evasion scenarios (Sections 5.4, 5.6, and Appendix A.5). Coverage therefore expands to additional model families, partial model reuse, and deliberate fingerprint evasion. The original populations are retained.

E2.justification: v3 Table 7 adds TRAP, LLMmap, IPGuard, and LLMPrint-CA comparisons for Mistral-7B-v0.3, which previously had only LLMPrint results. The original Meta-Llama-3-8B comparator set and results remain unchanged in v1 Table 5 and v3 Table 4.

E3.justification: New protocols include ROC-AUC evaluation, shared-vocabulary controls requiring single-token words under both tokenizers, GCG-iteration sweeps, larger-model configurations, and knowledge-specific adaptive attacks targeting previously detected suspects. Original default settings and calibration models are retained. The introduction's correction from 233 to 230 quantized models matches the unchanged model-count table and does not establish sample removal.

E4.justification: Sections 5.4–5.6 and Appendix A.5 add substantive tests of tokenizer confounding, negative-token necessity, optimization-budget sensitivity, fingerprint distinctiveness, partial model reuse, and adaptive evasion. The original failure analysis, detector tests, prompt/token-selection ablations, and Figure 2 sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 13 newly reports Hamming-distance means, standard deviations, medians, and quartiles across suspect models. These describe variation across models rather than repeated-run uncertainty. Gaussian threshold calibration remains unchanged, and neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original numerical result tables and Figure 2 are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. These include ROC-AUC values of 0.938–0.994, Mistral baseline comparisons, larger-model and tokenizer-control results, detection of 64/70 merged models, and adaptive-attack TPRs of 0, 0.167, and 0.967 under white-, gray-, and black-box attacker knowledge. These are additional evaluations, not demonstrated improvements under unchanged conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 changes gray-box scores from log probabilities to probabilities while retaining zero for tokens absent from the top-k list. This changes the stated decision rule when only one target token is returned, correcting an ordering inconsistency. Fingerprint construction, losses, and black-box verification remain unchanged; implementation changes or reruns are not established.

P1.justification: Most original prose and section ordering are retained, with localized editing, paragraph splitting, and terminology corrections. New experimental and limitations subsections, acknowledgements, author contact information, and an appendix LLM-use declaration extend the structure without extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.
