P2.justification: The document changes throughout from single-column to two-column layout, with much denser tables and abbreviated Table 1 headers. Dataset counts, failure-analysis results, and the top-20 comparison move to the appendix. Six new tables are added, while both original figures retain their content and are resized or repositioned.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Phi-4 technical report and GPT-OSS model card citations for the new evaluations. The provenance-detection literature, comparator positioning, and claimed novelty relative to prior approaches remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 revises the mathematical definition of gray-box scores so that zero-filled missing tokens are compared with probabilities instead of negative log probabilities. Because missing-token values remain zero, this is mathematically consequential. Equations 1–3, bitwise accuracy, the Gaussian assumption, and threshold formulas are retained; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses substantial validation gaps through tokenizer and single-token controls, partial-reuse tests, and adaptive attacks, while adding practical cost information, code access, and a correction to the top-k rule. These improve the paper's evidential basis and reproducibility. The attack results expose important failures, and their optimistic interpretation and limited fine-tuning details remain weaknesses, but the added evidence and transparency provide a clear substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLMPrint and retain matching methods and original experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, figures, and tables, support comparison despite substantial reformatting and table relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds larger-model evaluations, tokenizer controls, model-merging tests, adaptive attacks, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original provenance-detection experiments, baseline comparisons, failure analyses, and ablations across five base models and their post-processed variants.

results.title: Fingerprinting LLMs via Prompt Injection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: training-free adaptive MCTS planning, strong multi-attribute control across models and domains, and preserved summary quality. The added comparisons support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the matched-generation results as evidence for structured planning and sequential refinement (Section 5), and adds a beam-search rationale in Appendix B. It also softens the limitation discussion by removing the explicit limited-scalability warning while retaining computational expense and suggesting approximation strategies.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies beam size 3, temperature 1.0, top_k 50, and top_p 1.0, and documents generation-count matching for the new controls. Hardware, existing search hyperparameters, Algorithm 1, and detailed prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same attributes on MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, and DialogSum, covering meetings, news, and everyday dialogue. The added comparisons use retained datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds Joint-iterative and Random sequential as evaluated 70B comparators on both MACSum datasets (Section 3.2; Tables 1–2). These introduce a substantively stronger comparison class that controls generation effort; all existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: The new comparisons match generation counts to PACO's eight simulations and select the best-controlled candidate (Section 3.2; Appendix B). This adds a focused experimental control. Retained metrics and search limits are unchanged; beam-search settings are newly disclosed rather than explicitly revised.

E4.justification: The added controlled comparisons examine whether gains reflect structured planning rather than additional attempts, and whether sequential adjustment helps relative to joint revision. Existing value-function ablations, control-pattern analyses, and Appendix D's attribute-weight sensitivity study are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-evaluation seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added generation-budget information describes candidate-search effort, not statistical replication or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add substantive results against the new controls while retaining existing numerical results. On MACSumDial, length MAD is 11.19 for Joint-iterative and 11.16 for Random sequential, versus PACO's unchanged 7.63; on MACSumDoc, the corresponding values are 7.15, 6.62, and 4.81. PACO leads these controls on deterministic attributes, but not topic alignment.

M1.justification: PACO retains its summary-level nodes, single-attribute actions, PUCT search, rewards, and final-summary selection procedure. Algorithm 1 and the appendix prompts are unchanged. Heuristic scoring moves into a variants subsection; the newly disclosed decoding settings do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: v2 presents PACO before the comparison methods, introduces Problem formulation and MCTS design subsections, and groups self-planning and heuristic scoring under Methods Variants. It also revises selected explanations, affiliations, and acknowledgments, while retaining most prose and the broader document structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 group results by backbone, highlight PACO rows, and change bolding to comparisons within each backbone; Tables 1–2 also accommodate the new comparators. Appendix tables receive related formatting changes, and figures undergo sizing or caption adjustments. The existing plots and illustrated findings are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Retkowski and Waibel (2025) and Gu et al. (2025) to the single-attribute control discussion. PACO's research positioning remains stable; publication updates for Lee et al. and Ryu et al. concern already cited works.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and search equations retain their substance. The displayed heuristic-probability equation becomes an equivalent prose definition in Section 3.3; equation renumbering and leaf-index notation cleanup introduce no new mathematical reasoning or proof.

improvement.justification: The equal-generation controls address an important weakness in v1: its comparisons did not isolate structured planning from additional generation attempts. PACO's deterministic-attribute advantage over both new controls on both MACSum datasets substantially strengthens validation of the central contribution. Appendix B also improves reproducibility. Generation matching does not establish equal runtime, and the scalability warning is softened, but these qualifications do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PACO and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–H. Their content can be reliably matched despite section reorganization and added comparisons.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluations of two generation-budget-matched comparison methods in Tables 1–2.

before.justification: v1 reports original summarization experiments, value-function ablations, attribute-weight sensitivity results, and runtime measurements in Tables 1–6.

results.title: Adaptive Planning for Multi-Attribute Controllable Summarization with Monte Carlo Tree Search

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about uneven instruction degradation, dependence on model/policy/order, system-prompt leakage, and mitigation through whitelisting and fair eviction. Listing the evaluated methods and models in the revised abstract makes existing coverage explicit without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Sections 2.3 and 8 explicitly delimit offline compression and discuss instruction-span and fairness assumptions. Appendices I, J, and N add long-context failure conditions, policy-specific mechanism hypotheses, and automation discussion. Section 4 also changes flipped-order defense eviction from 'less frequently' to 'more frequently' despite retaining the corresponding keep-rate curves, introducing a local inconsistency.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project repository link, the LongBench defense template, complete judge prompts, runtime hardware and precision details, batch size, query count, generation limit, and span-matching explanations. These substantially expand reproducibility information. One new identifier remains inconsistent: Appendix L names Gemma 4 32B, whereas its reference names 31B.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained modified IFEval coverage, v2 adds LongBench TREC question classification with protected contexts spanning 1,000–4,000 words (Appendix I). This introduces substantially longer inputs and a distinct task. It also reports exploratory findings for SAMSum and TriviaQA, although detailed results focus on TREC.

E2.justification: The matched IFEval and mitigation comparisons retain StreamingLLM, H2O, K-Norm, SnapKV, and TOVA. The new LongBench experiments use existing methods from this pool. Gemma serves as an evaluator, while the interpolation settings are variants of the proposed approach.

E3.justification: v2 introduces combined accuracy/leakage scoring, parameter sweeps with Pareto-frontier evaluation, LongBench length buckets and a different defense template, LLM leakage-severity scoring, and controlled timing over 500 queries. These are new evaluation protocols. The model label also changes from Llama3.1 8B to Llama3 8B, without establishing a checkpoint replacement or rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine partial debiasing and its trade-offs (Appendix H), context-length sensitivity (I), leakage under a semantic LLM judge (L), and retention differences across layers (M). The original instruction-order, whitelisting, and fair-eviction analyses remain after renumbering.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 introduce ± values, and Figures 23–24 introduce shaded runtime bands. Neither reporting practice appears in v1. However, v2 does not define these dispersion or uncertainty statistics or provide a repeated-run or seed protocol.

E6.justification: v2 adds aggregate scores, Pareto frequencies, long-context, runtime, judge-based, and per-layer outcomes, and extends the normal-order fair-eviction curves through r=0.9. Newly reported Table 3 gives 75% average Pareto optimality for fair StreamingLLM versus 45% for default. Table 2 includes a negative mean improvement of -0.0068 for fair K-Norm on Qwen2 over r=0.1–0.7.

M1.justification: Appendix G adds eviction debiasing through a parameter that interpolates between default and fair token budgets. This is a limited extension: whitelisting, proportional fair eviction, and policy-specific scoring remain substantially unchanged from v1 Section 5 and Appendix E, now Appendix F.

P1.justification: v2 makes numerous local prose edits, standardizes terminology such as 'fair eviction' and 'difficulty,' moves the policy taxonomy to Appendix A, and adds dedicated evaluation, limitations, and ethics sections. The existing pitfall-to-mitigation narrative and most retained exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. Figure 1 is rearranged vertically, v1 Figures 2–3 become panels of v2 Figure 2, and existing plots are redistributed. Four tables and new Pareto, long-context, runtime, judge, and layer-heatmap displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LongBench, Raccoon, Pareto optimality, and Gemma, and removes Zhang et al. (2024), 'A First Look at GPT Apps.' The original KV-compression taxonomy and broad research positioning remain, with the taxonomy relocated to Appendix A.

T1.justification: Section 6 defines a new combined improvement score, and Appendix G formally defines interpolation between default and fair retention budgets. The original fairness definitions and policy-specific mathematical descriptions are retained. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's IFEval and ROUGE-L evidence through long-context tests, semantic leakage evaluation, debiasing sensitivity analyses, and measured runtime costs. Explicit offline limitations and documented failure cases better establish applicability, while added access and protocol details improve reproducibility. Undefined uncertainty statistics, inconsistent judge identification, and the flipped-order wording error limit parts of the revision, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core experiments, methods, and figures. The main text and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original debiasing, LongBench, runtime, LLM-judge, and per-layer results.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction-following, leakage, token-retention, and mitigation experiments in Sections 3–5 and Appendix D.

results.title: The Pitfalls of KV Cache Compression

C1.justification: The central contribution remains proactive token-level self-reflection through transient hidden-state correction. V2 adds an explicit contribution claim about gains over strong baselines with lower latency overhead and broadens the conclusion to general reasoning and code generation. It removes the abstract's specific Cons@5 improvement and replaces the conclusion's approximately 50% overhead claim with qualitative wording.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning hidden-state and gradient access, imperfect critical-position selection, and model/task-dependent hyperparameter tuning. These qualify the retained plug-and-play applicability claims. The principal interpretations of critical tokens, contextual fidelity, self-consistency, and exploration remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds GPQA and EvalPlus prompts. Conversely, v2 removes v1 Appendix B.2's practical optimization, stopping, numerical-stability, and diagnostic guidance, together with the dedicated reproducibility statement. Core hardware and hyperparameter disclosures remain, and the same code URL is retained as a footnote; no changed repository availability is established.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluations on GPQA for general reasoning and EvalPlus for code generation, substantially extending the mathematical-task coverage. AIME2024/2025, HMMT2025, AMC, and MATH500 remain; MATH500 was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: V1 Table 2 compares the base models with SRGen and explicitly excludes head-to-head post-hoc reflection comparisons in Appendix D. V2 adds Self-Refine to Table 2 and evaluates MI-Peak and SLOT in the accuracy and efficiency comparisons of Tables 3–4. SLOT already appeared in v1's combination experiment, but its additional comparisons are new.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 replaces the full-AIME2024 latency-versus-iterations experiment with MATH500 workload scaling and a 100-problem comparison reporting runtime, tokens, and peak memory. V2 also adds greedy comparisons involving Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. The principal sampling temperature, top-p, generation limits, and five-run accuracy aggregation remain unchanged; the runtime results therefore do not demonstrate a same-setting speedup across versions.

E4.justification: V2 extends the voting analysis from AMC to AMC and MATH500, and replaces the single aggregated critical-token analysis with distributions for two models on MATH500 and GPQA. The old latency/activation sweep disappears, and the lambda-sensitivity plot changes. Most hyperparameter analyses, loss-dynamics plots, and both case studies are retained, with substantial relocation.

E5.justification: Five-run accuracy averaging remains, but v2 removes v1's reproducibility statement mentioning fixed random seeds in the companion artifact. This reduces seed documentation without establishing fewer runs or changed seed use. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests for the main accuracy results.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, comparator, and resource-cost results and removes v1 Table 2's detailed Cons@5 and Pass@5 results. Matched five-run accuracy entries also change: Distill-Qwen-7B on HMMT2025 changes from 18.0 to 19.3, and Distill-Llama-8B on AIME2025 from 32.7 to 36.0. Voting and lambda-ablation curves are revised, while the SLOT-combination results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core dynamic trigger, corrective vector, hybrid loss, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. However, v1 Appendix B.2's optional online adaptive-lambda procedure is omitted in v2, removing an explicitly described procedural variant. This does not establish a change to the algorithm used in the main experiments.

P1.justification: The introduction gains an explicit contribution list, experimental discussion is extensively rewritten, hyperparameter ablations move to Appendix G, and critical-token analysis moves into Section 5.6. Practical guidance, baseline-scope discussion, and the reproducibility statement disappear, while limitations are added and ethics text is rewritten. V2 also contains an empty 'More Results' appendix heading and an unfinished sentence in Section 5.5.

P2.justification: V2 switches to two columns, restructures Tables 1–2, adds comparison Tables 3–4, and substantially revises the efficiency, voting, critical-token, and ablation displays. Retained figures and case studies are resized and relocated. Figure 1's three loss-equation boxes become blank in v2, although the corresponding equations remain in the main text.

R1.justification: V2 adds the GPQA and EvalPlus references, Rein et al. and Liu et al., while retaining the related-work taxonomy and most citations. Removing the baseline-exclusion discussion and adding direct comparisons shifts some positioning toward empirical competitiveness, but the claimed distinction from post-hoc refinement and sample-level optimization remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, its assumptions and proof, the Lagrangian correspondence, and the joint-descent lemma are retained after Appendix B.1 becomes C.1. A localized mathematical correction appears in Appendix I: the displayed sine-power derivation replaces an inappropriately invoked cosine-sum identity with the sine-difference identity actually needed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's explicit avoidance of direct reflection-baseline comparisons by adding Self-Refine, MI-Peak, and broader SLOT comparisons with measured resource costs. GPQA/EvalPlus evaluations and concrete deployment limitations also strengthen the evidence for applicability. Removing the detailed Cons@5/Pass@5 results and practical guidance, plus unfinished text and blank diagram labels, are drawbacks. Nevertheless, the new comparisons resolve an important evidential gap and provide a substantially stronger basis for assessing SRGen's advantages and tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRGen work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization and layout changes.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds general-reasoning, code-generation, and comparative accuracy and efficiency results.

before.justification: V1 reports original mathematical-reasoning evaluations, latency measurements, hyperparameter ablations, token analyses, and generation case studies.

results.title: Self-Reflective Generation at Test Time

C1.justification: The central contributions remain history-aware repair, Edge Impact scoring and MANGO refinement. v2 softens the dataset claim from eliminating structural conflicts to removing many inconsistencies, and foregrounds a natural-text recall benefit with explicit over-generation caveats instead of v1's broadly stated correctness and robustness benefit.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the simple component-synergy narrative with model-dependent recommendations and explanations of high-density failures. It adds substantial discussion of conflict reduction versus structural preservation, literary recall versus over-generation, limited single-novel validation and absent theoretical guarantees. The five-edge scoring correlation is explicitly qualified as a sanity check.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-and-experimental-data repository pointer, graph-generation and error-injection instructions, paragraph-level literary processing, expert ground-truth annotation details and the model-access proxy. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although precise discretization and elastic-optimization settings remain unspecified. The original six cleanup operations and edge-removal totals are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates MANGO interactive-fiction mapping. v2 retains that coverage and adds controlled synthetic error scenarios, procedurally generated TextWorld environments and mapping from Chapters 16–17 of Dream of the Red Chamber, substantially extending input conditions and domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds heuristic_remove and heuristic_modify as evaluated non-LLM comparators in the MANGO comparison. It also omits the VC-only comparator from that experiment, although VC-only remains in the synthetic ablation. These changes materially revise v1's comparison against unscaffolded and component-only LLM repair.

E3.justification: The stated repair budget changes from 10 attempts per conflict to 20 outer iterations and 3 attempts per conflict. v2 changes repair backbones, evaluates 42 GPT-4.1-built MANGO graphs containing 534 conflicts, and introduces controlled error-injection protocols. Evaluation expands from loops, conflict repair rate and repair accuracy to graph-level conflict-free rates, residual conflicts, structural preservation and natural-text recall.

E4.justification: v2 adds error-type and density ablations, an iteration-budget sensitivity sweep, six controlled algorithmic scenarios, a 1,160-graph LCA analysis and a structure-preservation analysis. The earlier advent walkthrough/repaired-map example and conflict-distribution visualization are removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no seed counts or uncertainty intervals. v2 reports 20 independent seeds per synthetic cell, 30 game-seeds per TextWorld cell and 95% Wilson confidence intervals in Table 1. Appendix B adds variability reporting, while the cross-vendor discussion explicitly states that statistical significance was not formally assessed.

E6.justification: The original aggregate and per-game results are replaced by substantially different result sets. New findings include VC+EI achieving 25% conflict-free repair versus 70% for the baseline with eight directional errors (Table 1), and heuristic_remove leaving 98 conflicts versus 396 for the best LLM configuration (Table 3). Table 4 adds literary node/edge recall of 94.3%/88.2%. These are new evaluations, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core repair pipeline, normalized Edge Impact Score and Version Control operations remain. Appendix A adds a natural-text adaptation using angle and distance discretization with conflict-dependent elastic tolerances. The expanded history-based LCA description is presented as clarification, not evidence of a wholly new repair algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten, retained related-work and method explanations are condensed, and LCA exposition is expanded. Conclusion and Limitations become separate sections, while the long walkthrough appendix is replaced by a structured algorithmic-validation appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and replaces the conceptual Figure 1 with literary mapping comparisons and a rendered-map illustration. Figures 2–3 are retained, while the standalone version-history diagram and old appendix figures disappear. The aggregate and per-game table layouts are replaced with new experimental and algorithmic-analysis tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds the TextWorld citation and removes several supporting references, including Jericho, g2o, bundle adjustment and some incremental scene-graph studies. The central positioning around SLAM-inspired consistency maintenance, knowledge-graph error management and LLM spatial reasoning remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces the earlier spatial-path LCA expression with a timestamp argmax over reasoning-history paths, formally introduces the commit-dependency domain and explains the local directional-conflict special case. v2 also removes the formal Conflict Revelation Gain definition and the assertion that PageRank convergence justifies equal feature weights, substantially revising the mathematical grounding.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through controlled ablations with confidence intervals, independent algorithmic tests and non-LLM comparisons (Tables 1–3 and Appendix B). It also exposes failures and quantifies structural loss and over-generation, making the claims better calibrated than v1's broad reliability narrative. Removing per-game tables reduces audit detail, and the prose adaptation remains underspecified, but the gains in experimental rigor and interpretation outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-MapRepair work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, TextWorld, MANGO and literary-text experiments, plus algorithmic simulations in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original MANGO graph-construction and repair experiments, component ablations and model comparisons in Tables 1–2 and Appendix Tables A1–A4.

results.title: Constructing coherent spatial memory in LLM agents through graph rectification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion extend the claimed performance scope from 1.5B/7B to 1.5B/4B/7B models. The central contributions—strict language consistency, self-generated English reasoning alignment and multilingual generalization—retain their original meaning.

C2.justification: V3 attributes judge effectiveness to multilingual capability rather than simply size, explains capacity-dependent hard/soft reward trade-offs, and argues against translation-based alignment in Appendix D.2. It also acknowledges CTA overhead and unreliability when judges cannot understand extremely low-resource languages. Section 4.3 moderates the claim of almost overcoming the accuracy-consistency trade-off to mitigating it.

D1.justification: V3 adds direct model and dataset collection links, explicitly identifies cold-start SFT initialization for Naive-RL and SLC-RL, and documents the two-stage human annotation procedure in Appendix D.3. The existing implementation frameworks, hardware and 1.5B/7B hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use Light-R1-SFTData, MMATH and the same ten overlapping PolyMath languages, with the same five training languages. The new backbone and human-validation experiments reuse existing mathematical reasoning coverage.

E2.justification: V3 removes DeepSeek-R1-0528 from the 7B MMATH comparison and adds the reward-matched SLC-RL-s comparator in Appendix C.4. Section 4.2 also adds format gating to SLC-RL's stated reward expression. The other principal comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: V3 adds Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 evaluation with one GRPO iteration, two additional judge configurations, controlled reward-magnitude comparisons, and an English-versus-other-languages GAP metric. Human validation introduces random sampling of 30 training examples per language and expert assessment. Existing MMATH/PolyMath metrics and documented training and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether gains depend on hard language constraints rather than reward magnitude, whether smaller contemporary judges work, and whether CTA scores agree with human assessments. These extend the original ablations and judge comparison substantially (Section 5.4 and Appendices C.3-C.4). The original language-transfer analysis is retained.

E5.justification: V3 adds Pearson correlation estimation between human and LLM alignment scores in Section 5.4 and Table 6. Both versions retain four-run averaging for benchmark evaluation; no increase in repeated runs or new confidence intervals is reported.

E6.justification: V3 adds 4B, judge, human-validation and reward-control results, and revises DIT/QRT and 7B Iter-2 scores. The latter's all-language MMATH LC&Acc changes from 62.24% to 63.25%; its PolyMath LC&DW-ACC changes from 19.22% to 36.24%. These are reported value changes, with no explanation establishing their cause. The 1.5B M-Thinker MMATH results and original ablations remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed LC and CTA rewards, overall reward, rejection sampling, cold-start SFT and iterative GRPO procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithm 1. The additional backbone and judge experiments reuse this procedure.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized abstract, introduction and conclusion edits, rewrites the judge-analysis discussion, and organizes Appendices C and D into additional subsections. Most original prose, method explanations and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The results presentation is substantially reorganized: the 7B table leads, while 1.5B results receive a compact main-text summary and full appendix table. V3 expands the judge table with additional rows and GAP, and adds 4B, human-validation and reward-comparison tables. The four original figures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds MAPO (She et al., 2024) and a focused discussion contrasting its translation-based alignment with CTA's logical-step equivalence, also drawing on the already-cited CM-Align. The main related-work section otherwise remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Limited formal changes concern comparison rewards: Section 4.2 adds a format gate to SLC-RL's mathematical definition, and Table 11 specifies the new SLC-RL-s reward cases. The core GRPO, LC, CTA, overall-reward and DW-ACC definitions remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for the central reward design by addressing v1's missing human validation of CTA and testing the reward-scale confound through controlled comparisons. Additional backbone and judge experiments, plus explicit failure conditions, improve the evidence and its interpretation. These gains are tempered by unexplained benchmark-score revisions and Appendix C.1's overbroad accuracy claim: Table 8 reports 74.17% raw accuracy for M-Thinker-4B versus 77.96% for its backbone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same M-Thinker study. All 13 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds a 4B backbone evaluation, further reward comparisons, and human validation of CTA scores.

before.justification: V1 reports original MMATH and PolyMath experiments, reward and training ablations, judge-model comparisons, and language-transfer results.

results.title: Think Natively: Unlocking Multilingual Reasoning with Consistency-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three contributions and the headline BRIGHT score of 38.1. The added introduction reference to the triviality analysis supplies evidence for an existing claim rather than redefining it.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning transfer to ordinary retrieval, robustness to weaker candidate miners, and low training overhead; the existing limitations remain. It also corrects DIVER's description from 'strongest' to 'competitive': Table 3 reports RaDeR at 35.19 versus DIVER at 32.23 in both versions.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1 and A.3 newly disclose SGLang inference, while Appendix B.3 reports 1,304 training steps and runtimes of 13,144 seconds for contrastive learning and 13,378 seconds for Redapter. Core hyperparameters, prompts, hardware, licenses, and promised resource access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds non-reasoning-intensive retrieval evaluation on TREC-COVID and KAPR, substantially extending the task coverage beyond BRIGHT and R2MED. Natural Questions, previously cited but not experimentally used, now supplies training data for a comparator. The original synthetic training corpus is retained.

E2.justification: The main BRIGHT and R2MED comparator rosters are unchanged. New targeted comparisons include an NQ-trained Qwen3-8B model, Qwen3-Embedding-4B and BGE-M3 as alternative candidate miners, and direct teacher/zero-shot comparisons for annotation quality (Tables 4, 5, 10, and 12).

E3.justification: V2 introduces held-out annotation evaluation on 60,000 pairs and human validation on 360 pairs by three authors, ROUGE overlap measurements, and controlled candidate-miner comparisons. Appendix C.4 compares 58,568 NQ training examples with three synthetic-data sizes. Tables 2-3 also correct Qwen3-4B-ms from 8B to 4B; this reporting correction does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands pipeline validation through direct annotation-quality assessment (Section 5.3), lexical-overlap diagnostics of triviality (Section 5.4.1), sensitivity to the initial retriever (Appendix A.2), and training-cost analysis (Appendix B.3). The earlier component ablations, scaling analysis, and contamination checks remain.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 newly reports Cohen's kappa as a chance-corrected statistical assessment of annotation agreement with the teacher. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so the addition does not establish improved uncertainty reporting for retrieval performance.

E6.justification: Main retrieval and existing ablation scores are retained, including Qwen3-8B's BRIGHT/R2MED averages of 38.1/43.18. New outcomes include kappa 0.6001 versus 0.4314, distilled/teacher annotation accuracy of 85.0%/86.1%, alternative-miner BRIGHT scores of 37.2 and 35.9, ROUGE measurements, runtimes, and TREC-COVID/KAPR scores (Tables 4, 5, 7, and 10-12). These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The ReMixer pipeline, distilled annotator, and Redapter weighting procedure are unchanged. V2's explanation of positive/negative label thresholds restates information already shown in v1 Figure 1. Alternative candidate retrievers are tested as ablations without replacing the default method.

P1.justification: V2 adds an annotation-quality research question and section, appendix subsections for runtime and general retrieval, and acknowledgments. It makes localized wording, explanatory, and cross-reference edits while retaining most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence.

P2.justification: V2 adds six compact result tables (4, 5, 7, and 10-12), relocates existing displays as text flows, and gives reasoning intensity a numbered equation. The three original figures and established table designs are retained; appendix prompt captions receive small corrections.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for KAPR (Capari et al., 2024), TREC-COVID (Voorhees et al., 2021), and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024a). The related-work discussion and positioning of the central contributions are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Candidate selection, InfoNCE, the clipped reasoning-intensity ratio, and batch normalization retain their mathematical definitions. V2 displays the previously inline reasoning-intensity definition as Equation 2 and renumbers subsequent equations; no new assumptions, derivations, or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: V1 supported annotation quality mainly through downstream retrieval; v2 adds direct teacher agreement on 60,000 pairs and author judgments on 360 pairs. Together with lexical-overlap diagnostics, retriever sensitivity, and runtime analysis, this substantially strengthens evidence for the central synthesis and training pipeline. The general-retrieval comparison remains limited by unequal training-data sizes and an unnamed metric in Table 12, but these limitations do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same ReasonEmbed study with ReMixer and Redapter. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-C are readable and matchable across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds annotation-quality evaluation, retriever sensitivity, runtime measurements, and general-retrieval experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original BRIGHT and R2MED retrieval experiments, component ablations, data-scaling results, and contamination analysis.

results.title: ReasonEmbed: Enhanced Text Embeddings for Reasoning-Intensive Document Retrieval

C1.justification: The central contributions remain Stackelberg modeling of dialogue and reinforcement learning for persuasive utterance refinement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the claimed demonstrated scope from three SDGs to include Sotopia, without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 newly identifies increased utterance length as a limitation and explains excessive intent targets as potentially introducing low-quality reward signals. It adds interpretations of data-size and response-alignment analyses. It also removes v1's detailed explanation of the negative reward component and its stronger 'universal persuasion plugin' passage.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data access statement, substantially revises Appendix C's prompt templates, and documents new training-data construction, judging, embedding-model, and human-study details. Some transparency is lost: Table 1 removes participation counts, and Figure 3's caption still describes identical Refiner/Measurer copies despite the stated 7B/72B models.

E1.justification: The three original SDGs remain. v2 additionally trains and evaluates on Sotopia's open-ended social scenarios and AmazonHistoryPrice bargaining, and evaluates Werewolf with human participants. These additions substantially broaden task requirements, domains, and the population of interaction partners.

E2.justification: The original SDG comparator sets are retained. New comparisons actually evaluate SOTOPIA-π, SOTOPIA-Ω, SDPO, and MetaMind in Table 3, and MADeN in Table 7 alongside ReAct and ReCon. Table 4 also reports human performance.

E3.justification: v2 changes the reported Refiner and Measurer backbones and introduces substantial new protocols: Gemini-2.5-Flash judging of Goal/Overall scores on 450 Sotopia tasks and 90 hard tasks; 16 volunteers playing five Werewolf games each; and Buyer evaluation against a ReAct Seller using Deal Rate, SNP, and Share. The original 500-match and 50-match-per-setting SDG designs remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to K=1,3,5,7 (Figure 4), training-data requirements from 1,000 to 4,000 instances (Figure 10), and whether follower responses increasingly align with intended responses across training epochs (Table 6). Appendix E adds a Sotopia case study. Existing reward and two-stage ablations are retained with revised results.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-training-run or seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added match, participant, and interaction counts describe evaluation design rather than new uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results change: Table 1 reports Ours + LSPO's overall Werewolf win rate as 44.1% in v1 and 44.7% in v2, and Ours + Strategist's Avalon rate as 60.6% and 61.3%. Ablation values also change, and substantial new results cover Sotopia, humans, bargaining, and sensitivity analyses. Changed models and rewards prevent interpreting these revisions as controlled same-setting gains. The cross-model chart is retained.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.3 replace one desired/undesired response pair with sets of K=3 responses and sum their log-probabilities in the reward. The shared Llama-3-8B implementation becomes a Qwen2.5-7B Refiner and Qwen2.5-72B Measurer. These change the training objective and key model components.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, Sections 2.2–2.3 are condensed, and some interpretive prose is shortened. New named sections and appendix subsections organize the added material, while the LLM-use statement moves from Appendix F to H. Most existing prose and the core narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: The predominantly single-column ICLR layout becomes a two-column document. Figure 3 is revised, Table 1 loses participation columns, and new tables, sensitivity plots, a human-study interface image, and a Sotopia case display are added. Existing cross-model and game-case figures are resized and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Sotopia, its associated comparison methods, and Qwen2.5, while removing several background references, including Fudenberg and Tirole, ARGS, and the Llama 3 report. The central positioning of direct utterance optimization relative to strategy-selection approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1 and 5 generalize the formal intent and reward definitions from a single response pair to K response sets. Appendix B's winning-probability formulation and underlying Stackelberg reasoning remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support through open-ended social tasks, bargaining, and actual human interaction, extending v1's AI-only game validation. The response-alignment and sensitivity analyses also provide important evidence about the intended influence mechanism and design choices. These gains outweigh the loss of participation counts and new documentation inconsistencies, such as Figure 3's outdated model description. The continued absence of uncertainty estimates limits confidence in precise performance differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Stackelberg-based persuasive-agent framework. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, format, method details, and experimental scope.

after.justification: v2 reports original game experiments, additional Sotopia and bargaining evaluations, a human-player study, and new sensitivity and response-alignment analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original gameplay results on Werewolf, Avalon, and ONUW, together with reward ablations, cross-model evaluations, and the two-stage refinement experiment in Appendix D.

results.title: The Stackelberg Speaker: Optimizing Persuasive Communication in Social Deduction Games

C1.justification: The headline claims of 100% refusal, at most 7% utility degradation and at most 5% attack success remain. The introduction qualifies the contribution as the first method satisfying all four requirements within the evaluated setting and acknowledges that prior password-locking methods are not uniformly vulnerable to adversarial prompting.

C2.justification: v2 refines the existing interference discussion by distinguishing it from catastrophic forgetting and interpreting the eight-feature degradation as an overlap problem. It adds an economic-feasibility interpretation of runtime measurements and proposes overlap removal and vLLM serving as future mitigations. The warning about stronger future attacks is retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies A100 40GB hardware, updates reported total computation from approximately 5,000 to 6,000 GPU hours, discloses adapter parameter counts and identifies PEFT as the source of additional merging implementations. The original training and attack hyperparameters move from Appendix B to E unchanged; the promise to release code upon publication remains.

E1.justification: The original datasets remain. Appendix I adds selective locking of Law, History, Psychology, Politics and Philosophy as separate MMLU-derived features, previously covered collectively by general knowledge. This introduces finer-grained authorization tasks among overlapping subdomains, without adding a new source dataset.

E2.justification: Table 12 adds an evaluated password-locking-plus-circuit-breaking comparator, PWD + CB. Table 8 substantially expands merging comparisons with SVD, TIES SVD, four DARE variants and two magnitude-pruning variants. The original PWD and Linear/CAT/TIES comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce 4-bit Llama-3-70B-Instruct, temperature-1 sampling, progressive locking up to eight features, and adapter attachment/detachment and time-to-first-token measurements. Table 8 reports averaged locked-feature accuracy alongside unlocked accuracy. Original data splits, training settings and main evaluation metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a stochastic-decoding robustness check in Appendix F, expands merging analysis to distinguish over-refusal from ineffective locking in Appendix G, and tests scalability and interference through eight-feature locking in Appendix I. The original clipping-threshold sensitivity plot and jailbreak analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 adds runtime averages over five runs with ± values and ten independent temperature-1 inference runs with reported ±1% and ±2% variation. These additions are localized; the main result tables still lack uncertainty estimates, and the meaning of the ± quantities is unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparator, scalability, runtime and sampling results. Table 9 reveals incomplete locking in some configurations and Philosophy accuracy falling from 0.49 to 0.34 with seven features locked. Retained results also change: Table 4 swaps Llama Math's final two entries from 0.00/0.23 to 0.23/0.00; Table 5 updates Locket's MMLU score with M+Q locked from 0.51 to 0.53; v1 Table 8/v2 Table 10 changes locked Math from 0.92 to 0.00. Tables 2–3 are numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 moves merging, clipping and adapter attachment from the per-request inference routine into a separate per-client routine; Section 7 specifies attachment once per session. The feature-specific adapters, adversarial training objective and spectral-norm merging rule remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, problem statement and evaluation prose are extensively rewritten or condensed. Unlearning moves into the alternative-techniques discussion, applications move to Appendix D, and discussion/limitations topics are reorganized. The appendices expand from A–C to A–I with additional explanatory sections and analyses.

P2.justification: v2 adds full-width merging and eight-feature matrices in Tables 8–9 and separate PWD + CB and 70B comparisons in Tables 12–13. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Algorithm 1 gains a separate routine block, and several tables move. Original appendix Tables 8–9 become Tables 10–11. Both original figures retain identical graphics, with caption edits.

R1.justification: Sections 2–3 add pay-to-unlock literature and substantially revise the assessment of prior defenses. Table 1 changes existing methods' utility-preservation ratings from satisfied to unsatisfied and naive-jailbreak resistance from unsatisfied to satisfied, while recognizing Hofstätter et al.'s circuit-breaking robustness. Additional citations cover circuit breakers, preference/adversarial training, PEFT and vLLM.

T1.justification: The FLoTE mapping, loss expressions, perturbation optimization and spectral-norm formulas retain their mathematical substance. Naming the averaged refusal loss Lrobust and adding an informal feature definition clarify existing concepts; no new theorem, proof or substantive formal assumption appears.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly left broader model coverage and scalability beyond four features unresolved. v2 substantially strengthens these central aspects through 70B and eight-feature evaluations, a stronger PWD + CB comparator, expanded merging comparisons, and runtime and stochastic-decoding checks. Updated table entries also improve consistency. The new experiments usefully expose locking and utility limitations, although the abstract's perfect-locking and 7% headline claims need clearer scope in light of those results, and uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Locket research work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model, eight-feature, additional-comparator, runtime and stochastic-inference results in Section 7 and Appendices F–I.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix C report original measurements of feature locking, utility, jailbreak resistance and scalability across three language models.

results.title: Locket: Robust Feature-Locking Technique for Language Models

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes reward enrichment and fuller candidate utilization. V2 centers its contribution on recovering intermediate partial-error signals through semantic gating and hierarchical contrasts. The headline empirical claim changes from 7B competitiveness on WMT21–22 to effectiveness across 4B/9B models and 9B parity with GPT-4o/Gemini on the revised benchmarks.

C2.justification: V2 develops explanations involving sparse errors in the 'Zone of Uncertainty,' model confidence as a stabilizer, and SAC's complementarity with continuous QE. It adds interpretations of weighting tradeoffs and proprietary independence. A new limitations section explicitly addresses larger-model scalability, low-resource languages, and commercial-API reproducibility.

D1.justification: V2 adds the SAC prompt, exact proprietary-model versions, sequence length, warmup and clipping settings, vLLM use, H100 hardware and training time, API cost accounting, dataset statistics, and filtering details. It also supplies a code-availability link. V1 provides substantially less implementation and resource documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds WMT23/WMT24 evaluation and IWSLT spoken-domain training; WMT21 disappears and WMT22 becomes training material. Language coverage changes from English↔{Czech, German, Icelandic, Chinese, Russian} to English↔{Chinese, German, Japanese}. FLORES-200 and HalOmi remain in use.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include Set-MPO, LiPO, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Aya models, TowerInstruct, and GRPO/GSPO. NLLB is removed. Standard DPO leaves the main benchmark comparison but remains alongside KTO, SimPO, ORPO, and CPO in objective-generalization experiments.

E3.justification: V1 uses ALMA-7B, 16 candidates per source, and beam search with beam size 5; v2 uses GemmaX2-28-9B and Qwen3-4B, eight candidates, and sampling with temperature/top-p 0.3. FLORES-test moves from training to held-out evaluation. V2 adds stratified blind human evaluation and matched-reward online-RL controls.

E4.justification: V2 adds model-confidence and partial-error distribution analyses, SAC and alternative-reward ablations, proprietary-dependence controls, data scaling, gold-reference SFT comparisons, and ranking/curriculum sensitivity studies. Existing component ablations are revised. V1's three-way comparison of many-versus-many, many-versus-one, and one-versus-many pairing is removed.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 1 explicitly displays mean XCOMET with a one-standard-deviation band; v2 Figure 2 uses box-and-whisker distributions, without specifying the whisker convention. This changes dispersion reporting. Neither version provides training-run counts, seeds, benchmark confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V1's WMT21–22 ALMA results are replaced by results under different benchmarks and backbones, including v2's WMT23 Gemma-M2PO averages of 97.87 Coverage and 89.67 XCOMET. Human evaluations and numerous control results are added. The retained HalOmi XCOMET hallucination correlation also changes from 0.7061 to 0.6972 after rescaling v2 Table 8; this is not rounding.

M1.justification: V1's additive KIWI-XXL plus WSPAlign reward becomes multiplicative gating by an LLM-based Semantic Alignment Classifier (SAC). V2 also revises confidence fusion, replaces softmax-weighted preference learning plus single-best behavior cloning with margin-weighted pairwise CPO, and changes the ranking target from static to fused scores (Section 4).

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, motivation, and method narrative, organizing the method around two conceptual components. The appendix structure expands from A–B to A–J, with existing metric analysis and prompts relocated and expanded. The title, author list, and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework, replaces the original metric line plot with three boxplot panels, and moves the updated quality–faithfulness scatterplot to the first page. It restructures main tables around Coverage/XCOMET pairs and colored model groups, separates the pairing illustration, and adds distribution, scaling, case-study, sensitivity, and implementation displays.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded and repositioned around online versus offline alignment and reward reliability versus data efficiency. V2 introduces discussion of Set-MPO, LiPO, GRPO, and GSPO, and explicitly argues that set/listwise methods inherit unreliable MT rewards. Traditional word alignment is newly contrasted with SAC as inadequate for subtle semantic errors.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions change substantially: additive reward becomes discrete multiplicative gating, confidence becomes length-normalized with sigmoid fusion, pair weights become normalized margins, and the listwise target changes (v1 Equations 2–9; v2 Equations 2–7). These revise the formal objective, although neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through direct human assessment, additional controlled comparisons, matched-reward online-RL experiments, and an open-source pipeline test that better separates optimization gains from proprietary supervision. Expanded implementation details and explicit limitations improve transparency. Narrower language coverage, continued absence of run-level uncertainty, and an unexplained static-only ablation discrepancy between Tables 5 and 16 limit the conclusions, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of M2PO for machine translation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original WMT23, WMT24, and FLORES-200 experiments, a 450-instance human evaluation, and extensive analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original WMT21–22 translation experiments, HalOmi metric analyses, preference-method comparisons, and ablations, including appendix results.

results.title: M^2PO: Multi-Perspective Multi-Pair Preference Optimization for Machine Translation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: directly optimizing KG construction through RL, introducing two task-aware rewards, and improving downstream QA utility. The additional comparisons strengthen the supporting evidence rather than redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: New Section 7 discusses dependence on frozen retrievers, reward-computation overhead, untested large-model and multilingual generalization, and the need for associated supporting passages. Appendix A adds substantive interpretations of RL versus RAFT, judge capacity, transferability, and reward-dependent graph structure.

D1.justification: Section 5.6 newly reports training times for four configurations and a 2–5-document pool for graph-retrieval training. Conversely, v3 removes the code and data/model links, VeRL implementation disclosure, and reproducibility statement with release commitments. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish withdrawal of the underlying resources.

E1.justification: Both versions train on HotpotQA and Musique and evaluate on NQ, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and Musique using the same described corpora. The additional experiments reuse this coverage; larger models and another HippoRAG implementation do not introduce new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 5–6 add evaluated zero-shot constructors DeepSeek-V3, GPT-5-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B, and gemini-2.5-flash-lite, plus reward-ranked fine-tuning through RAFT. The original constructor and retrieval comparisons remain, substantially expanding the comparator set.

E3.justification: The original 1,000-question evaluations and retrieval settings remain. Appendix A adds offline reward-filtering and fine-tuning, a 3B-versus-7B reward-judge comparison, testing within the official HippoRAG implementation, and structural count/diversity measurements. These substantially extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses testing whether on-policy RL outperforms reward-guided offline training, sensitivity to judge capacity, transfer to an existing HippoRAG pipeline, and how rewards affect graph topology. The F1-reward ablation, training curves, and two qualitative case studies already existed in v1 and are largely relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and training curves without experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional descriptive graph statistics do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical evidence in Tables 4–8 and 12. For example, RAFT achieves 41.77 average ToG F1 versus GRPO's 41.28, while the separate official-HippoRAG experiment reports 32.09 versus 32.47 average F1. Original benchmark scores are retained; two Qwen-3B PopQA recall-gain annotations are corrected from 4.20 to 3.50 and 3.40 to 3.20.

M1.justification: The constructor, frozen retrieval pipeline, two utility rewards, and GRPO optimization without KL regularization remain unchanged. The Llama repetition penalty moves to Appendix D. RAFT and different judge sizes are comparison experiments, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: Llama results and adaptation move to appendices, the existing reward ablation moves into Section 5.5, and training-input construction moves into Section 4.3. Appendices are restructured, a limitations section is added, and the reproducibility section is removed, although much core prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 switches to two-column layout, revises Figure 1, consolidates the main F1/recall and reward-ablation tables, and separates Llama results into appendix tables. It adds several comparison, timing, and structural-statistics tables. Existing training plots and case-study displays are rearranged rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including RAFT, LightRAG, TERAG, AtlasKV, and prior RL-based KG reasoning, while removing the Llama 3 and HybridFlow references. Section 2.2 more explicitly distinguishes graph generation from corpora from refinement of existing KGs. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, reward equations, and clipped GRPO objective remain substantively unchanged. However, Section 4.3 removes v1's explicit mathematical definition of the policy probability ratio and associated token-sequence definitions, leaving a limited loss of formal specification. No new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: The larger-constructor comparisons and RAFT control substantially address v1's limited evidence against alternative constructors and training strategies. before.justification: v1 reports original QA performance, passage recall, intrinsic graph-quality evaluations, reward ablations, and training dynamics.

results.title: AutoGraph-R1: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Knowledge Graph Construction

V1's central claims concern codec reconstruction, semantic representations and disentanglement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAC research work. All pages, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, are readable, and retained experiments and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds TTS experiments, human listening scores, training-data-scale comparisons, speed measurements and semantic-representation ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original SAC reconstruction, representation, ablation and disentanglement results, including noisy-speech experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: From Local to Global: Revisiting Structured Pruning Paradigms for Large Language Models

The benchmark contribution and reliability–capability trade-off remain.

It adds interpretations distinguishing hallucination from general instruction-following failure and discussing drift even on the tool-training domain. D1.justification: New Appendix B documents initialization, regularization, optimizers, learning rates, dimensions, training steps, checkpoint selection, and steering optimization, substantially expanding v1's sparse implementation account. E1.justification: Section 4.3 adds decoding of weekday names, month names, and written numerals from 'one' to 'ten', extending the evaluated task beyond digit-valued number representations. The original eight natural-language datasets across four domains and the BBC multi-token-number setting remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds lin, bin, and log comparators to the arithmetic output-decoding experiments, where v1 examined sinusoidal probing (v2 Figure 7 versus v1 Section 4.2). The prior sin probe also becomes the explicit comparator in the new steering and ordinal experiments. The earlier TunedLens comparison is retained.

E3.justification: The Figure 3a probe comparison changes from synthetic arithmetic contexts to natural-language contexts, and Figure 5b expands held-out-layer evaluation from three to six models. New protocols include leave-one-out ordinal validation and steering incorrect predictions with an interpolation factor optimized per layer, operation, and probe. Newly disclosed hyperparameters alone do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a mechanistic intervention study comparing activation steering across layers and probe types (Figure 9), plus an error analysis reporting that temporal decoding failures persist at the first position when token order is reversed. V1's layer-removal, sparsity, and transformer-component analyses remain in Appendices A.6–A.8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a defined uncertainty-estimation procedure. The added leave-one-out evaluation changes validation design rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds output-probe results, steering that corrects up to 30% of multiplication errors and 42% of division errors under optimized settings, and ordinal results including 11/12 month names decoded by param-sin across six models. Input, cross-layer, and conditional output-recovery plots also change alongside the new probe and settings. These are not straightforward same-setting gains over v1; Table 2's earlier results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 introduces param-sin, assigning each latent feature a sine wave with learnable frequency, phase, and amplitude, beyond v1's inherited sinusoidal-basis probe (Section 3.2, Equation 2). It also adds target-conditioned activation steering using optimized patch embeddings and interpolation; v1's intervention removes layers.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around universality and specialized probing tools. V2 adds an explicit contribution list, reframes Section 4, moves several mechanistic analyses into the appendices, and adds Limitations, Experimental Details, and an LLM-use disclosure. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main layout from one column to two, reorganizes existing figures, and moves several displays into the appendices. It adds output-comparison and steering figures, an ordinal-results table, and a non-number Fourier-spectrum display. Figures 3 and 5 gain new series, and Figure 4's caption clarifies the color and line-style meanings.

R1.justification: V1 primarily extends Kadlcik et al.'s probe; v2 positions its own architecture against that probe's generalization limitations and explicitly challenges Zhou et al.'s gradual-refinement interpretation. It adds connections to Engels et al. on ordinal representations and Mickus et al. on embedding structure, while removing broader motivation references such as Kalai et al. This substantially revises the contribution's positioning.

T1.justification: Equation 2 adds a mathematical definition of the parameterized sinusoidal probe and its single-sine-wave constraint. The revision does not add formal theorems or proofs; its principal new mechanistic support is experimental.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central probing evidence through explicit output-baseline comparisons, targeted interventions, and ordinal generalization tests. Appendix B addresses v1's sparse implementation documentation, while new limitations clarify applicability. These gains improve the paper's assessability and reproducibility. The stronger causal wording still needs qualification: steering uses known correct targets and optimized interpolation, so its reported benefits do not establish a generally deployable error-correction method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching analyses moved into v2's appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and adds experiments with a new probe, activation steering, and ordinal-data decoding.

before.justification: V1 reports original representation-similarity measurements, probing experiments, cross-layer and cross-context evaluations, and arithmetic layer-removal results.

results.title: Language Models Learn Universal Representations of Numbers and Here’s Why You Should Care

C1.justification: The abstract replaces consistent superiority over existing reweighting methods with strongest overall average performance, emphasizing lower-capacity models. The introduction similarly narrows the performance contribution. The central optimization-based reweighting and improved RL-initialization contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses failures to outperform baselines when models already reason strongly or supervision mismatches the target task. It adds explanations for declining performance with larger training sets and for simple-task degradation, softens the RL-ceiling interpretation, and limits the AdamW analysis to a local approximation. Appendix I also introduces a mechanism interpretation involving more exploratory, self-corrective reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies probing-batch size 32 and practical loss-ratio scaling in Algorithm 1, corrects the forward-pass accounting, and documents parallel probing, GPU configurations, and measured step times. It also supplies settings for the added SGD/DAPO experiments and a planned code-release address. These expand implementation and resource documentation; the PDF does not establish that code has been released.

E1.justification: The math/code training corpora, BigMath RL data, and evaluation tasks are retained, including GSM8K and MATH500. Added models, optimizer comparisons, and computational experiments reuse existing task coverage rather than introducing new datasets, domains, or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds GRPO and DAPO as direct competitors to VCORE in Appendix F and Table 11, extending comparisons beyond SFT reweighting approaches. v1 uses GRPO only for downstream training of DFT/VCORE initializations and merely cites DAPO. Existing comparator sets in retained experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Qwen3-1.7B and Mistral-7B configurations, batch sizes 16/64, learning rates 1e-5/1e-4, plain SGD without momentum or weight decay, and probing-batch/hardware variations. The direct RL comparison also introduces a DAPO protocol with filtering disabled. Retained training, inference, and downstream RL settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds learning-rate/batch-size sensitivity tests (Table 3), probing-size and computational scheduling trade-offs (Appendix G), optimizer robustness (H.2), and qualitative CoT case studies (I). These substantially expand the existing data-size, reweighting-hyperparameter, and loss-scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 for main training and inference. Neither reports repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original results in Table 1 and v1 Tables 2–3, retained as v2 Tables 4–5, are numerically unchanged. v2 adds substantial new results in Tables 2–3 and 11–14. For example, Table 11 reports AIME accuracy of 40.00/43.33/48.33 for GRPO/DAPO/VCORE; Table 13 adds SGD averages of 38.69/38.14/40.11 for SFT/DFT/VCORE. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to retained scores.

M1.justification: The core Gibbs reweighting and variance-scaling pipeline remains. Appendix H.1 adds an optimizer-aligned extension using Jacobian-adjusted token utilities and probing directions, extending v1's SGD formulation. This does not establish that the implementation underlying the retained main results changed.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the abstract, preliminary motivation, method explanation, and experimental observations. Acknowledgments are added, and existing appendices are renumbered around new material. The original main-section order and most retained exposition remain, rather than undergoing wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables and the computational execution diagram in Figure 5. Table 1 gains shaded average columns and includes the Original model in best/second-best highlighting. Existing figures and tables are retained and reflowed around these substantial display additions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gema et al. and Stechly et al. to contextualize CoT failures, and removes the distinct high-entropy-token study by Wang et al. and exploration study by Vassoyan et al. Section 4.1 instead emphasizes confidence- and importance-based comparators. The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 1 and its proof concerning strict first-order improvement over uniform weighting. Appendix H.1 additionally develops a local Adam/AdamW extension with explicit assumptions, approximation bounds, optimizer-aligned utilities, an unbiased probing derivation, and an explicit Adam Jacobian. These go substantially beyond v1's derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct RL comparisons, optimizer and hyperparameter checks, and measured computational overhead, while narrowing the headline superiority claim to better match the unchanged main results. These substantially improve assessment of effectiveness and practicality. The gains are qualified: repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and Appendix A's assertion of a finite Gibbs temperature for every positive KL budget overlooks saturation cases.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VCORE research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model comparisons, robustness experiments, computational measurements, and qualitative reasoning examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning experiments, benchmark accuracies, and analyses of training-set size, reweighting hyperparameters, and loss scaling.

results.title: VCORE: Variance-Controlled Optimization-based Reweighting for Chain-of-Thought Supervision

C1.justification: The central claims of competitive accuracy, much smaller models, efficiency, and transparency remain. v1's explicit headline claim of greater interpretability is narrowed in v2 to insights obtained from inspecting embeddings, rather than retained as a principal comparative advantage.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning greater GEMS–LLM error complementarity on unseen questions, message-passing advantages over classical baselines, affordable ensembling, and diminishing returns from larger prompted LLMs. Most existing limitations remain. However, the Setting 3 discussion drops v1's explicit acknowledgment that GEMS does not outperform few-shot fine-tuning.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new baselines' per-question one-hot inputs and factorization objective, and specifies probability averaging for the ensemble. Appendix C.3 corrects the stated expected-performance subgroup count from 11 to 10 while retaining the listed bins. Existing GEMS hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts, and code-access information are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate OpinionQA, Twin-2K, and Dunning–Kruger responses under missing-response, new-individual, and new-question settings. The added comparisons and analyses use this existing coverage; the change from discrete-choice to close-ended terminology does not introduce a different task.

E2.justification: v2 adds XGBoost in Settings 1–2 and matrix factorization in Setting 1 across all three datasets (Table 5). It also adds GPT-5-Mini, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Flash prompting comparisons on OpinionQA (Table 9). Qwen2.5-7B, evaluated in v1 Table 5, is removed from the corresponding extended comparison in v2 Table 8.
