E4.justification: v2 adds error-overlap analysis (Table 4), classical controls examining the contribution of graph structure (Table 5), and an ensemble study testing whether inexpensive repeated training improves accuracy (Table 6). The earlier LoRA-capacity, hidden-layer, and projection-pair ablations are retained in Appendix F.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies 11 different model initializations for the ensemble. This is ensemble construction, not an increase in uncertainty-estimation runs for the existing results. Tables 1–3 retain the same three-split mean-and-standard-deviation reporting, and the LoRA ablation remains explicitly single-seed.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds classical-baseline, proprietary-model, error-overlap, and ensemble results. For example, Gemini 3 Flash reaches 52.78% with 8-shot Agentic CoT on OpinionQA Setting 1, while the new GEMS ensemble reaches 51.65% in Setting 3 versus 50.13% for the retained single-model result. Extended-table values are also corrected: Mistral-7B zero-shot accuracy changes from 35.60 in v1 Table 5 to 34.63 in v2 Table 8, matching Table 1; this does not establish a same-setting performance change from rerunning experiments.

M1.justification: The graph construction, encoders, decoder, losses, and LLM-to-GNN projection remain unchanged. v2 adds an inference variant that averages predicted probabilities from 11 differently initialized GEMS models (Section 6, Table 6).

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction, replaces much discrete-choice terminology with close-ended simulation, and restructures the narrative. Related work moves before the problem definition, while limitations and ethical considerations move from Appendix A into main-text Sections 8–9.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, substantially reflowing equations, tables, and prompt examples. v2 adds Tables 4–6 and 9 and restructures the extended LLM table. The original three-panel compute figure is retained as appendix Figure 4, alongside a revised Setting 1 display in main-text Figure 3.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Bianchi et al. and Zhou et al. on open-ended simulation and Lakshminarayanan et al. on ensembles, while removing works including Tang et al. and the Qwen2.5 report. Its positioning between LLM simulation, graph recommendation, and classical discrete-choice modeling remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, mathematical objectives, and encoder/decoder equations are retained. Changes such as replacing the GraphSAGE root-transformation symbol with the self-transformation symbol are not substantive mathematical revisions. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important comparative gap in v1 by adding learned classical baselines, allowing readers to assess whether graph modeling offers value beyond simpler non-language methods. Four proprietary-LLM comparisons, error-overlap analysis, and measured ensemble gains substantially strengthen the evidence supporting the paper's central argument; corrected extended-table scores also improve consistency. The added comparisons still provide limited uncertainty and implementation detail, and the Setting 3 discussion is less explicit about trailing fine-tuning, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GEMS research, despite a changed title and document format. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original classical-baseline comparisons, proprietary-LLM evaluations, error analysis, and ensemble results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GEMS and baseline experiments across three datasets and settings in Tables 1–3, with additional evaluations and ablations in the appendices.

results.title: Graph-Based Alternatives to LLMs for Human Simulation

C1.justification: Both versions claim an automated black-box framework that learns reusable strategies from successful, partial, and failed attacks, using three strategy libraries. The central claims of superior attack effectiveness, query efficiency, and strategy transferability remain. Revised numerical summaries and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds reward-shaping and sparse-feedback interpretations, explains why abstracted strategies outperform raw logs, and interprets the new defense, judge, and redundancy analyses. It also introduces substantive qualifications about internal computation, latency, token consumption, and strategy-library initialization, alongside an argument about amortized costs in Appendix C.6.

D1.justification: V2 names embedding alternatives and documents additional component configurations and token accounting. Algorithm 1 corrects the judge input from the attack prompt to the target response, aligning it with the existing prose. However, v1's explicit 1024-dimensional embedding specification, zero target-temperature statement, and retrieval threshold are omitted. Baseline recipes, system prompts, and code-on-request access remain.

E1.justification: HarmBench's 400 queries and AdvBench-50 remain the datasets. V2 adds defended-target scenarios involving paraphrasing, perplexity filtering, and external safety classifiers in Section 4.5. Changes to the evaluated LLM configurations are addressed under E3.

E2.justification: The six main attack baselines remain PAIR, TAP, GPTFuzzer, ReNeLLM, CipherChat, and CodeAttack. V2 adds a defense comparison against an undefended control using Paraphrase, Perplexity Filter, Llama Guard 3, and OpenAI Moderation in Table 5. The latest-model comparison uses existing attack baselines.

E3.justification: The main evaluation replaces Qwen3-8B and GPT-4o-mini with DeepSeek-R1; Appendix C.2 adds GPT-5.1, Gemini-3-Flash, and Qwen3-max. New protocols include retrieval-count sweeps, embedding and component-model substitutions, validation on 700 attack-response pairs, and judge-agreement and token-cost metrics. The main ten-query budget and ASR/AQ definitions are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds binary-scoring and raw-interaction-log ablations, retrieval-count sensitivity, defense tests, embedding and weaker-component analyses, alternative-judge validation, redundancy analysis, and token-cost analysis. It also expands strategy examples and adds a case study. V1's w/o ALL results match v2's w/o Retrieval results exactly; those values are retained evidence rather than a new ablation result.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's alternative-judge agreement percentages add validation outcomes, rather than uncertainty estimates or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Shared-target scores in Tables 1-3 are retained. ASTRA's overall ASR/AQ changes from 82.7%/2.3 to 80.6%/2.4 with the changed target set, so this is not a same-setting deterioration. Numerous results are added, including average ASRs of 62.1% and 61.7% for the binary-scoring and raw-log variants in Table 4, plus the defense, sensitivity, validation, and cost results in Tables 5-12.

M1.justification: The core architecture, three strategy libraries, and prompts match. However, v1 specifies a similarity threshold of 0.50 plus three retrieved strategies per library; v2 retains three per library but omits the threshold. Sections 3.4 and 4.1 do not establish whether the gate was actually removed or merely omitted from the description.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and condenses the abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and results narrative. It introduces a Formulation subsection, moves Algorithm 1 into Appendix A and ethical considerations before the references, adds a separate Limitations section, and reorganizes the appendices.

P2.justification: V2 substantially changes the document format, redraws Figures 1-2, transposes and expands Table 4, and revises the target columns in the main tables. Figures 5-7 and Tables 5-12 add new visual material, including sensitivity plots, a workflow diagram, and supplementary comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 adds JailbreakRadar, recent jailbreak studies by Yan et al. and Zheng et al., and sources for the evaluated defenses. It removes several references associated with v1's web-focused introduction, including PagedAttention, WebGPT, and Toolformer. The central positioning around continuous strategy accumulation remains.

T1.justification: V2 introduces Section 3.1 and an explicit optimization objective defining the optimal strategy through maximization of the judge's scalar score. This adds a limited mathematical formulation to v1's procedural description. No theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: V2 fills an important validation gap by directly testing graded scoring and strategy extraction, which v1 supported mainly through library ablations. Alternative-judge validation, defense tests, and explicit computational limitations substantially strengthen the evidence and qualification of the central claims. Reproducibility concerns remain: the retrieval threshold is unexplained, and Table 7 reports PAIR query averages above the stated ten-query budget. These issues limit some added evidence but do not outweigh the stronger component validation and clearer efficiency tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASTRA and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The retained framework and experiments can be matched despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds component ablations, defense evaluations, and appendix analyses of judges, embeddings, redundancy, and token costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original HarmBench and AdvBench-50 experiments, including attack success rates, query counts, transfer tests, and library ablations.

results.title: ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs

C1.justification: V2 adds explicit core contributions concerning quantitative ICL hallucination assessment and dependency-based formalization-difficulty assessment. M1.justification: The Qwen3-32B fine-tuning, dependency-name generation, suffix-array verification, and dependency-conditioned formalization pipeline are retained. Suffix Array Check names the existing verification procedure; the new integrations do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten, and parts of the methodology are condensed. Detailed setup moves into Appendix C, the discussion is redistributed between results and a dedicated Limitations section, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 transposes and expands the retrieval table, separates SFT and ICL results, adds a hallucination table, removes the retrieval-dispersion figure, and replaces the multi-attempt displays with new curves and appendix grids. Figures 1–2 and the examples are retained with relocation or caption changes. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

improvement.justification: V1 tests DDR retrieval chiefly against R@5/R@10 and downstream integration with RA. Prompt disclosure and specific limitations improve transparency. Retrieval-dispersion reporting is lost and cross-version score replacements remain insufficiently explained, but the stronger controlled evaluation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Direct Dependency Retrieval study. Their complete texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original hallucination, retrieval, and autoformalization results in Tables 2–5, with further multi-attempt results in Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original dependency-retrieval and autoformalization experiments in Tables 2–3, with retrieval dispersion and multi-attempt analyses in Figures 3–5.

results.title: Improving Autoformalization Using Direct Dependency Retrieval

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the conceptual comparison table and substantially expands experimental displays through Tables 5–9 and a full-width Algorithm 1. Several existing figures and tables are relocated, including the reward-shaping table becoming Appendix Table 10. All eight original figures retain their graphical content.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, another model family, non-math evaluations, embedding correlations, and tool-execution analyses.

results.title: Empowering Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Agentic Reasoning with Group Turn Policy Optimization

This substantially expands v1's stated data contribution and incorporates capabilities previously described as future directions.

Its limitations retain cardinality bias but add the absence of dense grounded understanding and conversational capabilities. v1's specific adaptive-routing/MoE and broader ReasonSeg evaluation outlooks are removed.

D1.justification: Appendices B and D add detailed annotation workflows, point-to-mask assignment, JSON export information, adapter insertion sites, bottleneck dimension 64, 1024-dimensional four-head attention, and approximately 311.9M trainable parameters. v3 also specifies rho, margin, and temperature settings and explicitly states dataset availability alongside code. The existing hardware and batch-size disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: PACO-LVIS-Instruct evolves into HMPL-Instruct with explicit part-level annotations and one-to-many subset grounding, including 2,941 subset samples, substantially expanding v1's reported object-level dataset. v3 also evaluates RefCOCO and Ref-ZOM in Table 4; these were not evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The main SAM3 comparison drops the Qwen3-VL-2B agent variant while retaining the 8B variant under the shortened SAM3 Agent name. v3 adds LISA and UniPixel to HMPL-Instruct comparisons in Tables 3 and 8, and evaluates LISA, ReLA, UniPixel, and SAM3 Agent on the external benchmarks in Table 4.

E3.justification: The ablation protocol expands from component removal in v1 Table 2 to stagewise training, individual-loss additions, and a single-adapter control in v3 Table 5, with explicit rho and margin sweeps in Appendix C. Dataset sample totals also change. The gIoU/P@50 metrics, inherited PACO-LVIS split policy, batch size 32, and three-round agent limit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands the retained curriculum and alignment analyses with C-Adapter-only and cascaded-versus-single-adapter controls, tests of the new losses, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies. Tables 3 and 8 analyze target cardinality and object/part performance, while Figure 8 adds qualitative comparisons with UniPixel on challenging instruction-grounding cases.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The uncertainty-aware hard-region loss concerns training supervision and does not constitute statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports SAM3-I simple/complex gIoU/P@50 of 54.0/59.6 and 51.0/56.4; v3 Table 2 reports 59.7/65.3 and 49.0/51.0 on the revised dataset and method. These are replaced results under changed conditions. Numerous results are added, including Table 4's RefCOCO gIoU of 76.3 versus UniPixel's 78.1 and Ref-ZOM gIoU of 73.6 versus 67.0.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the frozen SAM3 backbone and cascaded adapters but adds instruction contrastive and parent-rank concept anchoring losses. It changes one-way mask KL alignment to symmetric KL and replaces cross-entropy between branch predictions with ground-truth supervision for both branches. The reported adapter activation also changes from ReLU to GELU.

P1.justification: Existing abstract, introduction, SAM overview, and training explanations are extensively rewritten. Section 5 becomes dataset-centered, experiments gain separate metrics, quantitative, qualitative, and ablation subsections, and Discussion and Outlook is replaced by separate limitations. Appendices A–E reorganize related work, construction details, experiments, implementation, and artifact statements.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn to show the new embedding losses, and v3 adds dataset, granularity, benchmark, and sensitivity tables plus annotation-tool and example figures. Existing visuals are matched: v1 Figure 5 becomes v3 Figure 4, and v1 Figure 4 moves to the appendix as Figure 5. Typography, captions, and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial related-work review in Appendix A covering open-vocabulary, referring, and reasoning segmentation, plus benchmark positioning in Table 1. New cited work includes UniPixel, MMR, InstructPart, Sa2VA, and contrastive-learning research. The earlier MoE-related citations disappear with the corresponding outlook, materially changing positioning beyond the SAM-family overview.

T1.justification: v3 Section 4 introduces formal definitions for weighted bidirectional instruction contrastive learning and margin-based concept anchoring in Equations 1–4. Equations 5–6 substantively revise the mask-alignment and hard-region objectives. These expand and alter the mathematical formulation rather than merely restating v1's equations; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's narrow feasibility study through external benchmark comparisons, subset and part-level evaluations, and direct controls testing the cascaded-adapter design. Appendix D resolves important implementation omissions, while the expanded mathematical definitions and annotation documentation improve reproducibility. Training and split details for the new external comparisons remain sparse, and statistical uncertainty remains absent, but the gains in evidential support and technical completeness are substantial. Changed headline scores alone do not establish a same-setting accuracy improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAM3-I and its instruction-guided extension of SAM3. All nine pages of v1 and eighteen pages of v3 are readable, including figures, tables, equations, and v3's Appendices A–E. v1 has no appendix. The substantial revisions remain reliably comparable.

after.justification: v3 reports original HMPL-Instruct, RefCOCO, and Ref-ZOM evaluations, expanded ablations, sensitivity studies, and qualitative predictions in the main text and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original PACO-LVIS-Instruct segmentation results, baseline comparisons, component ablations, and qualitative predictions in Tables 1–2 and Figure 5.

results.title: SAM3-I: Segment Anything with Instructions

Appendix A introduces explanations contrasting adaptive selection with human-defined boxes and Sketchpad's global alignment, while explicitly qualifying Sketchpad results as tentative. Section 4.4 also adds a causal interpretation of the latency advantage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated VisionR1, PixelReasoner, and Bagel-Zebra comparisons; Bagel-Zebra is excluded from Zebra-CoT OOD because of training overlap. Appendix A adds matched-training LVR and tentative Sketchpad comparisons. These substantially broaden v1's standard-baseline and Mirage comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-VL-8B evaluations on COMT/VSP, a matched Visual-CoT training protocol for LVR, and inference-latency measurements on an H200 GPU. Existing main-text settings largely persist. Table 7 specifies 1.5 Stage 2 Zebra-CoT epochs, conflicting with the retained two-epoch main-text statement; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 adds inference-efficiency analysis, and Appendix C.1 adds six inference case studies across retained benchmarks. Existing component and alignment-weight ablations remain. The latent-size analysis loses v1 Figure 4's subtask-level curves, retaining only the benchmark and overall averages in v2 Figure 3.

E5.justification: Both versions specify random seed 42 and report point estimates. v2 introduces no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; its latency averages do not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The original Qwen2.5-VL table values remain unchanged. Added results include Qwen3-VL ILVR accuracies of 70.5% on COMT and 82.8% on VSP, new comparator scores, and 15.9-second average ILVR latency in Figure 5. The new Visual-CoT comparison is mixed: ILVR exceeds LVR overall, 32.6% versus 31.9%, but trails on EMMA, 21.5% versus 24.0%. New case outputs are added, while subtask-level latent-size results disappear.

M1.justification: The reported teacher-query aggregation changes: v1 Equation 8 uses the preceding latent state, whereas v2 Equation 4 explicitly averages all prior latent rationales. This is a limited component revision; interleaved generation, the momentum teacher, feature selection, and the two-stage objectives remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work, method exposition, and results discussion are extensively rewritten or condensed. v2 separates analysis into Section 4.4, reorganizes the empirical narrative, standardizes single-step terminology, and adds limitations, an AI-assistance disclosure, and appendices.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands to two backbones, Table 2 gains comparator groups, and appendix tables and six case-study figures are added. Figure 1 now illustrates final-state prediction, and a new latency chart appears. The latent-size figure contracts from four panels to one; the existing attention visualization moves from Figure 3 to Figure 4.

R1.justification: v2 adds Latent Sketchpad to related work and removes several tool-use references, including WebWatcher, Vtool-R1, OpenThinkImg, and Chain-of-Focus. It refines the prior-method critique to acknowledge single-step prediction of final states, while retaining the central positioning around missing intermediate-state updates.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the formal query definition from the preceding latent-state term in v1 Equation 8 to cumulative latent-history averaging in v2 Equation 4, also explicitly defining cumulative textual averaging. Other mathematical content is retained or restated in prose; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support where v1 had important gaps: it tests another backbone, broadens comparisons beyond Mirage, evaluates LVR under compatible training conditions, and measures the computational benefit previously asserted qualitatively. Implementation details and explicit limitations also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the removed code link and sample-count disclosures, reduced sensitivity detail, and inconsistent epoch reporting, although the Sketchpad comparison remains provisional.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ILVR research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The complete v2 appendices were inspected; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds backbone evaluations, baseline comparisons, inference-time measurements, and case studies in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity experiments, and latent-attention visualizations in Section 4.

results.title: Interleaved Latent Visual Reasoning with Selective Perceptual Modeling

C1.justification: The central contributions and headline LLaDA-8B gains remain the same. v3 expands the introduction's claimed empirical generality to two backbones and reframes the theoretical contribution around prediction probabilities rather than joint parent-to-child transition probabilities.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning unverifiable objectives and zero-shot/pass@1 coverage, plus a reported Dream output-format failure. It interprets matched-budget controls as evidence for granular credit assignment and adds hyperparameter failure explanations in Appendix E. v1's explanation of generation-length sensitivity is removed.

D1.justification: v3 adds exact prompt templates and task-specific reward definitions, discloses rollout temperature 0.9 and gamma 2, and supplies code and checkpoint links. E3.justification: v3 adds LLaDA-MoE-7BA1B-Instruct evaluations, training/inference comparisons with block lengths 32/64/128, controls matched at 16 completions per query, four hyperparameter sweeps, and an estimation-error diagnostic using 100 samples per task. Retained headline evaluations keep their original settings. The height analysis is now described as covering 30 batches rather than 30 training steps, without establishing that it was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test equal-budget credit assignment (Table 2), decoding robustness (Figure 3), and probability-estimation error (Table 4). Appendices D–F add broader training dynamics, self-distillation hyperparameter sensitivity and a comparative GSM8K case study. Earlier tree-height, branching, self-distillation and reverse-schedule analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports explicitly defined means and standard deviations for probability-estimation error in Table 4, using Monte Carlo estimates from 32 decoding orders per sample. Neither version reports repeated-training seeds or seed-based uncertainty for headline benchmark accuracy; the addition does not establish more training runs.

E6.justification: Shared LLaDA-8B accuracy rows and the original self-distillation ablation scores remain unchanged. v3 adds MoE results, including d-TreeRPO scores of 78.3/67.2/75.5/41.2 at 256 tokens, GDPO results replacing d2-stepMerge entries, and new control, estimation-error, sensitivity and case-study findings. These are additional or replaced results, rather than same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Tree rollouts, bottom-up advantages, block-aligned decoding, token-wise policy updates and scheduled self-distillation remain unchanged. The complete objectives in v1 Equation (16) and v3 Equation (19) match. v3 clarifies token-wise optimization already present in v1; its revised theoretical target does not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries and method explanations are extensively rewritten and condensed. v3 removes the experimental research-question list and separate algorithm-summary subsection, integrates the complete objective into Section 3.4, and adds a limitations section and organized supplementary sections. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is rearranged into a 2×2 grid, Table 1 gains a second backbone block, and the runtime table is transposed. Numerous diagnostic, sensitivity and case-study displays are added; retained figures are reformatted and relocated, and the algorithm display is removed.

R1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands descriptions of six baselines and their distinctions in credit assignment and probability estimation. Related-work coverage adds GDPO, BGPO, block diffusion and other works, while removing the SDAR citation. The revision goes beyond bibliographic updates and develops the research positioning.

T1.justification: v1 Section 3.3 and Appendix A bound the expected joint transition-probability ratio using a worst-case confidence gap across positions and decoding orders. v3 replaces this with a quantile-based, per-token high-probability log-ratio theorem and a new proof. Its bound concerns random path-wise probabilities, replacing the earlier joint-probability bounds and Taylor expansion.

improvement.justification: The matched-budget controls and probability-error diagnostic address important weaknesses in v1's evidence for its proposed mechanisms. A second backbone, sensitivity analyses, and explicit prompts and rewards substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. Removing d2-stepMerge reduces comparison coverage, and the replacement theorem has a different target rather than a stronger expected-probability guarantee. Nevertheless, the added controls and documentation provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe d-TreeRPO. Their full text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds a second model backbone, controlled comparisons, probability-error measurements, sensitivity analyses and case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on four reasoning tasks, self-distillation and tree-configuration ablations, and training-time measurements in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: d-TreeRPO: Towards More Reliable Policy Optimization for Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain training-free, black-box-compatible generation through determinant-based diversity optimization, scalability, and approximately 1.5–3 times greater diversity than baselines. New evaluations support these retained claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the approximation's accuracy near uniform spectra and introduces an empirical lower-bound interpretation. It discusses length as only part of the diversity gains and makes cost-benefit judgments application-dependent. Limitations now identify dependence on instruction-following and embedding quality; the earlier explicit discussion of DIVERSE's math failure is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix 1.4 newly documents Gemma training epochs, batch size, learning rate, LoRA rank, scaling, target modules, and gradient accumulation. v2 also discloses the 2048-token generation limit, attributes evaluation rubrics, and adds a project-page link. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed training.

E2.justification: The six comparison methods in Tables 1–2 are retained. VOYAGER-RANDOMEXPLORER is renamed VOYAGER-RE. Both GSM8K tables identify DEFAULT as the comparator; v2 aligns the prose with that existing label, resolving v1's inconsistent mention of a temperature baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds blinded human evaluation with three annotators, 200 pairs per task, and a four-point rubric; a poem experiment requesting at most 150 tokens; and a Dirichlet-spectra simulation. SUBSETSELECT's source-pool description also changes from mentioning temperature sampling to specifying vanilla sampling, without establishing that its unchanged results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an output-length control testing whether diversity gains merely reflect longer responses (Table 5), analysis of approximation accuracy across spectral conditions (Figure 3), and qualitative Sports and Math comparisons (Tables 7–8). The original explorer-selection and prompt-refinement ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The new human study introduces inter-annotator reliability reporting: Fleiss' kappa is 0.41/0.34 and Krippendorff's alpha is 0.74/0.72 for Sports/Math. Existing benchmark uncertainty reporting is retained, with no newly reported repeated-run or seed protocol.

E6.justification: Original generation scores, ablation scores, and GSM8K accuracies remain unchanged. New results include human ratings favoring VOYAGER over DEFAULT (3.82 versus 2.16 for Sports; 3.72 versus 1.56 for Math), length-controlled poetry results (Vendi 8.17 versus HIERARCHICAL's 6.65), spectral simulations, qualitative examples, and GSM8K generation-call counts.

M1.justification: The determinant-ratio acceptance rule, DPP selection of anchors and explorers, prompt refinement, and threshold initialization and decay are retained. Kernel symbols and sampler names are clarified without establishing a procedural change.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and background are substantially condensed and rewritten. Algorithms 3–4 and the proof move into a reorganized appendix, and the proof explanation is expanded. These are extensive narrative and structural revisions despite retention of the core method.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with reorganized flow and labels. v2 adds four tables and Figure 3, adds an LLM-call column to the GSM8K table, and relocates or resizes existing displays. Appendix prompt boxes also change styling while retaining their contents.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations covering creative prompting, Jaccard-kernel validity, and evaluation rubrics, including Mehrotra, Tian, Lu, Bouchard, and Paech. It removes the Chen 2018 and Li 2016 DPP references. The central positioning against decoding, prompting, dataset selection, and training-based approaches remains stable.

T1.justification: Lemma 1 and its second-order Taylor derivation are retained and relocated to the appendix; the entropy notation restates the existing mathematics. v2 adds reasoning establishing positive semidefiniteness of the RBF/Jaccard kernel mixture and explicitly notes constant trace for the fixed-size, unit-diagonal anchor matrix.

improvement.justification: v1's diversity evaluation was entirely automatic and left output length as an untested confound. v2 adds human diversity ratings and a length-controlled comparison, substantially strengthening evidence for the central claim. Approximation checks, explicit qualifications, and training details further improve interpretability and reproducibility. Human validation remains limited to two tasks, and the spectral lower-bound interpretation remains empirical rather than proved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VOYAGER work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, tables, and prompts, support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds human diversity ratings, a length-control experiment, and simulations evaluating the effective-rank approximation.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments, component ablations, and GSM8K results from models trained on generated data.

results.title: VOYAGER: A Training Free Approach for Generating Diverse Datasets using LLMs

C1.justification: v3 refines the novelty claim toward dynamically eliciting implicit user preferences through dialogue, while retaining unsolvable requests. v1 emphasized being first to combine multi-turn dialogues and unsolvable requests. The central contribution remains a broad, real-world travel benchmark with a reproducible tool sandbox.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of meta-judge calibration, tool-error penalties, difficulty and benchmark practicality. Appendix D distinguishes planning failures from tool-formatting failures, qualifying comparisons across model families. New limitations explicitly address restricted tool coverage and judge-dependent score comparability; Appendix F clarifies that unsolvability concerns unavailable capabilities or information, not merely model difficulty.

D1.justification: v3 supplies extensive information absent from v1: data provenance and collection dates, instance fields, profile de-identification and synthetic attributes, detailed tool descriptions, tool-simulator identity, framework/parsing details, and full assistant, simulator and evaluation prompts. It also adds code/data access information. These substantially improve documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed detail represents a changed implementation.

E1.justification: The three subtasks and five travel-intent domains are retained. v3 additionally evaluates agents with live tools alongside cached/simulated tools (Table 4), extending the tested environment conditions. Its new geographic and demographic descriptions do not establish an expansion to new domains or populations.

E2.justification: v3 retains the six original model comparators and substantially expands actual evaluations. Table 2 adds GPT-4.1, Kimi, DeepSeek, MiniMax and additional Qwen models; Appendix D and Table 10 add scored Ministral3, Gemma3 and Llama variants. These are evaluated comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: The scoring and meta-judge model changes from GPT-5.1 to Gemini-3-Flash-preview. Feasibility annotation changes from two-model to three-model consensus, the unsolvable subset changes from 103 to 100 instances, and the reported cache grows from approximately 100,000 to 200,000 responses. v3 also introduces live-tool, framework-control and human-validation protocols. These changes prevent treating updated scores as same-setting performance changes.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's main model comparison, v3 tests judge repeatability and human agreement, dataset-label validity, offline-versus-online fidelity, and dependence on the tool-use framework. It also validates tool-call count as a difficulty proxy and adds successful and failed trajectory case studies (Sections 5.4–5.5 and Appendices D–G).

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over three agent runs without dispersion. v3 retains that main repetition count but adds separate judge-repeat and end-to-end standard deviations (Tables 3 and 5). Appendix E adds three-annotator voting distributions, exact 95% binomial confidence intervals for label agreement, and judge–human versus human–human MAE reporting.

E6.justification: The main numerical results and rankings are replaced: v1 Table 3 reports GPT-5.1 leading overall at 68.89; v3 Table 2 reports Qwen-Plus leading at 76.29 and GPT-5.1 scoring 75.04. These use revised settings and do not establish performance gains. v3 additionally reports many model scores, tool-error rates, validation outcomes, stability results and dataset distributions.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction procedure is refined. v1 assigns single-turn status when all three assistant runs finish in one turn, and multi-turn otherwise. v3 uses six-run thresholds: at least four one-turn runs for single-turn, and none for multi-turn, excluding intermediate cases. The core sandbox, retrieval-based tool simulation and scoring components remain.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and results narrative. It merges the agent and agentic-RL discussions, separates evaluation into its own main section, and adds structured limitations, ethics and explanatory appendices. This is substantial rewriting and reorganization beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds a benchmark overview diagram, score and difficulty plots, dataset and cache distributions, validation tables, and boxed case studies and prompts. The main results table gains tool-error columns, and the benchmark comparison gains an implicit-preference column. The existing tool table moves to Appendix C. These substantially change visual presentation and organization.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to interactive preference benchmarks, multi-agent planners and adaptive planning. Table 1 adds FLEX-TRAVELPLANNER, TripTailor and COMPASS, and explicitly acknowledges earlier multi-turn benchmarks. Positioning consequently shifts toward implicit-preference elicitation and the combination of realistic data, broad tasks and tools.

T1.justification: The scoring equations retain the same rubric averaging, multiplicative meta-judge and tool-error factors, and three-subset aggregation. v3 changes normalization and makes instance indexing explicit without introducing a different mathematical construction. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the added clarifications are explanatory and empirical.

improvement.justification: v1's reliability claims lacked direct validation and detailed reproduction materials. v3 addresses these central weaknesses through human checks, uncertainty reporting, live-tool and framework controls, broader comparisons, and full prompts and data documentation. Reporting flaws remain: Table 15's counts total 1,489 despite its stated 1,500 trajectories. That inconsistency weakens the meta-judge analysis, but the wider evidential and reproducibility gains establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TravelBench, with matching core tasks, tools and evaluation framework. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes complete Appendices A–H.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations, human validation, stability experiments, framework controls and case studies in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of six LLMs on three TravelBench subsets, averaged over three runs (Table 3).

results.title: Beyond Itinerary Planning—A Real-World Benchmark for Multi-Turn and Tool-Using Travel Tasks

C1.justification: The three central findings and headline thresholds remain. v2 extends the stated empirical applicability to larger and reasoning models and explicitly qualifies the abstract: it does not claim all CoTs are faithful, only that missing hint words alone do not establish unfaithfulness.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of faithful@k's inability to distinguish occasional faithfulness from incomplete verbalization at the instance level, and incompleteness from non-exhaustiveness. It also introduces sycophancy as an explanation for Professor-hint behavior and interprets Qwen's negative Metadata indirect effects as suppression. The judge-error caveat itself already existed in v1's appendix.

D1.justification: The code disclosure changes from a promised future release to stated availability with a repository link. v2 also supplies the quantized Llama checkpoint reference and sampling parameters for the additional models. E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ARC-Easy, OpenbookQA and StrategyQA using Professor, Metadata and Black Squares hints. The added models use subsets of this existing coverage; no new dataset, task or input scenario is introduced.
