E3.justification: Section 7 adds a 4-bit Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct configuration and Qwen-3-32B in thinking mode on two retained datasets. Section 5.2 extends faithful@k from k up to 16 to k up to 32; retaining the n >= max(k) rule raises the reported eligibility threshold. These are substantive evaluation-setting additions and revisions.

E4.justification: v2 extends mechanism analyses and the strict lexical non-verbalization robustness check to larger and reasoning models, adds the GPT-4o judge crosscheck, and introduces four paired CoT case studies in Appendix E. The original smaller-model judge-error robustness analysis was already present in v1 and is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use 95% bootstrap intervals, including 10,000-resample BCa intervals for causal mediation. Added results retain these reporting practices; no change to seed reporting, repeated-run counts or uncertainty-estimation procedures is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the two additional models, k = 32, judge validation and qualitative examples. For example, Table 2 reports 47/65 Qwen-3-32B CoTs as faithful under Filler Tokens on OpenbookQA with Black Squares hints. Appendix D adds GPT-4o's 87% accuracy and 80% precision. The original five tables' numerical bodies are retained within their corresponding v2 tables.

M1.justification: The hint-injection procedure, faithfulness metrics, faithful@k estimator, unlearning procedure, Logit Lens method and causal interventions remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and sampling evaluations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: v2 revises portions of the abstract, introduction, metric explanations and results discussion, adds Related Work subheadings, and renames the concluding section Discussion. It inserts a generalization section and swaps Appendices A/B, while retaining the main methodological sequence and much of the exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds a causal graph, larger-model diagnostic plots and a paired-CoT example table, and expands existing result tables and plot panels. It rearranges faithful@k displays and standardizes plot colors and terminology. Figures 3–4 also correct the vertical-axis label from Unfaithfulness to Faithfulness.

R1.justification: v2 adds Arcuschin et al. (2025) and Paul et al. (2024), distinguishing its mediation setup from the latter. Related Work more explicitly acknowledges prior support for CoT monitoring and causal verification, positioning the paper as complementary while retaining its critique of hint-based evaluation.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same metric definitions, faithful@k estimator, activation decoding, mediation effects and unlearning controls. The new causal diagram illustrates existing mathematics; no new formal assumptions, theorem, proof or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The new larger-model and reasoning-model experiments directly address v1's explicit limitation of supporting broad conclusions using only small instruction-tuned models. Additional judge validation, qualitative examples and clearer qualifications strengthen scrutiny and applicability. The new monotonicity argument does not resolve faithful@k's ambiguity about occasional faithfulness, but the expanded relevant evidence and clearer boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and retain matching core experiments and equations. All 18 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds larger-model and reasoning-model experiments, another judge comparison, and qualitative CoT examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on three QA datasets, including faithfulness measurements, inference-time sampling, Logit Lens analyses, causal mediation and judge validation.

results.title: Is Chain-of-Thought Really Not Explainability? Chain-of-Thought Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about disentangled strategy control, efficient two-stage feature identification, over 15% better control effectiveness, and 7% absolute accuracy improvement. The additional experiments do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: The limitations now explicitly acknowledge dependence on manually specified keywords and the preliminary status of negative steering. Appendix F explains that continuous suppression may remove beneficial reasoning steps, trading accuracy for shorter reasoning; Appendix B.2 adds an interpretation of robustness to moderate keyword variation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository pointer, SAE latent width and expansion factor, and explicit single-feature usage. Appendix B.1 substantially clarifies keyword curation through the source model, 100 responses, 50 segments per strategy, annotator, filtering example, and 3–4 hours of effort. The latency experiment also identifies its A100 hardware.

E1.justification: v2 adds financial-domain evaluation on FinQA using Qwen3-8B (Table 10). This is a bounded extension beyond the retained mathematical and scientific evaluations; the existing training corpora and benchmark coverage remain.

E2.justification: Vector Steering is newly evaluated in the error-correction comparison for both models and all three datasets (Table 3). v1 compared only Self-Reflection and Budget Forcing there. The strategy-control and feature-identification comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The original main protocols are retained, but substantial additional protocols appear: evaluation requiring agreement between Gemini and DeepSeek while excluding GPT-4o, continuous negative steering throughout generation, keyword variation using three LLMs, and latency measurement on 100 GPQA samples.

E4.justification: v2 adds keyword-selection robustness analysis (Appendix B.2), a check excluding the feature-selection judge from evaluation (Table 11), and analysis of suppression, reasoning length, and accuracy under negative steering (Appendix F). Existing layer analyses and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates for feature precision and correction rates. v2 adds 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples to Tables 2 and 3 and the alternative-judge results in Table 11. This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting without establishing additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Retained Table 1–3 point estimates are unchanged apart from rounding. New results include Vector Steering correction rates, FinQA effectiveness averaging 0.84 for SAE-Steering versus 0.72 for Vector Steering, latency measurements, and stricter-judge scores. The new negative-steering experiment reports accuracy of 0.4333 versus 0.4667 without steering.

M1.justification: The SAE architecture, two-stage feature identification, additive steering, strength selection, and strategy router remain unchanged. Negative steering tests a different sign and duration of the existing intervention; expanded keyword-curation descriptions clarify the retained procedure.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Local changes clarify tokenwise intervention, expand and subdivide Appendix B, revise limitations, add Appendices F–G and acknowledgments, and update author affiliations and footnotes.

P2.justification: v2 adds five distinct tables (Tables 5 and 8–11), expands Table 3 with comparator rows, and revises uncertainty displays and captions. Figure 1 corrects the backtracking and verification examples. The pipeline figure and existing appendix prompt and case study are relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: The cited works, reference list, related-work discussion, and positioning against prompt-based control, contrastive steering, and activation-based feature selection are unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9, including SAE reconstruction, logit projection, control effectiveness, and the router objective, retain their mathematical content. The added explanations and experiments introduce no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through an activation-based error-correction comparator, bootstrap confidence intervals, and evaluation excluding the feature-selection judge. Added implementation details substantially improve reproducibility, and the negative-steering accuracy cost is explicitly discussed. Table 10 introduces a limited reporting flaw: Think Intervention's stated average is 0.58, while its displayed scores average about 0.51. This does not outweigh the stronger validation and disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAE-Steering. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds financial-domain evaluation, keyword robustness, negative steering, latency measurements, and alternative-judge evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on strategy control, feature identification, error correction, layer effects, and agreement between human and LLM judges.

results.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of a two-stage, trigger-agnostic, data-efficient defense that reduces attack success while preserving instruction-following ability. The additional experiments support these existing contributions without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new measurements as partial representation sharing with preserved output diversity. Appendix F adds an explanation that coherent defensive responses overlap with clean-response features, so suppressing them can damage utility; Appendix E explains poisoning-rate and loss-weight tradeoffs. The pretraining-scale explanation is also softened to a plausible explanation.

D1.justification: Section 4.3 newly specifies the default lambda as 0.1, and Appendix A fills v1's missing gradient-accumulation value with 8. New appendices document tested parameter ranges and coherent response templates. These are disclosures rather than established changes to the original training runs; hardware, optimizer, learning rates, and training times are retained.

E1.justification: The existing datasets and Toxic/Refusal tasks are retained. Appendix G adds a limited input scenario: Llama2-7B is attacked using the natural prompt prefix 'As my personal assistant,' extending trigger coverage without adding a dataset or application domain.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons in Table 1 and v1 Table 3/v2 Table 5 retain Clean-FFT, ONION, Fine-mixing, and the clean/attacked reference models. No comparison method is added, removed, or substantively redefined.

E3.justification: V2 substantially extends evaluation procedures with final-hidden-state PCA overlap, BLEU-2/ROUGE comparisons, attack-poisoning ratios of 10–30%, defensive-poisoning ratios of 0.001–0.01, and lambda values of 0.01–1.0. The original model lineup, splits, budgets, and main evaluation protocol remain unchanged. The 20% attack default was already stated in v1.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained trigger-count, behavioral-mixing, and poisoned-head analyses, v2 adds representation and lexical-overlap analyses, three hyperparameter sensitivity studies, coherent-versus-random defensive-response ablations, and a semantic-trigger robustness test (Section 5.2 and Appendices E–G). These examine previously untested mechanisms, design choices, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The new average overlap scores are additional results, without an accompanying change in uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: The matched original tables retain their numerical values. V2 adds substantial findings in Tables 2–3 and 6–10, including mean subspace overlaps of 0.558 for Toxic and 0.619 for Refusal, failures with coherent defensive responses, and defended semantic-trigger ASRs of 0.000 and 0.014. These are newly reported analyses and scenarios, rather than improvements to the original benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The defensive-poisoning procedure, default trigger–response construction, and training objective in Equations 1–3 remain unchanged. Weight Recovery is renamed Backdoor Neutralization; PCA measurements and semantic-response variants are introduced as analyses of the existing method.

P1.justification: V2 standardizes stage names, corrects local grammar and model-label errors, and updates headings and cross-references. Section 5.2 and Appendices E–G are inserted, with subsequent material renumbered; the existing narrative is largely retained.

P2.justification: Seven new tables—Tables 2–3 and 6–10—substantially expand the displayed evidence, sometimes reusing original default results as reference rows. Original Tables 2–3 become Tables 4–5. The pipeline labels and SCPN/Syntactic heatmap label are updated, and figures and appendix material are repositioned.

R1.justification: The reference lists match after normalizing line wrapping. Related-work coverage and the positioning against existing classification and generative backdoor defenses remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 introduces formal definitions of attacker- and defender-induced hidden-state shifts and a PCA projection-overlap ratio in Equations 4–6. The method equations and existing attention-head criterion are retained; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendices E–G substantially strengthen evidence for the central merging mechanism and previously unexamined choices of poisoning rate, loss weight, and defensive responses. They expose failures as well as successes, while the added lambda and gradient-accumulation details repair reproducibility gaps. PCA configuration and Appendix E.2's per-trigger versus total poisoning interpretation remain insufficiently specified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MB-Defense work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renaming, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds representation measurements, sensitivity experiments, defensive-response ablations, and semantic-trigger evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack and defense experiments across four language models, including accuracy and attack-success results in Tables 1 and 3 and analyses in Figures 4–5.

results.title: Merging Triggers, Breaking Backdoors: Defensive Poisoning for Instruction-Tuned Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about knowledge-graph grounding, implicit rewriting, and scalable cross-domain dataset synthesis. The additional evaluations support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: New Appendices C–E extend the interpretation to complementarity with jailbreak methods, generation-cost tradeoffs, reduced reliance on unnatural token patterns, and robustness across defenses and assessors. Appendix D also infers resistance to perplexity filtering without directly testing that defense. The original limitations concerning entity coverage and adversarial creativity remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds approximate input-token accounting, including 17,500 tokens per target for StealthGraph, and implementation information for the new defense evaluations. It also updates the advertised code/data repository. Existing hardware, training hyperparameters, graph settings, SPARQL code, and generation templates are retained.

E1.justification: v1 explicitly excludes jailbreak-based benchmarks such as TRIDENT. v3 Appendix C evaluates six such corpora, substantially broadening the tested attack-prompt population beyond the earlier public benchmarks and generated variants. The four application domains remain unchanged, and JailBreakV-28K is evaluated only through its text subset.

E2.justification: v3 Table 9 adds WildJailbreak, TRIDENT, FITD, JailBreakV-28K, H4rm3l, and HarmBench as evaluated dataset comparators alongside the retained benchmarks. Table 10 separately introduces estimated token-cost comparisons with FITD, PAIR, and TAP; PAIR and TAP are not separate ASR rows.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen3.5-Plus, GLM-5, and Gemini-3-Pro; LlamaGuard-4-12B; and SemanticSmooth with Vicuna-13B-v1.5 using summarization and paraphrasing. Appendix E adds StrongREJECT ASR@0.5, counting scores greater than 0.5 as successes. These extend the evaluation protocols without revising the retained experiments' settings.

E4.justification: Appendix D newly tests robustness against classifier-based and semantic-transformation defenses, while Appendix E checks whether the main findings persist under StrongREJECT. Appendix C adds approximate generation-cost analysis. The original rewriting-strategy, knowledge-graph, iteration-budget, and backbone analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify random seed 42 and deterministic decoding for the original judge ensemble. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. StrongREJECT is an additional assessment protocol, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original tables' numerical results are retained, but v3 adds substantial results in Tables 9–12. SG-Implicit✓ achieves 26.5% average ASR on the three new frontier targets, versus 11.5% for WildJailbreak; defense bypass rates are 75.0% and 71.5%; and average StrongREJECT ASR@0.5 is 85.5%. These are newly reported results under additional conditions, not improvements over earlier same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The knowledge-graph construction, generation and filtering procedures, alternating rewriting paths, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The SPARQL query and prompt templates also match. Replacing 'dual-path' with 'two-strategy' is a terminology change.

P1.justification: v3 consistently renames RiskAtlas and its variants, changes 'dual-path' terminology, polishes prose, expands affiliations, and adds acknowledgments. Three inserted appendices require updated cross-references, but the original narrative structure and most explanations are retained.

P2.justification: New Tables 9–12 substantially expand the visual presentation of evidence through frontier-model comparisons, token costs, defense results, and alternative-assessor scores. Existing figures and tables are retained with naming updates and reflow; v1's appendix Tables 9–12 become Tables 13–16.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds an explicit distinction from GraphRAG and corrects TRIDENT's described coverage from four domains to three. New benchmark, defense, and assessment references accompany the appendix additions. The central positioning as reusable dataset synthesis rather than target-specific jailbreak optimization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, the prompt-set construction, harmfulness and perplexity definitions, and the definition of successful obfuscation are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions, proofs, or derivations appear. The StrongREJECT threshold is an empirical evaluation addition.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central dataset contribution. Appendix C adds relevant jailbreak comparators excluded from v1, while Appendices D–E address robustness to dedicated defenses and dependence on the assessment framework. The cost comparison also makes the higher estimated input-token burden explicit. Cost estimates remain approximate, and resistance to perplexity filtering is inferred, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from RiskAtlas to StealthGraph. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. Original appendix material is retained and can be matched across renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds benchmark comparisons, defense evaluations, estimated computational costs, and alternative safety-assessment results in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, safety fine-tuning results, domain analyses, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: StealthGraph: Exposing Domain-Specific Risks in LLMs through Knowledge-Graph-Guided Harmful Prompt Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: architecture-preserving on-policy trajectory alignment using two complementary rewards, narrowing the modality reasoning gap, and state-of-the-art performance among 7B-scale models on MMSU and OBQA.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 interprets the Qwen ablation as stage-dependent over-regularization, qualifying the benefit of combining rewards. New discussion addresses preservation of text reasoning, transfer to real speech and paralinguistic tasks, and persistent semantic, domain-logic, and chronological errors. The scale limitation also explicitly expands to untested smaller models.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository pointer, identifies the MMLU auxiliary_train split, clarifies how the internal 7B Phi model relates to the official 5.6B architecture, and documents additional resource measurements. Existing LoRA hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained as Tables 5–6; relocated baseline and teacher-forcing descriptions are not new implementation details.

E1.justification: Section 5.5 and Table 4 add SD-QA, covering real spoken questions with diverse accents and open-ended answers, and the WANG et al. MMSU benchmark for paralinguistic perception. The latter is explicitly distinct from the VoiceBench MMSU used in both versions. Existing training and evaluation coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same comparators, but v2 adds Text-only GRPO to the Phi-4-MM comparison in Table 2. Table 3 additionally reports CoT, standard GRPO, and individual reward-component comparisons on Qwen, which v1 did not report for that backbone. SoundMind-RL is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds a text-only optimization control, free-generation reward tracking, and an explicit runtime/memory comparison on 8 H200 GPUs over three epochs, separating offline data-generation costs. Existing main experiments retain their reported sample counts, balanced eight-completion groups, decoding procedures, and hyperparameters. Identifying the auxiliary_train split clarifies the existing data source rather than establishing a changed split.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Phi reward ablations and layer analyses, v2 adds Qwen reward ablations, the text-only control, real-speech/paralinguistic generalization tests, a 12-domain breakdown, free-generation reward curves, efficiency analysis, and successful and persistent-error case studies. These substantially expand tests of mechanism, applicability, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals for layer-wise similarity, in v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 2. The averaging and confidence-interval description moves to Appendix E. v2 introduces no documented seed counts, repeated-run procedures, accuracy uncertainty estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and all pre-existing Table 2 values are unchanged. Added results include Text-only GRPO's 76.86% average audio and 83.76% text accuracy, Qwen behavior-only alignment reaching 77.71% versus 76.84% with both rewards, and TARS audio results of 57.40% on the new MMSU benchmark and 41.95% on SD-QA. Domain, efficiency, fallback-frequency, and qualitative findings are also added.

M1.justification: The joint speech/text GRPO-DAPO procedure, representation and behavior rewards, correct-text reference selection and fallback, and modality-specific normalization remain unchanged. v2 clarifies mean pooling and evaluates reward variants without changing the proposed TARS algorithm.

P1.justification: Editing concentrates on related work, reward explanations, and a condensed experimental setup. Existing analyses are regrouped and reordered under Section 5, baseline and teacher-forcing details move to appendices, and appendix headings are reorganized. Much of the introduction, original results discussion, and conclusion remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables, Tables 3–4 and 7–10, a training-reward plot in Figure 4, and a row in Table 2. Existing layer plots are relocated and exchange figure numbers without changed data. The hyperparameter and prompt tables become Tables 5–6, with the prompt table reformatted into one column. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of manifold mixup, contrastive learning, joint speech-text training, and interleaving, and distinguishes TARS from SoundMind-RL's sparse rewards. New benchmark and distillation references are included, while the central research positioning remains. Updated author or publication information for AlignChat, Kimi-Audio, and DeepSeek-R1 concerns retained works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same MRR definition, rewards, mean pooling, and modality-specific advantages. v2 adds explanatory prose but no new mathematical assumptions, formal results, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's validation centered on two multiple-choice benchmarks and Phi reward ablations. v2 adds an important text-only GRPO control, tests real/open-ended speech and paralinguistic perception, and reveals that combined rewards are not optimal for Qwen. These additions substantially strengthen evaluation of attribution and applicability, while efficiency measurements and failure cases improve scrutiny. Some added benchmark protocols remain briefly specified and accuracy uncertainty is still unreported, but the overall validation gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TARS study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Inspection of all 12 pages of v1 and 15 pages of v2 supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds text-only GRPO, Qwen reward ablations, generalization evaluations, domain-level results, efficiency measurements, and qualitative cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning-benchmark results, training and reward ablations, LibriSpeech WER, and layer-wise analyses in Tables 1–2 and Figures 2–3.

results.title: Closing the Modality Reasoning Gap for Speech Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace categorical geometric-collapse and knowledge-exclusion claims with associations and partly geometric explanations. V2 also claims preliminary effectiveness on logic and code generation. The headline 62.4% accuracy and 113.7% sampling-efficiency improvements remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 6.3 and Appendix D.3 introduce attention rerouting by semantically structured probes as a hypothesis and allow informational contributions. V2 explicitly states that rank augmentation does not guarantee better reasoning and interprets the new controls as evidence beyond verbosity. Section 8 revises generalization limitations to acknowledge larger-model and nonmathematical evaluations.

D1.justification: V2 documents optimized vLLM deployment, revised component timings, and approximately 3.6 seconds of end-to-end inference per problem. The advertised repository path changes from SOE- to spectral-orthogonal-exploration. Core probe and sampling hyperparameters remain, while the added experiments receive limited implementation detail.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning only. V2 retains the five mathematical benchmarks and adds actual evaluations on ZebraLogic and HumanEvalPlus (Section 5.5/Table 7), substantially extending coverage to logic puzzles and code generation.

E2.justification: V1 compares against Self-Consistency and a random-probe ablation. V2 retains both and adds PRM-guided, step-level Best-of-N comparisons on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and MATH-500 (Table 4). This materially expands the comparator set to reward-guided step selection.

E3.justification: The original difficult-subset Pass@16 protocol remains. V2 adds Qwen3-8B/32B Teachers, alternative 7B Students, matched sampling positions and continuation counts for PRM comparisons, and controls using 16 trajectories per problem with first/last 500-token measurements. Latency evaluation changes from Hugging Face generation to vLLM, and Table 6 introduces normalization by 1.128.

E4.justification: V2 adds controls contrasting short/long and correct/incorrect traces to examine verbosity confounding (Table 5), diversity-threshold sensitivity from 0.80 to 1.00 (Appendix C.3/Table 9), and wall-clock-normalized efficiency analysis (Table 6). The original random-probe ablation and orthogonality distribution are retained.

E5.justification: The three AIME 2025 seeds, 42, 1024, and 2024, and their reporting remain unchanged (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 10). Existing shaded plots are retained. V2 introduces no new uncertainty estimation, significance testing, or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark, ablation, seed, and exploration-curve results remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results for the new comparisons and analyses. Table 7 reports baseline/SOE accuracies of 56.23%/58.72% on ZebraLogic and 10.00%/16.67% on HumanEvalPlus. The 2.60-second Hugging Face latency is replaced by a 0.46-second vLLM measurement under different deployment conditions.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 retain greedy-trace truncation, Monte Carlo manifold estimation, Micro-SVD, eight-token Student probes, orthogonal-residual maximization, and Teacher continuation. Equations 3–7 preserve the same procedure; revised terminology and deployment do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, method exposition, theoretical discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting, with more qualified language and orthogonal-complement terminology. Section 6 is retitled, experimental and appendix subsections are expanded or reorganized, and author/affiliation information changes.

P2.justification: Figures 2 and 4 are substantially redrawn, Figure 1 changes its null-space label, and Figure 6 revises its categories and axis for vLLM timings. Six new tables display added experiments. The orthogonality distribution moves from main-text Figure 7 to appendix Figure 10, with corresponding layout and numbering changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Jiang et al. (2023) for Mistral 7B, Lin et al. (2025) for ZebraLogic, and Liu et al. (2023) for code evaluation. The principal related-work discussion and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V1's Theorem 2 claims exponential spectral decay; v2's Proposition 2 and Appendix D.2 narrow this to rank non-expansion and revise the attention-concentration argument. Section 6.3 removes the infinite-SNR argument and replaces unconditional rank augmentation by a nondecrease statement plus an idealized rank-plus-one case. Appendix D.1 also qualifies the nonlinear-layer argument.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparison/control evidence and overstrong theoretical guarantees. PRM comparisons, verbosity controls, threshold sensitivity, and broader model/task evaluations strengthen empirical support, while Section 6 and Appendix D narrow conclusions to better match the arguments. New experimental details remain sparse, and Table 6 uses arithmetic runtime normalization rather than a matched-time rerun, but the overall gains in evidential support and claim calibration are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOE research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds PRM comparisons, control experiments, larger-model evaluations, threshold sensitivity, and logic/code benchmark results.

before.justification: V1 reports original mathematical benchmark evaluations, rank-decay measurements, probe-selection ablations, and experiments across three random seeds in Section 5 and Appendices B–C.

results.title: Student Guides Teacher: Weak-to-Strong Inference via Spectral Orthogonal Exploration

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion add a quantified practical claim: approximately 50-fold throughput over manual inspection on an eight-H100 server. The central accuracy, cross-survey/task generalization and explanation-quality claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix G replaces the simple declining-tool-use account with explanations involving nonmonotonic exploration and evidence-dependent stopping, using unchanged Figure 6. V2 also interprets annotation efficiency and noise robustness, distinguishes bulk throughput from single-sample processing, and explains specialist DL screening as complementary to Spec-o3 vetting. The formal limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 documents the GPT-5.2 generator, Gemini-2.5-Pro filter, seed examples and expert acceptance used for synthetic data. It adds inference hardware and asynchronous tool-execution information and revises LAMOST instrument specifications. Existing core training disclosures and the project access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds high-redshift QSO evaluation and adaptation, plus CV verification under simulated severe noise (SNR below 5). These extend coverage to substantially different spectral morphology and degraded input conditions. The original LAMOST, SDSS/DESI and O/B/A coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds the science-specialized S1-VL-32B and its cold-start-fine-tuned S1-VL-32B-SFT variant. All previously evaluated comparators remain; these additions do not extend to the retained cross-survey and cross-task tables.

E3.justification: New protocols include QSO and low-SNR tests with 50 positives and 250 negatives, Gaussian-noise injection into CV positives, approximately 200 SFT trajectories followed by full-data RL, and incremental SFT on 96 synthetic QSO trajectories. V2 also introduces a throughput assessment. Existing benchmark splits, metrics and core training settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained training-stage and tool-access ablations, v2 tests cold-start data reduction, three trajectory-generation conditions, and lightweight QSO adaptation. The new QSO and low-SNR evaluations also probe generalization and robustness boundaries absent from v1.

E5.justification: The human/LLM score distributions and Spearman-correlation reporting are unchanged. V2 adds no repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests. Its new trajectory acceptance counts are additional outcomes rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–4 are unchanged. New results include S1-VL comparisons, QSO zero-shot F1 of 71.9 and low-SNR F1 of 78.2 for Spec-o3-7B, and 3B QSO F1 of 73.6 after adaptation versus 68.4 zero-shot. Tables 12–13 add data-efficiency and synthesis outcomes; Section 4.7 reports approximately 0.2 seconds per spectrum in throughput.

M1.justification: The core architecture, inspection loop, SFT/GRPO objectives and reward remain unchanged. Appendices H/J add an auxiliary QSO adaptation procedure using few-shot, answer-guided GPT-5.2 trajectories, Gemini filtering and expert acceptance, followed by incremental SFT.

P1.justification: V2 edits the abstract and contribution bullets, expands the training-dynamics discussion, and adds an efficiency subsection, acknowledgements and supporting appendices. Most existing prose and the main narrative order remain. Affiliation, contact and bibliographic text also receive limited edits.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains two rows, and six compact appendix tables are added. All seven figures retain their content and design. Existing displays are redistributed, including the human rubric moving from Table 7 to Table 11 and the unchanged rollout algorithm moving to a later page.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for S1-VL, post-training/distillation work and inference engines. Section 2.3 shifts its distinction from generic image agents toward scientific knowledge alignment, while Appendix F clarifies complementary screening/vetting roles. Publication-year and venue updates for retained references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The state and trajectory definitions, reward equation, and rollout algorithm are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's expanded behavioral explanations introduce no new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for practical extensibility. V1 left annotation burden untested; Table 12 now shows CV/CS performance within three F1 points using roughly one-fifth the demonstrations, while Table 9 demonstrates adaptation using 96 synthetic QSO trajectories. New science-specialized comparisons and QSO/noise tests strengthen the empirical case further. The throughput protocol remains sparsely specified and uncertainty reporting is unchanged, but the added controlled experiments address important gaps in the scalability argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spec-o3 work. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, with readable tables, equations and figures. Retained material can be matched despite appendix renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original QSO, low-SNR, data-efficiency, synthetic-trajectory and throughput results.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark and generalization experiments, training/tool ablations, and human evaluations of reasoning quality.

results.title: Spec-o3: A Tool-Augmented Vision-Language Agent for Rare Celestial Object Candidate Vetting via Automated Spectral Inspection

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the modular execution-grounded benchmark, atomic/composite separation, standardized execution protocol, and observed capability asymmetry. Five-round reporting strengthens the evidence supporting these retained claims without changing their scope.

C2.justification: V2 introduces an interpretation of tolerance invariance based on essentially exact-or-failed outputs. It replaces v1's treatment of early-terminated models as excluded coverage artifacts with discussion of measured interface failures. Section 7 replaces the single-run limitation with qualifications about overlapping confidence intervals and adds configurable fork-pinning guidance; new cases explain additional failure mechanisms.

D1.justification: New Appendix G details percentage-transfer generation, execution, validator weights, and task-specific amount and balance tolerances. Section 7 newly discloses configuration-based fork pinning, without establishing its use in the reported evaluations. Dependencies, runner interfaces, and the policy of withholding full outputs and traces remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 107 BSC tasks: 62 atomic and 45 composite, with the same transaction, DeFi, query, and advanced-operation coverage. Expanded breakdowns and case studies do not establish additional tasks or domains.

E2.justification: The main 20-model roster is retained after matching aliases. However, Table 2 expands the composite diagnostic comparison from 13 to 20 models, adding entries such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.1. The overhead comparison expands from nine models in v1 Table 9 to seventeen in v2 Table 11.

E3.justification: Table 10 changes reported composite coverage for Qwen3-Coder, Qwen3-Coder-30B, and Devstral-2512 from 0/45 to 45/45. Table 2 removes first-try and ethers-error-rate metrics. New Appendix D.3 introduces re-scoring with tolerance multipliers from 0.5× to 3×; the main execution settings and scoring rules remain stable.

E4.justification: V2 adds a benchmark-wide tolerance-sensitivity analysis and deviation breakdown in Appendix D.3/Table 8. It retains v1's two cases under H.1–H.2 and adds cases covering numerical misinterpretation, planning failure, and partial execution. Difficulty and overhead analyses are expanded, while quantitative first-try and ethers-error analyses are removed.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly reports only one run per model and cannot estimate uncertainty. V2 explicitly increases this to five independent rounds, reporting means, standard deviations, coefficients of variation, t-based 95% confidence intervals, and inter-round Spearman correlations with significance information in Section 5.1 and Table 1.

E6.justification: Scores and rankings are extensively replaced by five-round estimates. Table 1 changes from Gemini-3-Pro leading with 8,217 to Claude-Sonnet-4.5 leading with an 8,236 mean; Gemini-3-Pro's mean is 7,863. Retained case pass rates change from 45% to 59% and 40% to 56%. New tolerance results report invariant scores and rankings. Different repetition protocols preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The JSON task specifications, dynamic parameter sampling, TypeScript interface, composite planning procedure, weighted atomic validation, and step-efficiency scoring remain unchanged. The new walkthrough documents the existing pipeline rather than establishing an algorithm change.

V1 Figure 2 is split into v2 Figures 2–3; several plots are redesigned, a ranking chart and deviation table are added, and diagnostic table columns and figure placements are extensively revised.

R1.justification: The same 16 cited works and substantive related-work positioning are retained. Bibliography ordering, citation formatting, and added reference URLs are presentation changes.

T1.justification: The formal task definitions, planning objective, atomic scoring equation, and composite decay formula are retained. V2's standard confidence-interval formula documents statistical estimation without adding a theoretical result or revising the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit single-run weakness through repeated evaluations, uncertainty estimates, and ranking-stability checks, while adding benchmark-wide validator-sensitivity evidence. Internal score consistency also improves: GPT-5's composite scores conflict between v1 Tables 1–2 (2,443 versus 3,962), whereas both v2 tables report 3,646. These substantial reliability gains outweigh the removed first-try/ethers diagnostics and a limited reporting error: Section 5.1 claims 15 models have CV below 9%, while Table 1 shows 14.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVM-QuestBench research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: V2 reports original five-round evaluations of 20 models and a validator-tolerance analysis covering 10,700 task instances.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 20 models, including benchmark scores, execution diagnostics, and task-level failure analyses.

results.title: EVM-QuestBench: An Execution-Grounded Benchmark for Natural-Language Transaction Code Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about critic staleness, synchronized co-evolution, and saturation-aware refinement. Added experiments support these existing claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds substantive interpretations concerning benefits beyond extra sampling, RCO's fixed-policy disadvantage, critique granularity as a driver of alignment, and a favorable computational tradeoff. The original limitations concerning reward quality and separate reward/critique models remain unchanged.

Table 2 also extends ablation evaluation to Qwen2.5-7B. Existing main benchmark settings remain unchanged.

The detailed WebShop and SciWorld case studies in v1 Appendix E are removed.

The new analyses provide mean gains and percentages without uncertainty estimates; the eight-trajectory control concerns evaluation design rather than repeated-training uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original Qwen3-4B ablation scores remain unchanged. v2 adds second-backbone ablations and Tables 4–7; Table 4 reports overall scores of 20.22 for RCO, 65.18 for LUFFY, and 77.85 for ECHO. The new Table 2 average drop of 9.25 for the Qwen3-4B frozen critic is inconsistent with the displayed scores, whose mean drop is approximately 8.31.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same cascaded rollout, saturation-aware critic reward, group-relative advantages, and synchronized policy/critic updates. The algorithm and critic prompt move to Appendices D and E without procedural changes.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely verbatim, with limited punctuation and cross-reference edits. A new analysis appendix is inserted, the pseudocode and prompt appendices are renumbered, and the case-study appendix is removed. The non-binary-reward explanation moves from Section 5.3 into Table 2's caption.

P2.justification: Table 2 expands from a single-column, one-backbone display into a full-width table with two backbone blocks and an average-drop column. Four new tables replace the extensive boxed case transcripts as supplementary displays, and appendix material is relocated. Figures 1–5 retain their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Zhao et al. MAS-Bench citation and reference, and expands comparative positioning against the already-cited RCO and LUFFY methods. The related-work taxonomy and central distinction between static and co-evolving critics remain intact.

T1.justification: The weighting function, logarithmic gain derivation, additivity and antisymmetry properties, and GRPO objective are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: The matched-sampling control directly addresses an important alternative explanation left open in v1: that refinement gains merely reflect additional sampling. Established critique-method comparisons and second-backbone ablations substantially strengthen validation, while runtime reporting makes the cost tradeoff assessable. These benefits outweigh reduced case-level auditability and the new average-drop arithmetic error, although the alignment analysis lacks uncertainty reporting and does not establish its stronger causal interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ECHO framework and four-environment study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including identifying relocated material and removed case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Qwen2.5-7B ablations, additional baseline comparisons, refinement and alignment analyses, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results for two backbones, component ablations, failure-distribution analyses, and training/refinement observations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: No More Stale Feedback: Co-Evolving Critics for Open-World Agent Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: controlled real-photo counterfactuals, FOCUS, REFLECT's three tasks, and persistent demographic disparities that vary across tasks and models. Condensing four contribution bullets to three does not remove the empirical contribution, which remains stated elsewhere.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning residual editing artifacts, scenario-dependent refusals, template stability, and decoding sensitivity. It distinguishes robust distributional disparities from weaker mean effects, limits cross-editor conclusions to the tested MCQ subset, and explicitly distinguishes visual gender presentation from gender identity.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies a code repository link. Appendices add editor and evaluator identifiers, crop-construction details, biography-audit criteria, subset construction, and sampling settings. Existing main-task prompt templates and implementation descriptions are largely retained.

E1.justification: Appendices C.7–C.8 add MCQ evaluations for software developer and construction laborer, plus an exploratory androgynous-presentation condition. Mirroring and cropping also extend tested image conditions. These are targeted extensions; the original six-occupation, 480-image benchmark remains intact.

E2.justification: The five-model evaluation panel and VisBias comparison are retained. Appendix C.2 newly compares the original gemini-3-pro-image-preview editor against gpt-5-image through matched MCQ evaluations using GPT, Gemini, and Qwen.

E3.justification: V2 adds protocols for spatial transformations, editor substitution, explanation-augmented answers, template removal, and stochastic decoding at temperature 0.7, plus polarization metrics. Figure 8 revises the 2AFC description from the same person in two versions to different people edited from one photograph. This documents a prompt revision without establishing that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: V1 mainly provides face-localization and demographic-label checks. V2 adds extensive tests of face–body mismatch, expression drift, mirroring/cropping, biography quality, prompt framing, filtering, position bias, editor dependence, template sensitivity, explanations, and decoding randomness in Appendices B–C.

E5.justification: V1 already reports cluster-robust salary significance tests, retained as v2 Table 13. V2 additionally reports template-cluster bootstrap and Wilson confidence intervals and explicitly adds stochastic repeated sampling: five runs per MCQ query and three for Income 2AFC.

E6.justification: The original MCQ JSD tables and salary p-values are retained as v2 Tables 2, 3, and 13. Substantial new results include polarization, cross-model correlations, filtering diagnostics, robustness outcomes, and coverage extensions. Examples include 12.1% expression drift and 0.940 correlation after expression filtering; these are newly reported analyses.

M1.justification: The core face-editing pipeline, FOCUS construction method, and three-task REFLECT framework remain unchanged. Alternative editors, prompts, and presentation conditions are evaluated as auxiliary experimental variations.

P1.justification: V2 condenses and edits the introduction and findings, updates affiliations and corresponding-author information, and adds acknowledgments. Appendix subsections expand to organize the new analyses, while the main narrative structure remains substantially the same.

P2.justification: V2 adds ten analytical tables and redraws the main and appendix result charts with revised legends, axes, annotations, and panel arrangements. Figure 5 becomes full-width, and existing figures and tables are redistributed through the expanded appendices.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of VIGNETTE, hiring halo effects, multimodal debiasing, modality bias/conflict, and face-perception research, alongside additional model citations. These broaden supporting context while retaining the original positioning around realism and control in counterfactual bias evaluation.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 introduces formal definitions of the polarization index and extreme-cell rate over pairwise win rates. Existing win-rate, mean-gap, and JSD definitions remain substantively unchanged; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V1's attribution argument relied mainly on face-localization and label checks. V2 directly tests several residual confounds and quantifies template and decoding uncertainty, substantially strengthening empirical credibility. Table 9 also reveals weaker mean effects alongside robust distributional disparities. Signed gaps remain sensitive to editor choice in Table 8, limiting claims of complete robustness, but the added validation addresses important weaknesses in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FOCUS dataset and REFLECT benchmark. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original evaluations and adds empirical robustness checks, audits, uncertainty analyses, and exploratory coverage extensions.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM evaluations on three tasks, dataset quality checks, and salary significance tests in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Measuring Social Bias in Vision-Language Models with Face-Only Counterfactuals from Real Photos

C2.justification: Section 4.6 newly argues that history and mutation provide benefits beyond standard fine-tuning. D1.justification: The v2 abstract adds a stated code-availability link, absent from v1. Existing LoRA settings, training hyperparameters, synthesis model, embedding model, agent schemas, and mutation prompts are retained; repository contents are not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training sources, MCP-Universe domains, MCP-Mark environments, agent-routing benchmark, and expanded/noisy candidate scenarios. The human audit samples existing synthesized trajectories without adding a new domain or routing task.

The original comparators remain in Tables 1–2 despite Appendix A describing replacements.

The existing benchmark settings, training configuration, Gemini-2.5-Pro executor, and evaluation temperature remain unchanged.

Appendix B adds a human audit of simulated supervision. These directly examine component contributions and label reliability beyond v1's retained history and robustness analyses.

Appendix F calls these confidence intervals and asserts statistical significance, but specifies neither interval construction nor a significance test.

E6.justification: New MCP-Universe/MCP-Mark results include 47.12/44.00 without mutation, 46.70/42.00 for vanilla fine-tuning, and 44.88/42.00 for Qwen3-Embedding-8B, alongside BM25, Contriever, and kappa=0.93 results. Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 retain their original outcomes. Appendix Table 9 has small discrepancies from retained Table 2, including 52.59 versus 52.60 for the proposed router under MCP-Universe +LiveMCP.

M1.justification: The candidate graph, mutation operators, trajectory synthesis, history-conditioned router, and two-tool Light Routing Agent remain unchanged. ACE-Router is a renaming; the newly evaluated ablation variants do not revise the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 applies the ACE-Router name throughout, makes localized introduction edits, updates author information, and adds acknowledgments. Section 4.6 and new appendices extend the existing structure; most retained prose and the original appendix content remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 3 changes from a radar plot to sorted bars with explicit percentage labels, preserving its results. Tables 3–5 add displays for ablations, retrieval comparisons, and label agreement; Tables 8–9 redisplay existing comparisons with uncertainty. These substantially expand the visual evidence while retaining the original tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the new retrievers, recent agent research, and an explicit evolutionary-method attribution to Novikov et al. It removes citations including GraphOracle and SEAL-Tools. The central positioning against static retrieval and context-compressing routing remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The routing formulation, candidate specifications, selection rule, graph similarity definition, and trajectory representation in Equations 1–5 are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: The new component ablations and human audit address important gaps in v1's evidence for mutation's contribution and simulated-label reliability. Additional retrieval comparisons and variability reporting substantially strengthen empirical assessment while headline results remain stable. Sparse details for the added protocols and Appendix F's confusion between standard deviations, confidence intervals, and statistical significance limit rigor, but the new evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from ToolACE-MCP to ACE-Router. Their full text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable. The original appendices A–C are retained as C–E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, retrieval comparisons, human assessment of synthesized labels, and variability estimates.

before.justification: v1 reports original MCP benchmark experiments, agent-routing results, scalability and noise tests, and a history-removal ablation in Section 4.

results.title: ACE-Router: Generalizing History-Aware Routing from MCP Tools to the Agent Web

Updated dataset counts and supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

Appendix K.3 explains authenticity ambiguities and cross-property errors. Discussion also revises the interpretation of open-model competitiveness and adds limitations concerning ambiguous claims, satire, and evaluation of evidence quality.

The longitudinal sample grows from 2,400 to 2,500. Appendix J.1 retains temporal search filtering but no longer specifies v1's fact-checker-domain blacklist, leaving its continued use unresolved.

It also adds language/integrity breakdowns, baseline confusion matrices, and detailed analysis of human–model disagreements.

Human integrity accuracy changes from 96.8% to 97.5% on an expanded sample. Numerous new subset, ablation, and sensitivity results are reported.

P1.justification: V2 makes local language corrections, expands scoring and metric explanations, rewrites parts of the Discussion, and reorganizes the appendices. The main section sequence and most introductory and methodological prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are refreshed or redrawn, and v1's compact statistics table becomes v2's substantial Figure 4 infographic. The principal results table gains grouped subset columns. New discretization diagrams, analysis tables, distribution plots, confusion matrices, and browser screenshots substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The reference lists and related-benchmark comparison are substantively unchanged. Updating XFacta's stated time since its last update from five to eight months preserves the same research positioning.

Stale appendix counts, conflicting smoothing-window labels, and unclear blacklist documentation remain, but these reporting issues do not outweigh the stronger validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VeriTaS benchmark. All 27 pages of v1 and 35 pages of v2, including their appendices, tables, figures, and scoring definitions, support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original Q1 2026 evaluations, expanded human validation, and new shortcut, duplication, and pipeline-backbone sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark statistics, human annotation validation, Q4 2025 model evaluations, and longitudinal performance analyses.

results.title: VeriTaS: The First Dynamic Benchmark for Multimodal Automated Fact-Checking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about reusable RL skill vectors, orthogonal updates, efficient adaptation, and benchmark improvements. V2 adds supporting evidence without revising those central claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking orthogonality to principal versus off-principal updates, explaining refinement benefits as regularization and excessive sharding as an unstable RL signal, and assessing how much target-RL benefit PaST recovers. Appendix C broadens the interpretation of orthogonality across tasks and domains. The explicit limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds a front-page MuLabPKU/PaST code-repository link and documents hardware and per-document RL runtimes for the new comparison. Existing implementation recipes, prompts, hyperparameters, and data-processing details are retained. The link establishes an access pointer, not verification of repository contents.

This directly tests the alternative computation PaST avoids, which v1 did not evaluate. Existing SEAL, synthetic-data, target-SFT, and transfer-strategy comparators are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds supplementary protocols: a LooGLE refinement sweep with ten source documents and fixed total RL steps; target GRPO at 25, 50, 75, and 100 steps on the existing first-ten-document evaluation subset, timed on eight A100 GPUs; and cross-domain update-pair controls. Existing main evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3.1 expands LooGLE refinement analysis to test finer sharding and excessive iteration. New Section 5.3.3 examines the accuracy-cost tradeoff against target RL. New Appendix C tests orthogonality across the three benchmarks and across source/target update combinations, extending v1's LooGLE heatmap and SFT–SFT control.

E5.justification: Both retain three-run averaging for the main LooGLE and ToolBench results and the same LooGLE three-generation sampling protocol. V2 introduces no new run-count disclosures, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Headline benchmark scores are unchanged. New Table 6 reports target-RL accuracies of 38.2, 41.2, 44.0, and 46.2 at 33, 52, 72, and 91 minutes per document, against PaST's retained 44.6. Table 4 retains LooGLE results 42.9 and 44.6, adds 45.3 and 42.1, and omits the previous five-document single-round result of 41.7. Tables 10–11 add numerical orthogonality results.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same sequential SFT/RL skill extraction, linear target injection with lambda = 1, and iterative refinement procedure. Additional refinement configurations are experiments with the existing method.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites the task-vector discussion, expands the ablation narrative, adds Section 5.3.3 and Appendix C, and updates subsequent appendix references. It also changes an affiliation and adds acknowledgments. The overall narrative and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 4, 6, 10, and 11 and restructures Table 3 to cover SQuAD alone, presenting the expanded LooGLE analysis separately. Existing figures and other tables are retained with relocation and renumbering; the overall visual design is unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 expands the comparison with the already cited Reasoning Vectors, emphasizing sequential versus parallel extraction, orthogonality evidence, and iterative refinement. Section 3.2 adds Zhu et al. (2025) to support the optimization-subspace interpretation. The broader related-work coverage remains stable.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix C becomes v2 Appendix D with the same assumptions, equations, expectation calculation, Hanson–Wright argument, and functional-disentanglement conclusion. The newly cited theoretical explanation does not introduce a new formal derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 claimed an efficient alternative to target RL without directly measuring that accuracy-cost tradeoff. V2 Table 6 addresses this important evidential gap: PaST reaches 44.6 versus 46.2 for 100-step target RL, which takes 91 minutes per document. The refinement sweep and cross-task/domain orthogonality controls also substantially strengthen support for the central mechanism. These gains concern validation rather than higher headline scores. Their limits remain clear: timing covers target-side RL only, and the added results provide no new uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PaST research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds target-domain RL comparisons, refinement sensitivity results, and further orthogonality analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original PaST evaluations on SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench, including ablations, parameter-update analyses, and case studies. Some comparison scores in Table 1 are explicitly attributed to SEAL.

results.title: Knowledge is Not Enough: Injecting RL Skills for Continual Adaptation

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies the weakest-link claim by the 18-document, three-bucket setting, while the contributions and conclusion explicitly claim replication across additional datasets, hop counts and model scales. The central account of divergent MFAI effects changes from real-world versus synthetic data to vertical versus horizontal task topology.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the synthetic-data/model-prior explanation with task topology and distractor homogeneity. Section 3.1 acknowledges oracle access and search-space reduction, treating matched-MFAI gains as an upper-bound estimate of recognition difficulty. The limitations additionally acknowledge answer-format confounding and strict-EM sensitivity.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code/data release; v2 supplies a repository link and reports release of code and curated artifacts under a permissive license. It also specifies the heatmap layer range and priority sampler, higher-hop placement rules, quantized checkpoint and token-counting procedure, and documents residual batching nondeterminism.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on the Compositional and Inference subsets of 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue three- and four-hop questions. It also tests NeoQA with random-timeline distractors instead of only same-timeline distractors, expanding both reasoning requirements and input conditions.

The reported heatmap sample increases from 20 to 100 examples, with priority-fill selection specified in v2. The original two-hop dataset sizes and accuracy metrics remain.

It extends gold-only and no-document ablations to higher hops. The earlier unmatched-variant analysis is retained and consolidated in Appendix A.9.

Its rewritten attention appendix drops v1's description of standard-error intervals for focus curves. Seed 42 remains fixed; no increase in independent experimental seeds is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive dataset, higher-hop, model-scale, robustness and compute-cost results in Tables 5–16. Retained results also change: Figure 3 reports MuSiQue Ministral-8B Unmatched accuracy for Beginning+Middle as 20.7% in v1 versus 22.69% in v2. The original two-hop gold-only and no-document table values are retained.

M1.justification: The original two-document MFAI prompt and training-free procedure remain. Appendix A.7.2 makes a limited higher-hop adaptation: instructions target three or four documents, and unmatched instructions mirror their indices into an empty bucket selected with T > M > B priority.

P1.justification: Substantial rewrites affect the abstract, contributions, unmatched-instruction discussion, conclusion and limitations. Appendix A.4 is condensed and rewritten, and the earlier unmatched-variant specification and analysis are merged into A.9. Terminology changes from 'Law' to 'Effect', alongside widespread language corrections.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial statistical, validation and robustness tables, expands ablation tables with higher-hop columns, and redraws the main bar charts with confidence intervals and revised overlays/legends. It replaces the displayed attention heatmap and adds a separate MuSiQue heatmap. v1 Figure 7 is retained as v2 Figure 8.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ho et al. (2020), Efron and Tibshirani (1994), and McNemar (1947) for the new dataset and statistical analyses. The main related-work positioning remains largely intact. Publication and author-metadata corrections concern already cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 newly defines paired binary outcomes, the continuity-corrected McNemar statistic and its chi-square null distribution. The weakest-link probability argument and attention aggregation remain substantively unchanged; the rewritten normalization exposition adds no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow empirical validation through additional dataset, hop-count and model-scale checks, targeted controls, and statistical uncertainty reporting. It also addresses important interpretation weaknesses by acknowledging MFAI's search-space confound and the datasets' answer-format confound, while improving reproducibility documentation and reporting code/data release. Some categorical causal assertions in Section 4 remain stronger than these qualifications permit, but the broader evidence and clearer limitations provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MFAI study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the expanded experiments and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations involving 2WikiMultiHopQA, higher-hop questions, a 32B model, distractor changes and instruction-order sensitivity.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuSiQue and NeoQA evaluations, attention analyses, and gold-only and no-document ablations in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Failure Modes in Multi-Hop QA: The Weakest Link Effect and the Recognition Bottleneck

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about GPT-5's synthetic-data advantage and the advantage enjoyed by models contributing to pooled ground truth. It recommends real data for absolute performance assessment and explains unsuccessful efforts to collect non-CS real examples. New analyses also support interpretations concerning reference-provider bias and long-context difficulty versus truncation.

Hardware, decoding settings, and code/data access information are largely retained.

E2.justification: The main evaluation adds Gemini 3.1 Pro, increasing the lineup from 21 to 22 models. The reported code-only comparison replaces GPT-5 Nano with Gemini 3.1 Pro. More substantially, pooled-ground-truth comparisons, previously reported for three models, now additionally cover all 22 models in v2 Table 6.

E3.justification: V2 accepts matches against either reference description where two exist, changing the main evaluation rule. Dataset composition changes from 81 real and 530 synthetic discrepancies to 92 and 543, including 13 targeted synthetic paper omissions. Human validation expands from 12 papers and 135 predictions to 20 papers and 224 evaluations; the pooled reference set grows from 67 to 129 discrepancies.

E4.justification: V2 adds an alternative Qwen3 32B judge check, reference-description agreement and provider-bias analyses, a relevant-file-position analysis addressing truncation, and a correlation analysis excluding the GPT-5 family. It also expands human error analysis and pooled evaluation. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's existing code-only, language, and synthetic-code analyses.

E5.justification: V2 adds Cohen's kappa estimates for agreement between judges and between evaluations using alternative reference descriptions (Section 4 and Appendix B.1). The existing fixed-seed, five-run mean and standard-deviation reporting remains unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is reported.

E6.justification: The main result tables change substantially: GPT-5's real-data recall is 45.7% in v1 Table 5 and 41.3% in v2 Table 9, while GPT-5 Mini and newly evaluated Gemini 3.1 Pro lead v2 at 46.7%. Changed samples and matching rules prevent interpreting these shifts as controlled performance gains or losses. New agreement, bias, truncation, and pooled-result entries considerably expand the reported evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes final discrepancy validation and rephrasing from GPT-5 alone to GPT-5 plus Gemini 3.1 Pro, with manual verification of disagreements. This revises one data-construction component; the synthetic generation and discrepancy-prediction procedures and substantive prompts remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The appendices undergo substantial reorganization: implementation information is consolidated in A, analyses and results are grouped in B and C, examples move to D and E, and prompts move from B to the final Appendix F. Main-text prose receives smaller edits, while limitations and evaluation explanations expand.

P2.justification: V2 adds the reference-comparison Figure 7 and Tables 5–8, revises the correlation plot with a second fit, and expands real examples to display both providers' descriptions. The error table moves into the appendix and gains categories. Prompt boxes are redesigned across full-width pages, substantially changing appendix presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting science automation, long-context limitations, incomplete pooled judgments, and verification-oriented peer review, including Boiko, Levy, Buckley and Voorhees, and You. The existing related-work categories and central positioning remain intact. Bibliographic updates to retained works are not new research relationships.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical propositions or proofs. The discrepancy definition and taxonomy remain substantively unchanged. Additional agreement statistics and alternative descriptions of existing mathematical examples do not introduce new formal reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for benchmark validity through second-provider verification with manual adjudication, explicit judge/reference-bias checks, and broader pooled validation. These address v1's dependence on GPT-5-generated references and narrow precision assessment; new synthetic-data and pooling limitations also improve interpretation. Local reporting defects temper the gain—for example, Appendix C.3 gives Gemini 3.1 Pro's final-bin recall as 31.3%, whereas Table 8 reports 37.3%—but do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SciCoQA by the same authors. Their complete text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material across the reorganized appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations of 22 LLMs, expanded human validation, and additional analyses of judges, reference descriptions, pooled results, and context effects.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 21 LLMs, code-only ablations, human validation of predicted discrepancies, and quantitative dataset analyses.

results.title: SciCoQA: Quality Assurance for Scientific Paper–Code Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, and conclusion retain the benchmark's novelty and scope, weak domain performance, limited specialization gains, forgetting findings, and Claude Code's 34.2% result. Additional supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly recognizes the agent-backbone confound and interprets the controlled results as showing a remaining agent-system gap. It also interprets tested sequence lengths as having limited influence on SFT performance and discusses multi-attempt performance ceilings. The original limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix K.2 newly documents random file concatenation, endoftext separators, fixed-length training chunks, and use of all chunks for SFT/LoRA. Section 4.1 clarifies agents' project/corpus access, and Appendix D identifies the new retriever and training-pair generator. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same six domains, eleven frameworks, twenty-five projects, code-generation tasks, and knowledge-understanding questions (Tables 1 and 7). The added experiments reuse this coverage; revised code-length statistics do not establish a dataset change.

E2.justification: Appendix D adds two variants within existing specialization families: Dense RAG using EmbeddingGemma and instruction tuning on Gemini-3-Flash-generated requirement/code pairs (Table 9). The original LLM, agent, and specialization comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial experimental controls: SFT sequence lengths of 4096 and 8192 alongside 2048, and Claude-Sonnet-4-5 as the shared backbone for agent comparisons (Appendices E and G). Appendix D also introduces instruction-supervised training. These supplement the retained original settings; ten-sample Pass@any at temperature 0.8 was already specified in v1.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether short training sequences explain weak SFT performance and whether different base models explain agent performance gaps (Appendices E and G). Appendix F also supplies evidence about success across multiple generation attempts. Existing forgetting, corpus-size, error, contamination, and case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix G.1 already specifies ten samples for Pass@any, retained in v2 Appendix K.1. The new sampling tables do not introduce seed sweeps, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 9-13 add baseline, ablation, sampling, and agent-control results. For example, Claude-backed SWE-Agent and OpenHands achieve 18.5% and 17.5% average Pass@1; these are new configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Original main result tables remain unchanged. Section 4.1 corrects 28.2% to 30.3%, matching Table 4; Table 1 revises maximum corpus/project lengths from 40.0k/67.4k to 400.5k/674.0k lines.

M1.justification: The proposed benchmark construction, knowledge-corpus organization, task formulation, and requirement/test creation procedures remain unchanged in Section 3. Dense RAG and instruction tuning are added comparison baselines, not revisions to the proposed benchmark method.

P1.justification: V2 makes limited prose additions around agent controls and implementation details, inserts Appendix sections D-G, and updates cross-references, author information, and funding acknowledgments. The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained.
