P2.justification: Five new tables present baseline variants, sequence-length ablations, paired Pass@1/Pass@any results, and agent controls, substantially extending the appendix's tabular presentation. The existing contamination table becomes Table 14. Table 2 is enlarged/reformatted, Figure 2 moves, Figure 3 is resized, and other retained material reflows.

R1.justification: V2 removes the RiskAtlas citation and reference. Research positioning otherwise remains stable. Duplicate Yu and Zheng bibliography entries are consolidated without removing the underlying cited works.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces a theoretical contribution. Existing task and metric definitions remain unchanged, including Pass@any already described in v1 Appendix G.1; the new sequence-length conclusions are empirical.

improvement.justification: V1's agent comparison mixes base models; v2 Table 13 controls that important confound and strengthens interpretation of agent differences. Additional retrieval/training baselines and sequence-length tests address plausible explanations for weak specialization performance. Corpus-packing documentation and corrected numerical summaries improve reproducibility and consistency. Together these substantially strengthen the empirical support for the paper, although equal inference budgets are not established for the new agent controls.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KOCO-BENCH research. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across appendix renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds baseline comparisons, a sequence-length ablation, sampling results, and agent-control experiments in Appendices D-G.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of LLMs, specialization methods, and coding agents, alongside continual-learning experiments, contamination measurements, and project-generation analyses.

results.title: KoCo-Bench: Can Large Language Models Leverage Domain Knowledge in Software Development?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the benchmark and two-stage framework contributions, joint reasoning/language-fidelity claims, scaling claims, and generalization claims. Headline performance numbers remain identical; the appendix experiments provide additional support rather than redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for MCQ-first data construction, interprets human-rating differences, and relates reversed ordering to transfer failures. Appendix F organizes and extends failure-mechanism discussion, but much of it reprises existing tables and the Spanish example. The stated limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices B and D substantially expand reproducibility documentation with exact SFT/RFT prompts, teacher-generated target construction and verification details, GPU memory and node configuration, software versions, and training-time estimates. These are newly disclosed details, without evidence that the retained experiments used different settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 15,774-instance, 13-language CUREMED-BENCH and the same MMedBench, MedExpQA, and MedQA evaluations. Additional models and curriculum ordering tests introduce no new datasets, languages, or task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix G and Table 13 add eleven evaluated comparators from DeepSeek-Qwen, Qwen3, MedReason, MedS3, and m1 families. This substantially broadens comparisons with reasoning-oriented and multilingual models while retaining the original baseline and proprietary-model comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix H introduces a reverse-order training control, proceeding from low- through medium- to high-resource languages at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B. Existing splits, evaluation metrics, judges, and stated training hyperparameters remain unchanged; additional execution details are disclosures rather than established protocol revisions.

E4.justification: V1's ablations compare supervised and reinforcement training variants without directly testing curriculum order. V2 adds a targeted ordering ablation across three model sizes in Table 14, substantially extending evidence about a central design choice. Appendix F mostly interprets existing results rather than supplying a separate new error-analysis experiment.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 newly specifies random seed 42. Three independent runs and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting already appeared in v1 and are retained for the new comparisons. No increase in run count or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Tables 13 and 14 add substantial baseline and reversed-curriculum results; Tables 2–12 retain their numerical entries. For example, the newly reported reversed 7B curriculum achieves 64.21% language consistency and 36.58% logical accuracy, compared with the unchanged default results of 85.21% and 54.35%.

M1.justification: The proposed code-switched SFT, composite reward, standard GRPO, high-to-low resource curriculum, and 0.85 retention ratio remain unchanged. The new training prompts document the existing procedure; reversed curriculum ordering is an experimental ablation.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering are retained. V2 adds appendix navigation and subsections, condenses Appendix E.4, and updates author information, acknowledgments, and citation style. These are limited editorial and structural changes beyond the separately assessed scientific additions.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, extensively resizing and relocating tables and figures. Figure 5 changes from side-by-side to vertically stacked panels. V2 also adds the training-prompt Figure 8 and Tables 13–14, with subsequent appendix figures renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations concerning healthcare generation, automation, and multilingual resources, including MedSumm, CAREPILOT, and RELIC. It also explicitly explains prompt adaptation from already-cited Hwang et al. The principal positioning around jointly improving medical reasoning and language fidelity remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The dataset definition, SFT objective, reward definitions, composite reward, and curriculum mixture equation are unchanged. V2 adds no theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V1 attributes benefits to curriculum training without directly testing its ordering. V2 addresses this important validation gap with the reverse-order control in Table 14, strengthens comparisons through Table 13, and supplies previously missing training prompts and execution details. Together these substantially improve support for the central contribution and reproducibility. The ordering evidence remains limited to 1.5B–7B, and much of the new failure discussion reuses existing evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CURE-MED study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and identifying v2's added appendices F–H.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluations of additional baselines and reversed curriculum ordering.

before.justification: V1 reports original multilingual model evaluations, component ablations, out-of-distribution experiments, and human verification scores.

results.title: CURE-Med: Curriculum-Informed Reinforcement Learning for Multilingual Medical Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add an explicit claim that probe ordering and competitive performance generalize across dense and MoE model families. v1 treated cross-backbone validation as future work. This substantially broadens the claimed applicability while retaining the original method and efficiency contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new results as evidence that the safety signal is not specific to Llama or dense architectures. Revised limitations restrict this evidence to ToxicChat and roughly 3B active parameters. A new failure-scenarios discussion identifies novel harms and evolving jailbreaks as situations where dedicated guards may remain necessary.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds backbone-specific hidden dimensions and hyperparameter ranges, plus A100 80GB extraction followed by RTX 3090 probe training. The code-access reference changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository. These are focused reproducibility additions; repository accessibility was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ToxicChat, WildGuardMix, IMDB, SST-2, and Emotion, including WildGuardMix-to-ToxicChat transfer. Additional backbones change model configurations, not dataset or task coverage. SST-2 already appears in v1's downcasting table.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds ToxicChat-T5 (780M) and WildGuard (7B) to the efficiency comparison previously using Llama Guard 3 (8B). Although these methods already appeared in classification comparisons, their efficiency participation is new. Classification comparator membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: ToxicChat evaluation expands from Llama-3.2-3B to GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, adding materially different backbone configurations. Appendix A specifies backbone-specific attention-head ranges and fixes downcasting to 32 for both additions. The SST-2 description changes from 'standard split' to Palma's 7,000-example subset, consistent with v1's limitations; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds an explicit architecture-robustness analysis testing whether probe ordering depends on Llama or dense architecture, finding the same ordering on two MoE backbones. This addresses a previously untested generalization question. Existing distribution-shift, attention, sensitivity, and downcasting analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The existing uncertainty-reporting practice is retained. Table 7 still specifies mean and standard deviation across three runs, while new Table 1 rows use the existing ± format. No new seed information, run-count disclosure, confidence intervals, or significance procedures appear.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds results for all three probe variants on two backbones, including MHA F1 scores of 86.17 for GPT-OSS-20B and 83.76 for Qwen3-30B-A3B. These are new configurations, not same-setting improvements. Table 5 adds T5 and WildGuard pipeline latencies of 88.33 and 100.32 ms. Original benchmark and appendix results are retained; the Llama Guard memory change is equivalent rounding.

M1.justification: The frozen-backbone, two-stage token/layer aggregation method, pooling and attention variants, and cross-entropy objective remain unchanged. Revised layer counts correct the formulation; the expanded refusal discussion does not establish an implemented procedural change.

P1.justification: Localized edits improve wording, clarify inference and dataset descriptions, and revise the experimental narrative and limitations. Appendix B now explicitly mentions the SST-2 ablation already tabulated in v1. The overall section organization and most prose are retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains backbone groups, Table 5 gains guard rows, Table 2 separates ShieldHead under a reuse heading, and Table 6 gains backbone-specific footnotes. Captions and pagination change, but the architecture illustration, attention plots, sensitivity figure, and downcasting table are retained without substantive visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds EAGLE-3 as supporting precedent for combining representations across depths, along with GPT-OSS and Qwen3 technical references. The existing positioning against logit reuse, fixed-layer probes, and standalone guards remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects off-by-one indexing and parameter-count expressions to include the embedding output: hidden states run from 0 through L, and aggregation-module counts change from L+1 to L+2. Figure 2's uniform-weight formula becomes 1/(L+1). These are limited mathematical corrections, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for portability and efficiency: Table 1 addresses v1's explicit single-backbone limitation, and Table 5 tests savings against a compact T5 guard as well as larger guards. More specific failure conditions and active-capacity qualifications improve the applicability discussion. The new backbones remain tested only on ToxicChat, and invocation-free re-prompting is asserted without evaluation, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence for the paper's central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. All 13 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, equations, figures, and tables, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds ToxicChat experiments with two additional backbones and efficiency measurements for two additional guard pipelines.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification results, latency measurements, attention analyses, hyperparameter sensitivity, and downcasting ablations.

results.title: A BERTology View of LLM Orchestrations: Token- and Layer-Selective Probes for Efficient Single-Pass Classification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: evidence-centric rebuttal planning, concern-conditioned evidence construction, inspectable verification, and RebuttalBench evaluation. Additional experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope or novelty.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of the checker's coverage/constructiveness tradeoff, interpretations supporting human-aligned judging and criticizing overlap metrics, and explanations of comparator weaknesses. New limitations address latency, cost, incomplete artifact reuse, and venue conventions; an ethics section discusses misleading responses and confidentiality. Some interpretations overreach, notably the zero-leakage claim despite Table 3 showing Tier 3 cases classified as Tier 1.

D1.justification: Appendix D expands documentation of filtering priorities, confidence tiers, ambiguous-case handling, and the 106-case benchmark count; it does not establish that the benchmark was resampled. v2 also identifies the RAG embedding model as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and documents new study procedures. The abstract's code-release promise is removed, while the project and demo links remain.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds a supplementary evaluation on recent CVPR 2026 submissions, comprising 33 review-comment cases assessed by nine authors. This extends the represented manuscripts and evaluation population beyond the retained ICLR 2023 benchmark, while preserving the rebuttal-generation task. Annotation of the existing 106 benchmark cases does not constitute additional dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares against direct-to-text outputs from four model backbones. v2 retains these comparisons and adds standard RAG, AutoGen, and Jiu-Jitsu in Appendix F/Table 7, all using Gemini3-Flash. These introduce retrieval-based, general multi-agent, and prior rebuttal-specific comparators, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include blind human annotation of 106 cases, an author study comparing four systems on 33 cases using three 1–5 rating dimensions, and rescoring Gemini-generated outputs with GPT-5-mini instead of the default Gemini judge. Appendix E also introduces a BLEU-4/ROUGE-L case comparison. The original main evaluation protocol and nine-component rubric remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds validation of outcome labels and confidence tiers, human–automated evaluation agreement, judge-model robustness, a case examining overlap-metric limitations, and a checker case investigating inflated coverage from verbose responses. These are substantial new analyses of benchmark reliability and system behavior. The original component ablations and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix E introduces statistical association estimation through Kendall rank correlation between human and automated scores, reporting tau = 0.646. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the system comparisons; the new assertions of statistical validation are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 are unchanged, but Tables 3–7 add substantial results. Examples include reported 100% outcome-label accuracy, alternate-judge averages of 3.84 versus 4.13, and human faithfulness scores of 2.88 versus 4.33 for Gemini and RebuttalAgent-Gemini. Table 7 reports RAG 3.11, Jiu-Jitsu 1.42, and AutoGen 3.56 against RebuttalAgent 4.23. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The Rebuttal Letter Writer prompt changes its missing-experiment rule: v1 Appendix D requires invented plausible numbers marked with an asterisk; v2 Appendix H prohibits fabrication and requires [TBD]. This changes the specified drafting procedure while retaining the architecture. However, the following rule still refers to speculative, asterisk-marked data. The PDFs do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. Changes include local wording and naming edits, removal of a duplicated filtering sentence, new limitations/ethics sections, and insertion of Appendices D–G. Existing prompt templates and case studies move from Appendices D/E to H/I without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds five substantive tables: an annotation confusion matrix, alternate-judge results, human-study scores, corresponding automated scores, and expanded baseline comparisons. Figures 1–3 and the original Tables 1–2 retain their content and basic presentation. Existing boxed prompts and case studies are retained with page reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds five references, including Kendall's rank-correlation paper and VBench++, primarily around the new evaluation discussion. Appendix F adds explicit positioning against RAG, AutoGen, and Jiu-Jitsu. The main related-work sections remain substantially unchanged; the LED-merging publication update is bibliographic rather than a new cited work.

T1.justification: The score-aggregation equations and existing mathematical case-study content are retained. The added discussions of information-theoretic arguments and Utility/Reward clarification describe illustrative rebuttal cases; they introduce no developed theorem, proof, or formal analysis of RebuttalAgent.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical case relies on an unvalidated single LLM judge and direct-to-text baselines. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through actual-author evaluation, alternate-judge checks, and RAG/AutoGen/Jiu-Jitsu comparisons. The drafting-rule correction also addresses an important conflict with the paper's faithfulness goal. These gains outweigh material remaining flaws: the prompt still mentions speculative asterisk-marked data, and Table 3 contradicts the claimed zero tier leakage by showing 2/6 human Tier 3 cases assigned Tier 1. The revision provides substantially better evidence, although its strongest reliability claims remain overstated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Paper2Rebuttal/RebuttalAgent. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. Existing prompts and case studies can be matched across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds human annotation, author evaluation, alternate-judge evaluation, additional baseline results, and qualitative analyses in Appendices D–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original RebuttalBench comparisons and component ablations in Tables 1–2, plus generated-response case studies in Appendix E.

results.title: Paper2Rebuttal: A Multi-Agent Framework for Transparent Author Response Assistance

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the empirical contribution from BFCL robustness to generalization across TAU-Bench and TAU2-Bench, claiming leading results across most settings and gains up to 17.4 percentage points. The original fission contribution and headline BFCL gains remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments separating fission benefits from teacher-provided feedback information and additional update counts, interprets simulator generalization and leakage assessments, and argues that training remains stable. The limitations now identify tool-calling as the evaluation boundary rather than BFCL alone and discuss costs at larger model scales or with expensive APIs.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code repository link and discloses alpha=0.5. Algorithm 1 is reconciled with the main text concerning ground-truth simulator input, deduplication by context and failed call, and composite-reward computation. The first two details already appeared in v1's prose. Hardware, principal training hyperparameters, and simulator prompt templates remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates on BFCL alone. v2 adds TAU-Bench Retail/Airline and TAU2-Bench Retail/Airline/Telecom, introducing simulated-user interactions and different tool environments. Section 4.5 also evaluates simulator failures from unseen e-commerce order-management and calendar-scheduling domains. The original training-domain coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds AWPO as an evaluated comparator at Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, including on the retained BFCL benchmark. The existing Base, GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, ToolACE-2-8B, and BitAgent-8B comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces pass@1 evaluation with GLM-5 simulated users, simulator judging on 200 in-domain and 200 out-of-domain failures, a 100-output human assessment, and comparisons matching 312 or 432 updates with G'=G. The trigger study's stated budget also changes from 234 total global steps to 234 standard updates; the PDFs do not establish that its retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The original feedback ablation, trigger sensitivity study, and recovery case remain. v2 adds simulator generalization and leakage assessments in Section 4.5, controls testing whether additional updates explain gains in Section 4.6, and training-stability analysis through reward curves in Appendix B.

E5.justification: v2 first reports inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa of 0.71 for two annotators assessing 100 simulator outputs. Both versions mention multiple runs for threshold selection, but neither specifies training-run counts, seeds, or benchmark confidence intervals. Increased repeated training is not established.

E6.justification: Existing BFCL scores, feedback-ablation values, and original plotted results remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive TAU results, simulator-quality findings, and matched-update accuracies: Fission-GRPO versus GRPO scores 46.75 versus 41.75 at 432 updates and 46.12 versus 43.75 at 312 updates. Added AWPO results also change the Missing Parameter leaders at 4B and 8B.

M1.justification: The three-stage framework and Error Simulator architecture remain. Section 3.2 revises the reported reward design: the maximum format contribution decays from 3 to 2 instead of 2 to 1, aggregation explicitly divides by three, and the length penalty is recast as a positive compliance reward. Whether these revisions reflect implementation changes or corrections to its description is not established.

P1.justification: Existing passages are substantially rewritten or condensed across the abstract, introduction, both related-work subsections, main results, feedback discussion, and limitations. Main-result subheadings are consolidated, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and a training-curve appendix is inserted before the retained algorithm and case-study appendices.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with model-group headers and three benchmark column groups; Tables 3–4 and training Figure 5 are added. Figures 1b and 3 are redrawn, with Figure 3 changing from horizontal to vertical panels. Table highlighting and placement change, while the simulator prompts and case visualization are retained as Figures 6–7.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench, AWPO, Silver and Sutton's experience-based learning perspective, and several online/deep-research agent works. These broaden the motivation and neighboring literature while retaining the central positioning against offline error corpora and existing GRPO variants.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the normalized composite reward, corrects the stated functional-reward range from [0,2] to [0,1], and replaces the gradient expression labeled as an objective in Equation 6 with a clipped-ratio/KL surrogate consistent with the existing pseudocode. These are limited mathematical corrections; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked evaluation beyond BFCL and direct simulator-quality or matched-update checks. v2 substantially addresses these gaps through broader interactive benchmarks, automated and human simulator assessments, and update-matched controls in Tables 1, 3, and 4. Corrected equations and pseudocode further improve clarity. Benchmark uncertainty and total simulator costs remain insufficiently quantified, but the added evidence materially strengthens the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fission-GRPO work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds TAU-Bench and TAU2-Bench evaluations, automated and human simulator assessments, matched-update comparisons, and training curves.

before.justification: v1 reports original BFCL experiments across three Qwen3 sizes, feedback ablations, trigger-frequency sensitivity results, and a qualitative recovery case study.

results.title: Robust Tool Use via Fission-GRPO: Learning to Recover from Execution Errors

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the benchmark contribution and central claim of difficulty with negation-based composition. The conclusion adds a more specific scientific claim that difficulty arises from interacting atomic plausibility, operator-grounding, and distractor effects.

C2.justification: v3 supplements the earlier heuristic and operator-grounding account with an interaction-based explanation supported by decomposition experiments. It also interprets human solvability, similar weaknesses across open and proprietary models, and lower composite diversity caused by deterministic reuse. The limitations are updated to reflect decoder-only fine-tuning and explicitly acknowledge untested downstream transfer.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3.1 supplies construction prompts missing from v1, whose prompt appendix contained evaluation templates only. Appendix A.5 adds the new LLaMA fine-tuning configuration, including NF4 quantization, LoRA parameters, learning rate, batch size, and hardware. Section 3 clarifies candidate counts, filtering, and annotation coverage. Code and dataset access destinations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same CommonsenseQA-derived data and four benchmark conditions are retained. Appendix A.7 adds diagnostic task coverage through independent atomic plausibility classification, operator verification given gold atomic labels, and composition without competing distractors, changing task requirements within the existing domain.

E2.justification: v3 adds Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview to zero-shot comparisons and supervised LLaMA-3.1-8B to fine-tuning comparisons, substantially broadening the evaluated model configurations. Section 5 also adds a small human performance reference. All earlier model comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces QLoRA fine-tuning for LLaMA-3.1-8B, human evaluation using 10 human-validated examples per condition, and controlled decomposition evaluations with gold atomic labels and with or without distractors. Diversity metrics are added and the annotation-agreement metric changes. Existing dataset splits, accuracy/macro-F1 metrics, and prompting settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 3 adds lexical and semantic diversity analyses addressing generation collapse. New Appendix A.7 separates atomic plausibility, operator grounding, and distractor effects through Tables 7–8, while the human evaluation checks task solvability. The original qualitative error analysis is retained as Appendix A.8 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 3 replaces Cohen's kappa with ordinally weighted Gwet's AC2 and reports awareness and consensus agreement separately. This changes the statistical estimator and reporting granularity, without establishing additional annotation rounds. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for model performance.

E6.justification: Previously reported model scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. On the human-validated NEITHER/NOR subset, Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview achieve 23.5 and 39.6 macro-F1, and fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1-8B achieves 89.5. New human, diversity, and decomposition results include NEITHER/NOR accuracy of 71.2 without distractors versus 46.8 with distractors in Table 8. Agreement results also change under the replacement estimator.

M1.justification: The proposed three-stage benchmark construction pipeline, GPT-4o-mini generation and refinement, deterministic composition, and operator semantics remain unchanged. Newly supplied construction prompts document the existing procedure; fine-tuned models and decomposition procedures are evaluation additions.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local terminology and count clarifications, expanded experimental discussion, subdivision of the prompt appendix into construction and evaluation templates, and insertion of decomposition analysis before the existing error analysis.

P2.justification: v3 adds diversity and decomposition tables, expands and compresses existing model-comparison tables, relocates the retained error table, and moves resource URLs into footnotes. These are localized additions and layout adjustments within the retained two-column design and table style.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations supporting Gemini evaluation, agreement estimation, and diversity measurement: Comanici et al., Gwet, Li et al., and Tevet and Berant. The related-work discussion and central research positioning remain unchanged. The revised Qwen citation identifies the same technical report.

T1.justification: The operator interpretations and benchmark formulation are retained. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs; the added standard empirical metrics do not introduce a new theoretical framework or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence about the source of benchmark difficulty and its missing construction prompts. The decomposition controls, supervised LLaMA comparison, broader model coverage, and construction and training documentation materially strengthen experimental support and reproducibility. The human study remains small, and replacing kappa with AC2 does not establish improved annotation quality; these qualifications limit the added validation without outweighing the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA, with matching benchmark construction, operator definitions, and retained experiments. The main text, appendices, and tables are readable, and relocated or renumbered content can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds model comparisons, human task performance, dataset-diversity measurements, and task-decomposition experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation agreement and label-validation results, model accuracy and macro-F1 experiments, and qualitative error analyses in Section 3, Section 5, and the appendices.

results.title: LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA: A Benchmark for Logical Commonsense Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: top-1 gaps provide membership signals, sequential smoothing exploits local correlations, and Gap-K% achieves leading WikiMIA/MIMIR performance. Added experiments do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking Pile-CC difficulty to entropy and preferred window sizes to architecture, plus interpretations of the new gap and selection analyses. Limitations now distinguish evaluated recent models and strong paraphrasing from untested larger scales and adaptive evasion. Appendix A newly discusses low-FPR variability.

D1.justification: New setup information specifies WikiMIA-25's length-64 split, DIPPER's diversity parameters, and Mistral-7B v0.1. These provide limited additional reproducibility detail. The original implementation defaults and code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains WikiMIA's original/paraphrased settings and MIMIR's seven domains, while adding WikiMIA-25 to address temporal overlap with recent models' training data. It also introduces strong DIPPER paraphrasing, substantially extending the evaluated temporal population and input-transformation conditions.

E2.justification: Loss, Zlib, Neighbor, Min-K%, and Min-K%++ remain the benchmark comparators, including in new Tables 6–7. The Min-K%++ formula correction does not establish a change to the evaluated implementation; corresponding retained scores are unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include LLaMA 3.1-8B and Gemma2-9B base/instruction-tuned models, window sizes 2–8 across OpenLLaMA/Mistral/LLaMA, and DIPPER with lexical and order diversity both 60. Existing benchmark splits, MIMIR overlap settings, detection metrics, and default k/window settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds large-gap token-frequency analysis, DIPPER robustness testing, domain-entropy analysis, architecture-focused window-size comparisons, and all/random/top/bottom token-selection controls (Tables 3, 7, 10–12). Earlier locality/component ablations, sensitivity plots, histograms, and qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2 Appendix A adds a qualitative explanation of TPR@5%FPR variability, without introducing uncertainty estimates or statistical testing.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and ablation values are retained. New results include Gap-K% versus Min-K%++ AUROC of 84.1 versus 82.7 on LLaMA 3.1-8B/WikiMIA-25 and 66.6 versus 65.5 under DIPPER. Table 12 adds bottom-selection versus all-token AUROC of 74.8 versus 68.6; other additions report gap frequencies, entropy, and window-sweep results.

M1.justification: The normalized top-1 log-probability gap, sliding-window averaging, and bottom-k% aggregation remain unchanged in Section 3.3, Equations 5–7. New experiments test the existing method and its variants without modifying the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 refines gap terminology and explanatory prose, revises the research questions, consolidates the author block, and adds acknowledgments and appendix subsections. The main section sequence and most of the existing narrative remain stable.

P2.justification: New tables substantially expand the visual presentation of gap statistics, recent-model evaluation, paraphrasing robustness, entropy, window sensitivity, and selection controls. Existing tables are retained and renumbered where necessary. All nine figures remain, with selected caption refinements and relocations as the analysis and appendix layouts expand.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting WikiMIA-25, DIPPER, Gemma2, Mistral, and OpenLLaMA, and replaces the LLaMA 2 reference with the original LLaMA paper. Section 2's related-work organization and central novelty positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 2 corrects Min-K%++'s selection set: v1 reuses I_k, defined using raw token probabilities, whereas v2 explicitly defines I'_k using the lowest normalized z_t scores. The proposed method's mathematics and gradient derivation remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's untested recent-model applicability (Table 6), directly examining the gap signal and bottom-k selection (Tables 3 and 12), and adding strong-paraphrasing evaluation (Table 7). These additions answer important validation questions while preserving earlier evidence and clarifying applicability limits. Uncertainty estimates and adaptive-attack tests remain absent, and the architectural and entropy explanations remain tentative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gap-K% research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, and retained material can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds recent-model evaluations, DIPPER paraphrasing experiments, and diagnostic analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gap-K% evaluations on WikiMIA and MIMIR, component and locality ablations, sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples.

results.title: Gap-K%: Measuring Top-1 Prediction Gap for Detecting Pretraining Data

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the open-weight failure claim to small models. The introduction corrects the named leading VLM from Gemini to GPT-4.1, and the conclusion changes the stated human–VLM gap from 10 to 12 points. GPT-4.1 already leads v1's Table 2, so its identification corrects the narrative. The central benchmark contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about humans receiving compass/context unavailable to VLMs, missing expert visual grounding, and unrecorded expert deliberation. It also interprets the new agreement, chain-length, and downsampling analyses as supporting the evaluator and visual-encoding explanation. The principal failure-mode interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: New Section A.5.1 documents sampling temperatures and generation limits, including larger Qwen completion budgets and judge output limits. These are newly disclosed settings; v1 supplies no corresponding budgets establishing a version-to-version change. V2 also identifies expert annotators and specifies CC BY/Apache licensing and code for reconstructing query images.

E1.justification: The 500-scene, 800-chain GeoRC dataset and geolocation task remain unchanged. Figure 25 adds a limited low-resolution test scenario: Gemma-3 processes two scenes at 256 × 256 alongside their original 2880 × 1546 resolution. Newly discussed external datasets are not evaluated.

E2.justification: Section 4.2 replaces Random Hallucinated chains sampled from unrelated locations with Random chains sampled from human-written expert chains. Table 2 includes this revised comparator. The other baselines, nine candidate VLMs, and three judging methods remain.

E3.justification: Judge evaluation adds Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation metrics to MAE, and Figure 25 introduces a controlled resolution comparison. Section 4.4 changes the stated country-accuracy reference from location coordinates to ISO-format country labels. The main sample counts remain unchanged; these descriptions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's MAE histograms and qualitative failure examples, v2 adds Bland–Altman judge-agreement diagnostics, chain-length versus F1 analyses, and an explicit two-image resolution ablation showing changed clues and location guesses. These substantially expand checks of scoring validity and visual sensitivity (Sections A.4–A.5; Figures 20, 22, 25).

E5.justification: V2 first reports 95% F1 confidence intervals for human experts and VLMs, inter-annotator ICC3/ICC3k statistics, and Bland–Altman limits of agreement (Tables 5–6; Figures 20, 23). V1 lacks this uncertainty and reliability reporting. V2 does not specify the confidence-interval construction or establish additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 broadly revises precision, recall, and F1 values: human-average F1 changes from 53.92 to 56.69, Gemma-3 from 31.21 to 25.23, and GPT-4.1 from 42.30 to 43.74; country accuracies remain unchanged. Table 1 changes one-to-all MAE for VLM candidates from 12.13 to 12.54. The appendix also adds agreement, uncertainty, chain-length, and downsampling results.

M1.justification: The three judging procedures, precision/recall/F1 scoring approach, and judge models remain unchanged. Appendix Algorithms 1–3 and the functional scoring instructions are retained; prompt edits are grammatical.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are partly rewritten, grammar and some cross-references are corrected, limitations and ethics become numbered sections, and the appendix gains an experimental-setup subsection. The overall narrative order and most dataset and method explanations are retained.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Tables 3–6 and Figures 20, 22, 23, and 25 covering positioning, agreement, uncertainty, chain length, and resolution. Table 1 gains a correlation row, Figure 6 is redrawn, and Table 2 is relocated. The existing generation prompt and supplementary failure examples are retained under new figure numbers.

R1.justification: Section 5 and new Table 3 substantially expand positioning through comparisons with GRE30K, MP16-Reason, GeoExplain, NAVIg, and GeoComp. V2 explicitly distinguishes its standardized expert annotation and human-calibrated evaluator from synthetic, scraped, and consensus reasoning datasets. Publication updates and consolidation of duplicate references are separate bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. The scoring definitions and algorithmic mathematics are retained; the added statistical evaluations do not introduce new mathematical reasoning or formal properties.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential basis: v1 relies chiefly on MAE comparisons and point estimates, while v2 reports annotator agreement, complementary judge diagnostics, and uncertainty intervals. It also corrects narrative/table inconsistencies, addresses closely related work, and improves reproducibility and disclosure of limitations. Important weaknesses remain: confidence-interval construction is unspecified, and the blanket no-correlation interpretation overstates results such as Qwen2.5-VL's r = -0.253. Nevertheless, the gains in validation and transparency constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GeoRC benchmark. Their complete text, figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: The original benchmark experiments remain, with additional agreement statistics, uncertainty estimates, chain-length analyses, and image-downsampling experiments.

before.justification: Tables 1–2 report original experiments comparing automated judges with human grading and evaluating human and VLM geolocation reasoning.

results.title: GeoRC: A Benchmark for Geolocation Reasoning Chains

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the claim that overall performance surpasses existing efficient methods to achieving the highest average score among the methods evaluated. The abstract and conclusion retain the same principal architecture, complexity, extrapolation, and application claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of model-dependent performance, the remaining Full Attention advantage on long documents, and RWKV7's prefill/memory tradeoff. Appendix J offers compression-related explanations for Qasper failures and qualifies their uniqueness. A new societal-impact section discusses privacy risks tied to processing user histories; the original limitations paragraph remains.

D1.justification: v2 changes the advertised code location from an anonymous host to a named GitHub repository. It additionally documents the 3.95M-parameter overhead, xRAG's vector encoding, 5–7-digit passkeys, and RWKV implementation details and kernel limitations. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 extends length-extrapolation evaluation from synthetic passkey retrieval to realistic GovReport and NarrativeQA inputs exceeding the 32k training length, reaching 484k tokens (Appendix D). Table 9 also adds NQ and NarrativeQA evaluations explicitly distinguished from SCROLLS. Original task coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Appendix G adds RWKV-7-Goose-World-2.9B-HF as an efficiency comparator; v1's efficiency comparisons used Full Attention. Comparator membership in the original Tables 2–4 is unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation configurations include Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, a 4,854-example SCROLLS subset above 32k tokens, and sweeps over adapter rank, chunk size, compression interval, and temporary-memory budget. The existing training settings remain unchanged; the agent experiment already used Qwen3-8B in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of backbone generalization, realistic length extrapolation, adapter-rank sensitivity, and chunk/compression/memory choices (Tables 5–7 and 9). Appendix J adds four Qasper failure cases examining detail loss, causal reasoning, and information aggregation. Existing memory ablations and gating analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. Substantial new results include CoMeT SCROLLS averages of 43.14 on Qwen3-14B and 40.55 on Llama-3.1-8B, and long-subset NarrativeQA F1 of 13.2 versus SWA's 5.8. Tables 6 and 8–10 add sensitivity scores, runtime measurements, and qualitative failure outcomes under additional settings.

M1.justification: The chunk-processing procedure, residual low-rank adapters, gated global memory, FIFO temporary memory, and layer-level pipeline parallelism remain unchanged. The added scheduling illustration and hyperparameter experiments document and evaluate the existing method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. Changes include localized wording clarifications, expanded abbreviations and affiliation information, additional analysis subsections, ethics and acknowledgments sections, and reorganized appendix labels.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables covering generalization, extrapolation, sensitivity, efficiency, and failure cases, plus a pipeline execution diagram. Existing illustrations and tables are repositioned, and captions gain clarification. The original graphics are retained, including the all-layer gating visualization renumbered from Figure 11 to Figure 12.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Related Work section are unchanged. The introduction qualifies its previously categorical criticism of context compression to typical settings, while Appendix G adds direct positioning against RWKV7's efficiency tradeoffs.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, RLA and gated-update equations, and complexity reasoning remain unchanged. The new pipeline diagram and empirical analyses introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the existing method: additional backbones and realistic extrapolation tests address important gaps left by v1's predominantly single-backbone academic evaluation and synthetic extrapolation evidence. The new ablations and failure analyses make design choices and limitations more assessable, including the remaining Full Attention gap and RWKV7 prefill advantage. Although statistical uncertainty remains unreported, the broader evidence provides a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoMeT study and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Existing material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, including the retained appendix analyses and gating visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original evaluations across model backbones, long-document extrapolation tests, hyperparameter ablations, an efficiency comparison, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, passkey retrieval experiments, memory ablations, and inference-efficiency measurements in the main text and appendices.

results.title: CoMeT: Collaborative Memory Transformer for Efficient Long Context Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from foregrounding conditional uncertainty reduction as the main proposal to three pillars: foundations, four technical challenges supported by numerical studies, and future directions. The original formalization remains central, while information gating becomes an appendix recommendation within the broader agenda.

C2.justification: v3 develops substantive interpretations concerning estimator access and cost, external-observation distribution mismatch, auxiliary world-model approximation, and weak trajectory discrimination. It also argues for evaluation beyond final task failure and substantially expands the multi-agent and self-improving-agent discussion. These extend v1's narrower focus on interactivity and reducible uncertainty.

D1.justification: v3 adds model and API-provider identifiers, inference settings, estimator implementation formulas, and exact prompts for verbalized confidence and observation approximation. Appendix E adds example action-classification prompts, and the front page supplies project and artifact-dataset links. v1 provides only a high-level implementation sketch.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluation on tau2-bench Retail order-management tasks and Telecom troubleshooting tasks. v1 uses benchmark scenarios only as conceptual examples. The change is the introduction of empirical task coverage, rather than the corrected tau2-bench naming.

E2.justification: v3 introduces empirical comparisons among NLL, token entropy, and verbalized confidence in Table 2, plus agent-based, auxiliary-LLM, and user-simulator observation estimates in Figure 8. v1 discusses estimator families without evaluating them. The information-gating proposal itself is not benchmarked against these methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces an experimental protocol using 114 tasks per domain, two agent models, a fixed Kimi-K2.5 user simulator, temperature 0, top-five-token entropy, and trajectory aggregation. Appendix F also specifies AUROC, Spearman and Kendall correlations, and normalized-turn trajectory comparisons. v1 has no corresponding experimental protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether agent probabilities approximate external observations, whether an auxiliary LLM reduces that mismatch, and whether uncertainty trajectories distinguish successful from failed tasks. Figures 3–4 and 8–10 provide empirical diagnostics beyond v1's illustrative examples.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports one trial per task, correlation significance markers at p < 0.05 and p < 0.001, and one-standard-deviation bands across trajectories. v1 contains no such reporting. Appendix F.2 calls the bands confidence intervals, although Figures 9–10 identify them as standard deviations; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds numerical and qualitative results absent from v1. For GPT-4.1 Telecom, Table 2 reports AUROC values of 0.624 for NLL, 0.611 for entropy, and 0.685 for verbalized confidence. New plots report observation-distribution mismatch and weak success/failure separation, while the benchmark survey finds turn-level evaluation in 4 of 44 benchmarks.

M1.justification: The action-dependent information gate, uncertainty components, and mutual-information reduction mechanism are retained from v1 Section 4.2 in v3 Appendix E. Added prompts illustrate previously proposed implementation options; the pilot experiments do not establish a revised gating algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution framing, and conclusion are rewritten around the broader agenda. Section 4 is extensively reconstructed into four challenges, the original proposal and supporting material are consolidated in Appendix E, and the appendices gain a contents page and revision history. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v3 adds empirical tables, observation-density plots, trajectory panels with dispersion bands, a benchmark-survey pie chart, benchmark inventories, and prompt boxes. v1 Figures 3–4 are retained as v3 Figures 6–7, and Tables 1–2 become Tables 3–4. The new displays and relocation substantially reshape the presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial benchmark-literature survey organized by evaluation granularity and expands positioning around recent agent UQ, multi-agent communication, and self-improvement research. Newly discussed works include Confidence Estimation for LLMs in Multi-turn Interactions, Agentic Uncertainty Quantification, and structured uncertainty-guided clarification. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The stochastic-agent definitions, uncertainty expansion, reductions to existing UQ settings, gating bound, and extrema proof retain their mathematical substance. v1's theory and appendices are reorganized into v3 Sections 3 and Appendices B–E. The new experimental estimator formulas document standard implementations rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's lack of empirical grounding for its critique of existing UQ through diagnostic experiments, a documented benchmark inventory, and concrete reproducibility information, while preserving the original framework. The evidence remains preliminary: there is one trial per task, only four Kimi-K2.5 Telecom failures, and an incorrect confidence-interval description of standard-deviation bands. The gating proposal also remains unvalidated. These limits constrain the conclusions, but the new evidence materially strengthens the paper's broader diagnosis of agent UQ challenges.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same agent uncertainty quantification work, despite the changed title and emphasis. v3 Appendix A explicitly identifies the revision, and the complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original experiments with GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.5 on tau2-bench Retail and Telecom, including estimator comparisons and trajectory analyses. It also reports an original categorization of 44 agent benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 presents a conceptual framework, proofs, illustrative trajectories, and action-category examples. It reports no original empirical study outcomes and explicitly leaves implementation for future work.

results.title: Uncertainty Quantification in LLM Agents: Foundations, Emerging Challenges, and Opportunities

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions and conclusion retain their scientific claims about AudioSeg, acoustic cues, ASR robustness and transcript-invariant evaluation. The added experiments support and investigate these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 identifies temporal localization as an MLLM bottleneck, interprets transfer to meetings, explains re-discretization artifacts, and connects duration with speaker complexity. It also adds an explanation for adapted encoders' weaker standalone performance. Limitations now acknowledge small-scale AMI validation while retaining generalization concerns.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future AudioSeg release; v2 reports its release and supplies a model-access link in the first-page footnote. Existing hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts and feature-extraction details are retained across appendix renumbering. Availability is reported by the PDF, not externally verified.

E1.justification: V2 extends v1's YTSeg-only coverage to AMI multi-party meeting segmentation, including training and evaluation in this distinct domain. It also tests explicit timestamp prediction with and without transcription. Title generation itself was already present in v1.

E2.justification: Table A11 adds BART as a title-quality comparison reference, with results attributed to Retkowski and Waibel (2024). Its oracle segmentation and reference-transcript setting are explicitly identified. The original segmentation comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds AMI-only versus YTSeg-to-AMI training comparisons, short-meeting and all-meeting evaluations, T1 evaluation at 8/10/12 seconds, and T2 scoring at ±3/±6 seconds. It also introduces temporal-matching and global-concatenation title evaluation using BERTScore and ROUGE-L. Original six-second evaluations and documented training settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test pretraining transfer to AMI, sensitivity to evaluation granularity, and timestamp-localization errors using predicted versus forced-alignment timestamps. Duration analysis gains segment-density and speaker-composition statistics. Existing acoustic-feature, DeepFilterNet and MLLM failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing plot bands and dataset summary reporting are retained. Neither new run counts or seeds nor new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are documented. Added performance tables report point scores.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial AMI, timestamp, title-quality, granularity and continuous-time results. For example, Table 7 reports 12.52 F1 using Qwen3-Omni's predicted timestamps versus 43.84 using forced alignment of the same outputs. Table A8 reveals AudioSeg/MiniSeg-with-features ranking reversals at 8/10 seconds. Original table scores are retained; Section 5.1 corrects 37.74 to 37.76, matching the unchanged Table 4.

M1.justification: Section 3.4.1 adds MLLM inference formulations producing timestamps and titles, either directly or alongside transcription. These extend the output procedure. AudioSeg's architecture, feature fusion and existing training objectives remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language and cross-reference corrections, adds a temporal-grounding research question and subsection, and inserts a title-quality appendix. Subsequent sections and appendices are renumbered, while most existing prose and the overall organization are retained.

P2.justification: The results presentation expands substantially: Table 7 gains a timestamp-variant block and explanatory notes, and new appendix tables display AMI comparisons, granularity sensitivity, continuous-time scores, title metrics and duration statistics. Existing figures and tables are retained, with several relocated.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds positioning against VAD and ASR chunking, while Appendix B discusses prior segmentation and title-evaluation approaches. Additional citations cover AMI, downstream chapter applications and encoder adaptation. The central novelty framing remains stable.

T1.justification: New Appendix B formally defines temporal title matching through endpoint tolerances and global title comparison through chronological concatenation, including unequal chapter counts. Existing segmentation definitions and alignment mathematics remain unchanged; no proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's single-dataset evidence and six-second main evaluation through AMI transfer tests and granularity/continuous-time checks (Tables A5–A9). Its same-output timestamp analysis also identifies a concrete MLLM failure mechanism. These additions address important validation gaps. Small AMI samples, ranking exceptions under re-discretization and an unspecified title-matching tolerance limit the conclusions, but the overall gain in empirical support and diagnosis is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AudioSeg study. All 19 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support comparison. Retained content can be matched across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original AMI, timestamp-prediction, title-quality and evaluation-sensitivity results (Table 7 and Tables A5–A11).

before.justification: V1 reports original YTSeg experiments comparing segmentation models, acoustic features and inference strategies, alongside ablations and failure analyses (Tables 4–7 and A1–A6).

results.title: Beyond Transcripts: A Renewed Perspective on Audio Chaptering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: anti-distillation while preserving teacher utility, and reliable watermark detection with nearly zero false alarms. The headline 61.3-point student accuracy reduction is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving rewriter error correction, degenerate repetition behind low baseline perplexity, and CDG-KD's mismatch with behavioral watermarks. Its answer-only interpretation is overstated: Table 4 shows one improvement over OPT, 6.5% versus 5.3% for Llama-3.2-1B on MATH. The main limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository URL in the abstract and identifies the reference, judge, and additional models used in the new analyses. Existing prompts, optimization settings, LoRA hyperparameters, preprocessing, and hardware disclosures are retained. Repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K/GSM8K-Platinum, MATH, MMLU, and MMLU-Pro. The additions reuse these datasets and downstream tasks; they vary distillation procedures, model configurations, or measurements rather than introduce new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the adaptive comparisons by evaluating KPOD against anti-distillation and CDG-KD against watermarking in Figures 5–7. Table 4 also introduces an answer-only comparator. ADS, DOGe, and the four existing watermarking baselines remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include perplexity and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judgments on 150 MATH traces, adaptive and answer-only distillation procedures, and varied teacher/rewriter configurations. The original dataset splits, standard SFT budget, and principal accuracy/detection metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of trace quality, resistance to KPOD and CDG-KD, removal of reasoning supervision, and dependence on teacher/rewriter size. The Direct ablation and paraphrasing/filtering tests already existed in v1; their relocation alone is not an addition.

E5.justification: New Table 2 reports mean perplexity with standard deviations across 150 traces. This adds sample-variability reporting, not evidence of repeated training runs. Both versions retain the 100 independent trials per query budget for watermark detection.

E6.justification: The retained headline comparisons in Figures 2–3 and Table 1 are unchanged, but substantial results are added in Figures 5–7 and Tables 2–5. Examples include quality scores of 3.83 for OPT versus 4.01 for original traces, answer-only accuracies, and a 27.5-point student accuracy reduction with a 7B teacher and 7B rewriter.

M1.justification: The semantic and optimized prompts, gradient-based variants, HotFlip procedure, and watermark insertion method are retained. The added attacks and model-size experiments evaluate the existing proposed methods rather than change them.

P1.justification: Related Work becomes a standalone section, appendix robustness material is consolidated into Section 6.4, and new analysis subsections and acknowledgments are added. There are localized wording and author-line edits, while most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 changes typography throughout, adds four tables, and relocates and expands v1 Figures 9, 14, and 15 into main-text Figures 5–7 with new attack series and revised legends/captions. The resulting display reorganization is substantial; other retained figures are principally renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Feng et al. (2024) and Yi et al. (2025) for the evaluated adaptive methods, plus Hsieh et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2025) for answer-only interpretation. The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: The formal objectives, rewriting constraints, prompt-scoring expression, and gradient/HotFlip derivations are retained. The single-source assumption emphasized in v2 was already present in v1. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central requirements that v1 evaluated incompletely: preserving trace quality and resisting adaptive distillation. Appendix B directly measures quality, Section 6.4 tests additional adaptive methods, and Table 5 establishes effectiveness beyond the original 7B-teacher/120B-rewriter pairing. These gains outweigh the limited overstatement of answer-only results, although that interpretation should acknowledge Table 4's exception.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same trace-rewriting study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds trace-quality measurements, adaptive-distillation comparisons, answer-only distillation, and model-size analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original teacher/student accuracy and watermark-detection experiments, including appendix ablations, additional benchmarks, and adaptive-distillation tests.

results.title: Protecting Language Models Against Unauthorized Distillation through Trace Rewriting

C1.justification: The introduction revises advertised error-recovery success from 88.7% to 90.0%, alongside the newly explicit success definition. The training-free FSM and grounding contributions, abstract's 95.6% compliance claim, and conclusion about the necessity of symbolic safety interlocks remain.

C2.justification: Appendix G introduces reasoning-context overflow as a limitation of thinking-model backbones and emphasizes efficiency with lightweight models. Section 4.6 interprets the revised 0.782 ablation score as unchanged corrupted-input compliance. Appendix F adds trajectory-complexity arguments and repair limitations; the original simulation and hardware-registration limitations remain.

D1.justification: Previously absent appendices now provide tool signatures, expanded FSM rules, representative hardware schemas, metric weights and thresholds, benchmark composition, and planner, alignment, and baseline prompts. These substantially improve implementation and evaluation documentation. Existing code and project links are retained.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same four extended BioProBench subsets and 22-device environment. Appendix F newly documents dataset composition and sample counts. Oracle-ReAct and thinking-model experiments use retained Subsets C/D; additional domains or task coverage are not established.

E2.justification: Section 4.2.4 adds Oracle-ReAct with forced verification, and Table 17 adds direct DeepSeek-V3.2-Think and Gemini-3-Pro-Think comparisons on Subsets C/D. These substantially strengthen the alternatives tested. Qwen and Kimi gain Table 3 rows but already appeared in v1's Figure 1.

E3.justification: Table 4 replaces Subset D sequence accuracy with correction success, explicitly defined as Cp > 0.8. Added experiments introduce forced-PASS termination for Oracle-ReAct and direct-versus-agent configurations for thinking models. Other newly supplied settings document existing experiments without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether mandatory verification rescues ReAct and whether stronger reasoning models replace or improve the framework. Appendix F.2 adds quantitative error-type breakdowns. Existing component ablations remain, with materially revised Subset D outcomes and explanations.

E5.justification: Both already report paired t-tests and cross-judge Pearson correlations. Tables 11 and 13 supply more detailed outcomes under those practices. No new repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Subset D Cp changes from 0.887 to 0.925. Table 6 changes w/o FSM from 0.000 to 0.782 and w/o Verification from 0.870 to 0.782. Added results include detailed judge/error breakdowns and Table 17's strong direct-model performance and agent-backbone failures. The new 90.0% correction success is a different metric from v1's 0.464 sequence accuracy.

M1.justification: The overall FSM, memory, and hierarchical verification architecture remains. The stated planner projection changes from symbolic keys alone to keys with semantic previews (Equation 2), and Equation 3 replaces the APPROVED-state execution condition with a verified-code condition.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most narrative remain. Localized rewrites expand memory/control explanations and revise error-correction and ablation passages. Grammar, affiliations, acknowledgments, and cross-references change, while the new appendices organize supporting material.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive appendix tables covering specifications, statistical checks, task complexity, error breakdowns, model scaling, and execution logs, plus boxed prompt listings. Table 3 expands and Table 4 changes its correction metric column. Existing figures are largely retained, with some displays relocated or elaborated.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds physics-aware rejection sampling through Hyun et al. New appendix citations include KeyBERT and Gemini 3 Pro. The broader research positioning remains; updates to SciAgents and other existing references principally correct bibliographic information.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces the five-bit signal space with mixed Boolean/ternary signals and revises formal grounding and execution definitions. Appendix E supplies custom score definitions, while Appendix F.1 adds a compounding-error calculation. The conditional safety assumptions remain, without a new safety proof.

improvement.justification: v1 directs readers to absent appendices for essential specifications and validation. v2 supplies much of that material and adds challenging controls that expose important strengths and failures, substantially improving reproducibility and assessability. Important issues remain: Appendix E.3 requires Cp = 1 for success, whereas Table 4 reports 100% success with Cp = 0.950, and Table 17's strong direct-model results qualify the retained necessity claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same BioProAgent study, with matching core sections, experiments, and figures. v1 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v2 supplies Appendices A-I. Newly documented material can be distinguished from retained content.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and reports additional Oracle-ReAct, error-type, and thinking-model evaluations.

before.justification: Sections 4.2-4.6 report original BioProBench simulation results, including benchmark comparisons, error correction, execution traces, and component ablations.

results.title: BioProAgent: Neuro-Symbolic Grounding for Constrained Scientific Planning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark, grounded pre-hoc detector, GSPO contributions, and principal performance claims. 'Expert-guided' becomes 'expert-aligned,' but the underlying account of guideline-based automated annotation remains the same.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds substantive interpretations of healthy-fundus false alarms, difficult MRI forgeries, coarse localization, and possible oversized-box solutions under the unchanged reward. It proposes size-aware regularization as future work. Section 5.2 also softens real-world applicability from a guarantee to a suggestion.

D1.justification: V2 adds per-editor counts and dataset identifiers in Table 10, identifies expert contributors, and advertises a named code/data repository plus model checkpoint instead of the anonymous code/data pointer. The appendix diagnoser becomes Gemini 3 Pro, consistent with the existing Figure 2. Core training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds evaluation on four external medical deepfake distributions: Med-Diffu, Synth-Pneumonia, Synth-Biomarker, and Med-Banana. This substantially extends evaluation beyond MedForge-90K and its internal cross-model and cross-forgery settings; the original modality and pathology coverage remains.

E2.justification: The original comparison lineups remain, and AIGC-Holmes is corrected to AIGI-Holmes, the same cited method. The added comparisons use narrower lineups: human evaluation omits SIDA-13B, while external OOD evaluation includes only FakeVLM, AIGI-Holmes, Qwen3-VL-Plus, and Gemini 3 Pro.

E3.justification: V2 introduces single-blind human ratings by two trained annotators on 100 cases and balances two fake-only external datasets with MIMIC-CXR real images at 1:1. It also revises the reported source-image count from 30,000 to 31,990. The original 50K/10K/30K experimental splits remain stated; rerunning those experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and qualitative example, Appendix B adds human checks on automated judging, external-distribution robustness tests, failure breakdowns by pathology, modality, edit direction and lesion size, and localization diagnostics addressing possible oversized-box reward exploitation.

E5.justification: Table 9 newly reports localization dispersion and distribution summaries, including standard deviation, median, percentile, and threshold-exceedance rates. These describe variation across samples, not uncertainty across training runs. Repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, and significance tests remain unreported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results. New results include a third-ranked human average of 72.7%, external-dataset accuracies of 90.7–99.6%, and detailed failure and localization statistics. Table 5 also shows Gemini 3 Pro exceeding the proposed method on Med-Diffu F1, 90.1 versus 89.8.

M1.justification: The detector architecture, localize-then-analyze output, SFT-to-GSPO training, and coverage, formatting, and classification rewards are retained. Changing the appendix wording from 'IoU coverage' to 'Mask Coverage' aligns it with the existing Equation 7 rather than introducing a new objective.

P1.justification: The retained text receives localized grammar, terminology, affiliation, and naming corrections. Funding and expert acknowledgements are added, and the original Appendices A/B become C/D after new acknowledgements and results sections. The main narrative is largely preserved.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with Tables 4–10 covering human ratings, external evaluations, failure categories, localization distributions, and dataset inventory. The four existing figures and main tables retain their basic designs, with limited caption and layout refinements.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting the external datasets and introductory discussion of medical AI and reasoning, and replaces the Stacchio inpainting citation with Rombach et al. The related-work argument and principal novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The task formulation, optimization equations, coverage definition, and reward formulas are mathematically unchanged. The new localization discussion adds empirical interpretation and limitations, without a new formal result, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central claims: v1 quantified explanation quality only through MLLM judges and evaluated generalization within MedForge-90K, whereas v2 adds human ratings and four external datasets. Failure and localization analyses also clarify important limitations. Reporting weaknesses temper these gains: the 95,276-image inventory is not reconciled with the retained 90,000-image splits, and Table 9 reports 20,000 true-positive forgeries despite 140 reported misses. The broader validation and more candid diagnostics nevertheless provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MedForge research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds human evaluations, external-dataset experiments, failure analyses, and localization statistics in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments, automated reasoning-quality evaluations, and component, optimization, and backbone ablations in Tables 1–3.

results.title: MedForge: Interpretable Medical Deepfake Detection via Forgery-aware Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract softens 'significantly outperforms' to 'consistently outperforms,' aligning the headline claim with the newly reported nonsignificant Claude comparison. The central contributions—motivation-grounded ideation, RL internalization, and complementary rewards—retain their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning cross-venue generalization, the separate contributions of motivation conditioning and RL, preferential selection of technical tokens, and adaptation of reasoning behaviors to problem structure. Appendix I qualifies the Claude comparison as complementary strengths without significant overall superiority. The original standalone limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 newly supplies an input/target example and inference prompt, clarifies paper-level sample accounting and entropy conditioning, and explicitly describes Full-SFT's two-stage inference. The abstract changes code availability from promised to available; this is a reported availability change, not independently verified access. Existing implementation and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from the ICLR holdout to include 67 held-out NeurIPS 2025 papers. This introduces an explicit venue-shift scenario with a different topical distribution, documented in v2 Table 7.
